summary: The paper addresses prediction of when monitored aircraft engines will fail and the difficulty of interpreting their degradation from many sensor signals. key_results: On the FD001 benchmark, the proposed method’s remaining-useful-life prediction had an RMSE of 25.41 using the mean of similar-engine failure times and 25.74 using the median. The mean-based proposed prediction had errors ranging from -57 to 58 and 7 correct predictions, compared with a range of -82 to 65 and 3 correct predictions for mean-based univariate functional principal component analysis. For the alarm assessment, 95 of 100 test engines had an alarm before the true failure point, while 5 alarms came later; the authors also report that 94 alarms occurred in the last 40 percent of total life. For sensor-curve prediction, the reported average multivariate-to-univariate RMSE ratios were below 1 at each tested observation level: 0.868084, 0.844954, 0.740571, and 0.941520 at 35, 50, 80, and 90 percent, respectively.

limitations_unstated: The evaluation uses only one simulated benchmark subset, with one fault mode and one operating condition, so performance on field engines, other failure mechanisms, or changing operating conditions is not established. future_work_stated: The authors propose applying multivariate functional data analysis to other prognostics and health management tasks, including condition monitoring, fault classification, real-time monitoring, and predictive maintenance.
future_work_unstated: Evaluate the method on field data and on datasets with multiple fault mechanisms and operating conditions, while testing whether lifetime registration preserves useful degradation timing. summary: The paper proposes a method to estimate extreme structural responses over long periods when environmental conditions and short-term responses are both variable. future_work_unstated: Future studies could test the method on field measurements and on simulators with changing operating conditions or multiple interacting failure mechanisms, and examine whether its uncertainty estimates remain reliable. summary: The paper addresses the way zero-valued observations can distort threshold selection and estimates of extreme-event tails when standard extreme-value mixture models do not represent those observations. Parameters are estimated by maximum likelihood, and the authors evaluate the method using simulations and two real datasets: weekly earnings for 2,000 observations from the CPS91 dataset and 441 monthly rainfall observations from Modikuppam station. Across the reported comparisons, the proposed model gives better parameter estimates and model fit than methods that omit zero inliers, although accuracy worsens as the proportion of inliers becomes large.
key_results: In simulations with a 20% inlier proportion and a heavy-tailed GPD, at sample size 1,000 the estimated shape parameter averaged 0.1977 when its true value was 0.2; its MSE was 0.0284, compared with 0.046 for the existing extreme value mixture model. In that same setting, threshold MSE was 0.8833 versus 3.4362, and scale MSE was 1.3209 versus 2.8026. For the CPS91 earnings data, the EVIMM had an nAIC of 9.6570, compared with 13.4020 for the standard mixture model and 13.4003 for the flexible mixture model; its Anderson–Darling, Cramér–von Mises, and Kolmogorov–Smirnov test p-values were 0.8340, 0.7918, and 0.7497. For the rainfall data, the EVIMM nAIC was 9.9677, compared with 11.3973 and 11.4083, and the three corresponding test p-values were 0.4716, 0.4190, and 0.4443; the competing models’ reported p-values were below 0.0001.

limitations_stated: The authors report that bias and MSE tend to increase at larger inlier proportions because fewer nonzero observations remain to estimate the bulk and tail parameters. limitations_unstated: The simulation evidence uses data generated from the proposed model, so it does not establish performance when the gamma bulk or GPD tail is misspecified. future_work_stated: The authors propose extending the model to inliers spread over a finite range or occurring at multiple points, testing alternative and multimodal bulk distributions, and developing change-point versions. future_work_unstated: Future studies could assess dependence and seasonal or operating-condition effects, especially for sequential rainfall or reliability observations, and could evaluate the method with censored lifetime and field data. summary: The paper develops inference for lifetimes assumed to follow the three-parameter XLindley distribution, rather than modelling a degradation path. future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to test model fit and prediction on larger, independent bearing-life datasets, including genuinely censored observations. summary: This paper studies when transformations of component reliability preserve comparisons between lifetime distributions. It models the reliability of a coherent system with identically distributed components as a distortion of their common reliability function, with dependence represented through copulas. The authors derive preservation conditions for the total time on test transform, excess wealth, decreasing mean residual life, and quantile mean inactivity time orders. They apply the results to coherent systems with exchangeable components, using theoretical examples based on copulas rather than empirical lifetime data. The main finding is that preservation can hold for broader distortion classes than convex or concave functions, but it does not hold for every distortion.
key_results: The total time on test transform order is preserved by starshaped distortions, and the excess wealth order by strictly increasing antistarshaped distortions. The decreasing mean residual life order is preserved by strictly increasing antistarshaped distortions, while the quantile mean inactivity time order is preserved when the strictly increasing distortion has an antistarshaped dual. The paper gives counterexamples showing that arbitrary distortions need not preserve the latter two orders: with the distortion h(p) = p to the fifth power, the decreasing mean residual life comparison fails for probability levels from 0 to 0.02632, and another example fails the quantile mean inactivity time comparison over times from 1.2539 to 1.3050. System examples demonstrate these conditions for systems with 3, 4, and 5 components, including distortions that are not convex or concave.
key_equations: Starshaped and antistarshaped distortion criterion: \[h(p)/p \text{ is increasing for a starshaped distortion and decreasing for an antistarshaped distortion}\] Here h is the distortion function and p is a probability level; whether their ratio increases or decreases defines the two distortion classes.
limitations_stated: The authors show that the decreasing mean residual life and quantile mean inactivity time orders are not preserved by general distortion functions, and they provide counterexamples. Their preservation theorems require specific distortion shapes and, in some results, strict increase and absolute continuity assumptions.
limitations_unstated: The examples are theoretical constructions rather than tests against field reliability data, so practical performance in operating systems is not assessed. The applications focus on exchangeable components and specified dependence models, which limits direct use for heterogeneous components or systems with nonexchangeable dependence.
future_work_stated: None stated.
future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to test the preservation conditions using field lifetime data and dependence models fitted to real systems. summary: Standard RUL predictors can degrade when machine conditions change and their deployment data differ from their training data. The paper proposes MDAN, which adapts a model trained on labelled source data to unlabelled target data using mixup in the source, an intermediate domain, and the target, together with self-supervised reconstruction and target pseudo-labels. The method is evaluated on the C-MAPSS aircraft-engine benchmark across twelve source-to-target cases and on the MFD bearing dataset across twelve operating-condition cases. MDAN achieves lower root mean square error than the compared methods in all twelve RUL cases and outperforms the leading bearing comparison in eight of twelve cases. The results are benchmark experiments, not evidence of a validated maintenance policy or deployed field system.
key_results: On C-MAPSS, MDAN has the lowest root mean square error in all twelve domain-adaptation cases; its reported values range from 13.34 to 16.12. For example, from FD001 to FD003, its root mean square error is 13.34 versus 39.58 for CADA, and its score is 417 versus 8,415. MDAN does not have the lowest score in every case: for FD002 to FD001, CADA scores 351 and MDAN scores 393. On the MFD dataset, MDAN outperforms SLARDA in eight of twelve cases; for a-to-c, the reported accuracy is 89.57 for MDAN versus 30.54 for SLARDA.
key_equations:
Source-target mixup: \[\tilde{x}=\lambda x_S+(1-\lambda)x_T,\quad \tilde{y}=\lambda y_S+(1-\lambda)\hat{y}_T\] The mixed input x tilde and mixed label y tilde combine source input x sub S and its known label y sub S with target input x sub T and its predicted pseudo-label y hat sub T, using mixup weight lambda.

Source-domain training objective: \[\min_{\phi,\psi} L_S^{or}+\alpha_1L_S^{mx}+\alpha_2L_R\] The model minimizes over predictor parameters phi and feature-extractor parameters psi the original source loss L sub S superscript or, source mixup loss L sub S superscript mx, and reconstruction loss L sub R, weighted by alpha sub 1 and alpha sub 2.

Intermediate-domain objective: \[\min_{\phi,\psi}\alpha_3L_{cd}\] The model minimizes over predictor parameters phi and feature-extractor parameters psi the intermediate-domain mixup loss L sub cd, weighted by alpha sub 3.

Target-domain objective: \[\min_{\phi,\psi}\alpha_4L_T^{or}+\alpha_5L_T^{mx}\] The model minimizes over predictor parameters phi and feature-extractor parameters psi the original pseudo-labelled target loss L sub T superscript or and target mixup loss L sub T superscript mx, weighted by alpha sub 4 and alpha sub 5.
limitations_stated: The authors state that MDAN requires access to source-domain samples, which may be unavailable for privacy reasons; does not address lifelong learning; assumes the source and target have the same label set; and does not explore multiple source domains.
limitations_unstated: Evaluation is limited to the reported benchmark datasets, and the paper does not report validation on operating fleet data or a deployed maintenance setting. For the RUL comparisons, results are averaged over three runs, and most baseline results are taken from an earlier publication rather than recomputed in the authors’ setup, which limits how fully the comparisons establish reproducibility across implementations.
future_work_stated: The authors propose studying source-free time-series domain adaptation, where adaptation uses a pretrained source model without access to source-domain samples.
future_work_unstated: Further work could test MDAN on field-collected RUL data with changing operating conditions and assess how prediction uncertainty and pseudo-label errors affect results. It could also evaluate whether adapted predictions improve maintenance decisions and system-level outcomes, rather than only prediction or classification metrics.

summary: The paper develops and studies a location-parameter-free method for estimating the scale, shape, and location of a three-parameter generalized exponential distribution used to model lifetimes and other skewed data. Ordinary maximum likelihood can fail for this model when the shape parameter is below one because its likelihood may be unbounded. The method estimates scale and shape by maximizing a likelihood based on differences between ordered observations, then estimates location with a bias correction and obtains quantiles by substituting the parameter estimates into the quantile formula. It is evaluated through simulations using standardized model data and through a sample of 40 electrical-component lifetimes. The authors show consistency of the estimators and report that the method can be substantially faster than the location-scale-parameter-free alternative while performing well for parameter and quantile estimation.
key_results: The simulations used 10,000 replications, sample sizes of 20, 50, 100, and 200, and shape values from 0.50 to 3.00. At shape 1.50 and sample size 100, the location-scale-parameter-free method took 33.90 hours for 25,000 iterations, compared with 3.60 minutes for the proposed method; the comparison method's results at sample size 200 were omitted because of a computational precision problem. For shape greater than one, the authors report that the proposed method performs better than the alternatives for scale estimation in bias and root mean square error, and they recommend it for quantile estimation, especially in that shape range. In the electrical-lifetime example, the proposed estimates were shape 1.0821, scale 91.1620, and location -2.7991; its Cramer–von Mises goodness-of-fit p-value was 0.9258, compared with 0.9252 for the location-scale-parameter-free method.
key_equations:
Location-invariant ordered-data statistic: \[V_{(i)}=X_{(i)}-X_{(1)},\quad i=2,\ldots,n\] V_(i) is the difference between the i-th ordered observation X_(i) and the smallest ordered observation X_(1), and n is the number of observations.

GE quantile: \[x_{\zeta}=\gamma-\alpha\ln\left(1-\zeta^{1/\beta}\right)\] x_zeta is the quantile at probability zeta, while alpha, beta, and gamma are the scale, shape, and location parameters.
limitations_stated: The authors say that proving uniqueness analytically is challenging and provide proofs only for particular cases; they also could not prove that the two-parameter likelihood is jointly unimodal. They omit location-scale-parameter-free simulation results at sample size 200 because likelihood calculations exceeded machine precision, and they exclude very small samples because estimates are unstable.
limitations_unstated: The method and its consistency argument assume independent observations from the same distribution, and the paper does not evaluate estimation with censored lifetimes, which commonly occur in reliability studies. The simulation uses standardized parameter settings and the real-data illustration is one sample of 40 components, so performance under varied operating conditions or on independent field datasets remains untested.
future_work_stated: None stated.
future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to extend the estimation procedure to right-censored and interval-censored lifetime data and test it on larger field datasets. Further studies could also incorporate operating-condition covariates and evaluate how component-level estimates support system-level reliability and engineering decisions.

glossary: FORM = First-order reliability method, which approximates a failure boundary by linearizing it near a design point.|S_i = First-order reliability sensitivity index for input i.|V_i = Variance contribution assigned to the main effect of input i.|p = Failure probability of the system being analyzed.|S_i^T = Total-effect reliability sensitivity index for input i, including its interactions with other inputs.|W_i = Variance of the conditional failure probability when all inputs except input i are given.|i = Index identifying an input variable.
summary: Failure probability estimation becomes difficult for engineering systems with several failure modes because the failure region can be complex and failure events are rare. The paper derives FORM-based formulas for first-order and total-effect reliability sensitivity indices for series, parallel, and more general systems. The method uses limit-state models, design points, and multivariate normal probability calculations, avoiding additional evaluations of the engineering model once the FORM results are available. The authors test the formulas using simulated numerical examples, including a frame, a component with two design points, and a beam-bar system. Their results show that the sensitivity estimates generally agree closely with Monte Carlo estimates, while computation of the required probability integrals can be demanding for highly correlated failure modes.
key_results: For the elastoplastic frame, the Monte Carlo failure probability was 5.32 × 10^-4 and the FORM estimate was 5.57 × 10^-4; the total-effect sensitivity estimates were close, including 0.293 versus 0.288 for the first plastic moment and 1.00 versus 1.00 for the load. For the parabolic limit state with two design points, the Monte Carlo and FORM failure probabilities were 3.02 × 10^-3 and 2.82 × 10^-3; the first-order index for the first input was 0.437 and 0.430, respectively. For the beam-bar system with Gaussian inputs, FORM and Monte Carlo sensitivity estimates agreed to the reported precision, including total-effect indices of 0.939 for moment strength, 0.117 for bar strength, and 0.323 for load. With non-Gaussian strength inputs, estimates still showed good agreement, though FORM slightly overestimated the first-order indices and underestimated the total-effect index for moment strength.
key_equations: First-order and total-effect reliability sensitivity indices: \[S_i=\frac{V_i}{p(1-p)},\qquad S_i^{T}=1-\frac{W_i}{p(1-p)}\] S_i is the first-order index, V_i is the main-effect variance contribution for input i, p is the failure probability, S_i^T is the total-effect index, and W_i is the variance of the conditional failure probability given all inputs except input i.
limitations_stated: The direct derivation assumes independent inputs, although the authors note that the formulas can be used for dependent inputs within an existing transformation approach. The required normal probability integrals have dimension twice the number of components and can need many samples when there are many components or strong correlations. In the non-Gaussian beam-bar example, using individual component design points rather than the optimal joint design points gives a suboptimal probability approximation.
limitations_unstated: The evaluation is based on numerical examples and Monte Carlo reference calculations; the paper does not validate the estimates using field observations or operational structural data. Accuracy may be less predictable for systems whose failure boundaries are poorly represented by the chosen design-point linearizations, beyond the cases examined.
future_work_stated: The authors propose developing efficient approximations for the FORM sensitivities, for example using system reliability bounds, to reduce the cost of the normal probability calculations. They also suggest extending decision-theoretic reliability sensitivities to system problems.
future_work_unstated: The method could be tested against field reliability records and across a broader range of operating conditions and uncertain material or load properties. Further work could also examine common-cause failures and model discrepancy, and assess whether the resulting sensitivity rankings lead to effective engineering decisions.

summary: Uncertainty in sensors, structural models, and operating conditions can make a deterministic digital representation unreliable as an indicator of structural safety. The paper introduces Risk Twin, which uses Bayesian updating to estimate uncertain system variables and structural reliability indices, then visualizes component risk and supports risk-informed control. Its online updates use samples and quantities computed in advance, avoiding repeated intensive simulations during operation. The approach is demonstrated using sensor measurements from laboratory plate and beam experiments and a simulated wind turbine. The demonstrations show that the system can update and display risk in real time and that control can improve reliability while balancing power generation and safety.
key_results: For the simply supported plate, reported relative position errors across five test positions ranged from 2.40% to 15.07% of the effective side length, and relative load-magnitude errors ranged from 0.25% to 18.5%. In the cantilever-beam control demonstration, the arm reached a target control location of 0.30 m at an actual location of 0.31 m, an error of 1 centimeter; the demonstration also showed motor reliability influencing whether to continue the control action. In the simulated wind-turbine example, one high-wind snapshot showed reliability indices of 2.2 for the blade, 18 for the hub, and 3.3 for the tower. In another snapshot, optimization increased the blade index from 2.9 to 13.4 and the tower index from 2.6 to 3.2, while the paper reports a trade-off between structural reliability and power generation.
key_equations:
Bayesian update for basic variables: \[p(x\mid y)\propto L(y\mid x)p(x)\] Here p is the probability density, x is a possible value of the basic random variables, y is the observed measurement, and L is the likelihood of that measurement given x.

Reliability index: \[\beta=-\Phi^{-1}(P(R))\] Here beta is the reliability index, Phi inverse is the inverse standard normal cumulative distribution function, P is the probability of the risk event under the updated distribution, and R is the risk event.
limitations_stated: The authors note that the accuracy of the simulation-free update depends on the number of precomputed samples and the accumulation of time steps, and that the available sample size may be insufficient for highly reliable components. They also say the Risk Shadow color map may need further study for scalability and differentiability, and that the simple linear interpolation used for arm control may not minimize total energy cost globally.
limitations_unstated: The wind-turbine demonstration uses a simulated physical system rather than field measurements, so the reported control and risk results do not establish performance under actual turbine conditions. The physical tests are small laboratory demonstrations, and the paper does not report independent validation of risk estimates or uncertainty calibration on a larger structural dataset.
future_work_stated: The authors propose exploring how Risk Twin can be applied and adapted to real-world civil structures and infrastructure.
future_work_unstated: Future studies could validate the reliability estimates against field measurements and observed structural failures, including whether the estimates remain calibrated under changing environments and sensor degradation. They could also represent additional failure mechanisms and system-level dependencies, and evaluate how control decisions should account for operational costs and consequences of failure.

summary: The paper concerns uncertainty in sample percentiles and tolerance intervals, rather than physical degradation or component failures. It derives confidence for percentile locations from the binomial distribution, assuming the observations are independent and identically distributed, and defines an assurance interval by matching its percentile level and confidence level. The authors also describe using Brent’s numerical optimization method to calculate assurance when the population distribution is unknown. Their demonstrations use simulated normal, uniform, and exponential data, including repeated samples of 1,000 observations. They find that interval widths narrow with larger samples and that assurance intervals give a direct way to communicate matched percentile and confidence levels.
key_results: In one simulated normal sample of 1,000 observations, the reported 95% confidence interval ranges were 0.14 for the median and 0.12 for the mean. In 100 repetitions with samples of 1,000 observations, median confidence intervals were wider than mean intervals for the normal and uniform distributions; for the exponential distribution, the intervals were about the same in the example, and the paper notes that the relationship depends on distribution parameters. The paper reports that tolerance intervals expand as the percentile level or confidence level increases, while expansion with increasing confidence is comparatively slight. Its assurance interval sets the percentile level equal to the confidence level and can be computed numerically with Brent’s method.

summary: The paper studies remaining useful life (RUL) prediction for turbofan engines and the need to quantify uncertainty so maintenance decisions can account for prediction risk. It trains Bayesian dense and convolutional neural networks using Stein variational gradient descent (SVGD), which represents the posterior over model weights with a set of particles. The authors compare these models with the same architectures trained using Bayes by Backprop and with non-Bayesian neural networks. Evaluation uses simulated run-to-failure engine trajectories and test trajectories that end before failure from all four subsets of the public C-MAPSS benchmark. The dense network trained with SVGD generally achieves the strongest prediction accuracy, and the authors also use predictive uncertainty to adjust estimates conservatively against late predictions.
key_results: Across the four benchmark subsets, the dense network trained with SVGD achieved RMSE values of 13.17, 18.27, 12.33, and 21.00, respectively, averaged over 10 random seeds. Its corresponding mean absolute error (MAE) values were 9.55, 13.81, 8.53, and 15.51. These dense-network results were generally better than those for the same model trained by Bayes by Backprop or ordinary backpropagation, although on the fourth subset the Bayes by Backprop model had a lower uncorrected asymmetric score: 6,320 versus 6,648. The uncertainty correction reduced the dense SVGD score on the first subset from 334 to 318, and the paper reports that it improved the score across all models.
key_equations:
SVGD particle update: \[w_i^{(l+1)}=w_i^{(l)}+\epsilon^{(l)}\hat{\phi}^{*}(w_i^{(l)})\] The weight vector w for particle i at iteration l is updated by adding the step size epsilon at iteration l multiplied by the estimated SVGD update direction phi at that particle.

Uncertainty-adjusted prediction: \[\mu^{*}=\mu-p_{\mathrm{late}}k\sigma\] The corrected prediction mu star equals the predictive mean mu minus the estimated probability of a late prediction p late multiplied by correction strength k and predictive standard deviation sigma.
limitations_stated: The authors say that the effect of the number of particles and the choice of kernel require further investigation. They also note that evaluating more competitive deep learning architectures was outside the scope of this study.
limitations_unstated: Evaluation is limited to simulated turbofan data, so the results do not establish accuracy or uncertainty calibration on field data or other equipment. The late-prediction probability is estimated on the training set, and the study does not report an independent calibration evaluation; moreover, its test trajectories end before failure, so performance on fully observed field run-to-failure cases is not demonstrated.
future_work_stated: The authors propose studying the number of particles and kernel choice, adding state-of-the-art transformer architectures to the comparison, and exploring neural variational gradient descent, which removes the need for a kernel.
future_work_unstated: Future studies could test calibration and RUL accuracy on field data, including changes in operating conditions and equipment populations. They could also examine additional failure mechanisms and covariates, evaluate system-level consequences of maintenance decisions, and assess the computational cost of the particle method at larger model and dataset scales.

summary: This paper develops a hierarchical maintenance policy for modular systems whose units can degrade through wear or fail because of environmental shocks. The system is represented with Markovian models and phase-type lifetime distributions, with states organized at the unit, module, and system levels. At periodic inspections, the system is left alone if optimal, its modules and failed units are maintained if critical, and the whole system is replaced if failed. The policy and its costs are illustrated using a simulated submarine electrical control unit with four modules, using component transition rates from a published study and cost values selected by the authors. The authors find that higher assumed downtime cost favors shorter inspection intervals and increases total maintenance cost.
key_results: For the four downtime-cost scenarios, the optimized inspection intervals were 8,300, 4,390, 2,200, and 980 hours, while the corresponding total costs were 17.4791, 24.4786, 42.0189, and 87.0051 monetary units. The respective inspection counts were 6, 11, 23, and 51. These results compare scenarios within the proposed model; the paper does not report a benchmark comparison with another maintenance method. For the system without maintenance, the reported mean lifetime is 24,000 hours and reliability at that time is 0.438.

Total expected maintenance cost: \[\mathrm{EC}_{\mathrm{sys}}(\tau)=\sum_{a=1}^{A}\mathrm{EC}_{\mathrm{sys}}(a,\tau)\] EC_sys of tau is total expected maintenance cost over the inspection intervals, a is the interval index, A is the maximum number of inspections, and EC_sys of a and tau is expected cost in one interval.

future_work_stated: The authors propose incorporating dependence between modules, distinguishing failure modes and their associated maintenance actions, and using empirical data to demonstrate the method.
future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to evaluate the policy on field records that include failures, repairs, and downtime costs, and to quantify uncertainty in the optimized intervals. summary: Noise in a limit-state model can make standard reliability calculations estimate a larger failure probability than the probability for the underlying noise-free system. The paper models the observed response as the noise-free response plus zero-mean noise and seeks the failure probability of the noise-free model. It uses Gaussian process regression to denoise model outputs, with active learning and a noise-aware learning function to choose additional evaluations. The method is tested on the R–S example, two benchmark functions, and a finite element model of a structural frame, using simulated data with added noise. It recovers the reference probabilities in the benchmark examples, while the structural-frame estimate is closer to the noise-free reference than the probability calculated directly from noisy outputs but remains higher than the reference.
key_results: For the R–S example, the reference failure probability is 1.35 × 10⁻³; the authors report that 100 design points suffice without noise, while larger noise levels require about 1,000 to 10,000 points for fairly accurate recovery. For the four-branch and hat benchmarks, the active-learning estimates converge to the reference probabilities of 4.51 × 10⁻³ and 9.76 × 10⁻⁴, respectively, and their convergence plots show estimates near the reference at about 200 design points. For the structural frame with 10 mm of added noise, the reference probability is 5.07 × 10⁻³, the direct noisy-model probability is 1.70 × 10⁻², and the median denoised estimate with one-point enrichment is 7.26 × 10⁻³. The structural-frame estimates improve with multi-point enrichment in the reported comparisons, although they remain above the noise-free reference.
key_equations:
Noisy limit-state model: \[\tilde{g}(x,\omega)=g(x)+\varepsilon(x,\omega)\] The noisy response g̃ at input x and noise outcome ω equals the underlying response g at x plus the noise ε at x and ω.

Noise-free failure probability: \[P_f=P(g(X)\leq 0)\] The noise-free failure probability P_f is the probability P that the underlying function g is non-positive for the random input vector X.

Active-learning point selection: \[x_{\mathrm{next}}=\arg\max_{x\in X_c}U_N(x)\] The next evaluation point x_next is the candidate x in the candidate set X_c that maximizes the noise-aware learning function U_N.
limitations_stated: The study focuses on homoskedastic Gaussian noise, and the effectiveness of Gaussian process regression with heteroskedastic, non-Gaussian noise remains unstudied. The authors also state that a suitable stopping criterion is still under investigation. In the structural-frame example, the one-point enrichment results remain above the noise-free reference, and the authors could not determine the exact cause of the learning function’s exploitative behavior.
limitations_unstated: The evaluation uses benchmarks and an artificially noise-corrupted finite element model, not field measurements from an operating structure, so performance with real measurement errors is not established. The structural-frame model omits geometric and material nonlinearities, and the paper does not report a measured computational-cost comparison that would establish savings across practical model sizes.
future_work_stated: The authors are exploring alternative noise-aware learning functions and enrichment strategies to address potentially exploitative behavior. They also identify the study of Gaussian process regression with heteroskedastic, non-Gaussian noise and development of a suitable stopping criterion as work still to be done.
future_work_unstated: Validate the method using repeated field measurements and independently characterized sensor errors, including noise that varies with operating conditions. Further work could also extend the reliability calculation to system-level failure events and assess how denoised probability estimates change engineering decisions.

computation_method: Monte Carlo simulation|MCMC or variational inference|Numerical optimization
glossary: HNN MC = Hamiltonian neural network Monte Carlo, the paper’s sampling method.|P(F) = Probability of the system failure event F.|F_i = The failure region used at subset level i.|n and i = The total number of subset levels and the index of a level, respectively.|g = The limit state function, whose nonpositive values indicate failure.|x = The vector of uncertain system parameters.|u_lim = The displacement threshold used to define failure.|u(x,t) = System displacement for parameters x at time t.|t = Time.
summary: Estimating very small structural failure probabilities is difficult when the uncertain-variable distribution is strongly correlated, high-dimensional, or concentrated in a narrow region, because conventional sampling may explore it poorly or require many costly model evaluations. This paper develops Hamiltonian neural network Monte Carlo (HNN MC), which uses a trained neural network to approximate gradients used by Hamiltonian Monte Carlo sampling within Subset Simulation. The method is tested on simulated Gaussian and Rosenbrock distributions, structural dynamics examples, and a system whose parameters are inferred from artificially generated noisy response data. The authors find that the approach estimates failure probabilities accurately in many examples while reducing sampling time, especially when model evaluations are needed to calculate gradients. Its accuracy can degrade in rare-event regions of especially difficult distributions, where the authors test error monitoring and network updates as remedies.
key_results: For the Bayesian parameter-inference reliability example, HNN MC estimated a mean reliability index of 4.35 with a coefficient of variation of 0.048; traditional Hamiltonian Monte Carlo gave 4.44 and 0.039. The corresponding computation time per Subset Simulation was 4,509 seconds for HNN MC versus 579,549 seconds for traditional Hamiltonian Monte Carlo, an improvement of more than 100 times. Across other examples, the paper reports at least 20 times faster sampling, including average times of 735 seconds versus 15,872 seconds for the Rosenbrock example. For the difficult Rosenbrock case with k equal to 100, standard HNN MC substantially overestimated the reference reliability index, but increasing to 10,000 samples per subset produced a mean of 2.781, compared with the reference value of 2.715.
key_equations:
Subset failure-probability decomposition: \[P(F)=P(F_1)\prod_{i=1}^{n-1}P(F_{i+1}\mid F_i)\] P(F) is the overall failure probability, F_i is the nested failure region at level i, n is the number of levels, and i indexes those levels.

Displacement limit state: \[g(x)=u_{\mathrm{lim}}-\max_{t\in[0,40]}|u(x,t)|\] g is the limit state, x is the uncertain parameter vector, u_lim is the displacement threshold, t is time in the interval from 0 to 40 seconds, and u(x,t) is the system displacement at that time.
limitations_stated: The authors state that HNN MC can lose accuracy for strongly correlated, high-dimensional problems and for thin Rosenbrock distributions, particularly in rare-event regions where steep gradients are difficult to learn. Online error monitoring and retraining can improve results, but monitoring reduces the computational savings; even with the tested remedies, the most difficult case did not match the accuracy of traditional Hamiltonian Monte Carlo in all configurations.
limitations_unstated: The structural response data used for parameter inference are artificially generated, and the paper does not validate the reliability estimates using measurements from an operating structure or field failures. Since the network is trained from sampled Hamiltonian trajectories, its predictions in rare-event regions not represented adequately in training may be unreliable, so performance on a new system or operating regime is not established.
future_work_stated: None stated
future_work_unstated: Evaluate the method with field measurements and observed failures, including uncertainty in both the physical model and the neural-network gradient predictions. Further work could also test additional failure mechanisms, varying operating and load conditions, and system-level failure events, then connect the probability estimates to engineering decisions such as inspection or design choices.

summary: Transmission-line failure risk is represented as the probability that a line’s energy exceeds its rating; estimating that risk directly from a high-dimensional power-system model can require many simulations. The authors derive a reduced-order probability density function (PDF) equation for a quantity of interest (QoI), such as one line’s energy or the joint energies of two lines. They estimate the equation’s coefficients by regression on simulated trajectories of a power-system model with correlated Ornstein–Uhlenbeck (OU) noise, then solve the resulting partial differential equation (PDE) numerically. Tests use simulated data from three benchmark power grids with 9, 30, and 57 buses, including scenarios with a line removed. The method uses fewer samples than kernel density estimation (KDE) for comparable density estimates and shows that assuming line failures are independent can give inaccurate joint-risk estimates.
key_results: For marginal line-energy densities, the authors report good agreement with a KDE benchmark built from 10,000 Monte Carlo samples, while the reduced-order estimates use 5,000 samples. For joint exceedance probabilities, the reported predictions include 0.658 or 0.659 versus an empirical 0.458, each in units of 10 to the minus 3 for the 9-bus case; 5.580 or 2.110 versus 2.112, each in units of 10 to the minus 2 for the 30-bus case; and 2.056 or 0.918 versus 1.029, each in units of 10 to the minus 2 for the 57-bus case. The paper reports that about 2 to the 10th samples with the reduced-order method achieved accuracy that required about 2 to the 14th samples with direct Monte Carlo simulation in the sample-scaling experiment. At a 1 percent error requirement, estimated sample use scaled with the number of lines to powers of 0.89 for the proposed method and 1.07 for Gaussian KDE. The independence-based joint estimates deviated notably from the empirical results, especially in the 30- and 57-bus cases.
key_equations: Reduced density equation: \[\frac{\partial f(U,t)}{\partial t}+\frac{\partial [c(U,t)f(U,t)]}{\partial U}=\frac{\partial^2[d(U,t)f(U,t)]}{\partial U^2}\] Here f is the density of the quantity of interest, U is a value of that quantity, t is time, c is its conditional drift coefficient, d is its conditional diffusion coefficient, and the derivative symbols denote partial differentiation.
limitations_stated: The authors identify estimation and time interpolation of the reduced equation’s coefficients as the main source of error. They also state that regression-method choice depends on the system dynamics and requires manual tuning, and that systematic study of regression methods remains open.
limitations_unstated: Evaluation is based on simulated trajectories and comparisons with estimates derived from the same modeled dynamics, not field measurements, so calibration to real grid behavior is untested. The experiments use a specified correlated noise model and a limited set of line-removal scenarios; the paper does not report uncertainty intervals for the rare-event probability estimates.
future_work_stated: The authors propose applying the framework to predict cascading failures in more complex energy-based power-system models that include line-tripping dynamics. They also note that the joint density formulation can be extended to three or more lines.
future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be validation with operational grid data and tests across changing loads, weather-related conditions, and noise-correlation structures. Further work could incorporate additional failure mechanisms and protection-system effects, quantify uncertainty in estimated tail probabilities, and connect those estimates to mitigation or maintenance decisions.

summary: Reliability estimates based only on system age and age at the previous test omit characteristics that may distinguish individual weapon systems. This paper models interval-censored failures with a Weibull failure intensity whose covariate effect can be linear or represented by a neural network, and compares Bayesian methods including a Laplace approximation. The evaluation uses simulated Banana and Moon datasets, heart-failure patient data, and two Navy weapon-system datasets. On simulated datasets with nonlinear failure patterns, the neural-network Laplace method generally gives the strongest predictive results. On the heart-failure and weapon-system datasets, the authors find little evidence that neural networks improve on linear models.
key_results: For the four synthetic datasets, the Laplace neural-network model reports the highest receiver operating characteristic area under the curve: 0.597 for Banana, 0.674 for Moon, 0.778 for Banana 2, and 0.804 for Moon 2. Its precision-recall area under the curve is also highest on those datasets, at 0.742, 0.812, 0.765, and 0.829, respectively. For heart failure, the best receiver operating characteristic area under the curve is 0.195 for the discrete spike-and-slab Markov chain Monte Carlo model, while the best precision-recall area under the curve is 0.712, shared by the Bayesian neural network and Laplace neural-network models. On the weapon-system datasets, the neural-network model improves both metrics relative to the baseline, but the reported increases are modest: 22.08% and 8.07% for System 1, and 18.12% and 10.72% for System 2, for receiver operating characteristic and precision-recall area under the curve, respectively.
key_equations:
Weibull covariate-dependent failure intensity: \[h(t,x)=q(x)(\lambda t)^{k-1}k\lambda\] The failure intensity h at time t and covariates x is the covariate multiplier q of x times a Weibull time component with rate lambda and shape k.

Likelihood contribution for an interval observation: \[L=p^y(1-p)^{1-y}\] The likelihood contribution L uses the modeled interval failure probability p and the observed label y, which is one for failure and zero for a pass.
limitations_stated: The authors could not calculate Kaplan-Meier survival functions for the two weapon-system datasets because of missing measurement recordings and unreliable unique system identifiers. They also state that details of the weapon systems cannot be disclosed because of data sensitivity.
limitations_unstated: The weapon-system model assumes no more than one failure between tests and treats covariates as constant within each observed interval; these assumptions may not represent all operational histories. Repeated intervals belong to the same items, but the model does not describe an explicit item-level random effect, and weapon-system results are reported only as percentage changes, limiting independent assessment of their magnitude.
future_work_stated: The authors expect larger, feature-rich weapon-system datasets planned for collection to be more likely to benefit from their artificial intelligence and machine-learning approach.
future_work_unstated: Further work could test sensitivity to multiple failures per interval and include item-level effects or other dependence structures for repeated observations. The methods should also be assessed on more complete operational records and across operating conditions, with absolute performance measures and a decision-focused evaluation of maintenance actions.

summary: This paper compares ways to estimate extreme wind-turbine blade loads for structural safety assessment. It models long-term wind speed and turbulence together with the random short-term response, and compares environmental contours with a sequential method that uses Gaussian process regression to guide response simulations. The analyses use simulated responses from a surrogate for a reference wind turbine, with one case based on an assumed wind model and another based on a South Brittany wind model fitted using 32 years of hindcast data from 1979 to 2010. At Site A, the contour and sequential estimates agree reasonably well when the 90% short-term response quantile is used, and the sequential estimates approach the brute-force results in about 10 to 20 iterations. At South Brittany, contour estimates are substantially lower than sequential estimates, consistent with extreme responses arising in frequently occurring conditions rather than only at the most severe environmental conditions.
key_results: For Site A, the 50-year response estimate using the 90% short-term quantile was 25.85 meganewton-metres with direct-sampling contours and 25.17 meganewton-metres with IFORM contours. These estimates compare reasonably with brute-force 50-year results of 24.649 meganewton-metres from 1,000 simulated years and 25.093 meganewton-metres from 10,000 simulated years. Sequential estimates generally converged toward the brute-force results within 10 to 20 iterations; using the median short-term response underestimated the 50-year response, while using the 99% quantile overestimated it. For South Brittany, the 90% contour estimate was 16.54 meganewton-metres for the 50-year response, and the authors report that it was substantially below the sequential estimate; brute-force comparison was not feasible.
key_equations:
Long-term response distribution: \[g_Y(y)=\int g_{Y\mid X}(y\mid x)f_X(x)\,dx\] The long-term response density gY is obtained by integrating the short-term response density given environmental conditions, gY given X, against the environmental-condition density fX over conditions x.

Sequential sampling acquisition rule: \[x_{\mathrm{new}}=\arg\max_x s(x)|\sigma_{\theta}(x)|\] The next environmental condition x_new maximizes the product of s, the estimated density of responses exceeding the 100-year return value, and sigma_theta, the uncertainty in the fitted response-distribution parameters.
limitations_stated: The authors state that the two-variable analysis omits wave effects, a simplification they consider particularly questionable for the floating South Brittany case. They also state that brute-force results were infeasible for South Brittany, so the true response there is unknown and firm recommendations cannot be made with high confidence.
limitations_unstated: The assessment uses a surrogate trained on a reference turbine and does not translate the environmental wind speeds to the surrogate turbine's hub height, limiting the direct applicability of the reported load magnitudes to actual offshore turbines. The sequential model also uses separate Gaussian-process outputs for the response-distribution parameters, which may not represent dependence between those parameter estimates; the paper does not test how this modeling choice affects rare-event estimates.
future_work_stated: The authors recommend further case studies to validate the sequential sampling method for other structural problems and to test higher-dimensional environmental inputs. They also recommend investigating how the number of response simulation seeds affects results in design applications.
future_work_unstated: Further work could validate the estimates against field or operational load data and against detailed simulations of floating turbines that include waves and platform motion. It could also test alternative response-tail models and parameter-dependence assumptions, and examine how the resulting uncertainty affects design decisions.

scope_reason: The paper develops methods to estimate seismic failure probabilities and fragility of engineered lifeline networks, directly addressing system reliability.

glossary: LSF = Limit-state function, a function used to distinguish network failure from survival.|SS = Subset simulation, a method that estimates rare failure probabilities through nested intermediate events.|HMC-SS = Hamiltonian Monte Carlo-based subset simulation.|RP = Most reliable path between an origin and a destination.|G^RP = The limit-state function based on the most reliable path.|z_i = The logarithmic safety margin of component i.|n_RP = The number of nodes on the most reliable path.|i = An index identifying a component or node.
summary: Binary network failure measures give subset simulation little information about how close a surviving sample is to failure, which makes rare seismic network failures costly to estimate. The paper proposes two continuous or piecewise continuous limit-state functions, based on the most reliable path and the shortest path, to guide sampling toward network failure. It also links intermediate failure events to earthquake magnitude so one specialized simulation can estimate a network fragility curve across multiple magnitudes. The method is tested using simulated ground motions and bridge-network models for a two-component system and highway networks in San Jose and San Diego. The most reliable path version generally estimates failure probabilities more accurately, while the shortest path version requires less computation time; the single-run approach can also substantially reduce the evaluations needed for a fragility curve.
key_results: For the two-component parallel system at moment magnitude 3.0, the most reliable path version estimated failure probability as 3.46 × 10⁻⁴, close to the numerical integration value of 3.40 × 10⁻⁴; its reported estimate at magnitude 4.0 was 1.00 × 10⁻³ versus an exact value of 0.98 × 10⁻³. A single specialized run estimated that system’s fragility curve with 12,700 limit-state evaluations, or 37.47% of the evaluations required by separate runs at each magnitude. In the San Jose network, dividing the magnitude range into intervals produced results consistent with crude Monte Carlo simulation and required 9.32% more samples than a single run, while avoiding the single run’s underestimation at lower magnitudes. Across the examples, the most reliable path approach generally had better estimation accuracy, whereas the shortest path approach reduced computation time compared with the other tested methods.
key_equations: Most reliable path limit-state function: \[G^{RP}(\mathbf z)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{\min_{i\in RP}z_i}{n_{RP}},&\text{if connected},\\0,&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}\] G with the RP superscript is the most reliable path limit-state function, z_i is the safety margin of component i, RP is the set of nodes on the most reliable path, n_RP is the number of nodes on that path, and i indexes its nodes.
limitations_stated: The most reliable path function is piecewise rather than globally continuous, so path changes can cause discontinuities and may lead to inefficient sampling or inaccurate estimates. The shortest path function has greater estimate variance, and a single specialized simulation can accumulate bias for complex network reliability problems; the authors demonstrate that dividing the magnitude range into intervals can reduce that bias.
limitations_unstated: The numerical tests use simulated models and fixed network layouts, so the reported performance is not validated against observed earthquake damage or field network outcomes. The analysis also relies on simplified assumptions, including peak ground acceleration as the intensity measure, lognormal component capacities, and a fixed epicenter for the magnitude-based fragility construction; performance under other ground-motion measures and varying event locations is not established.
future_work_stated: The authors propose developing limit-state functions tailored to different network reliability indices and alternative functions suitable for other sampling methods. They also identify more realistic network flow-capacity analysis, including multi-state or continuous component models, and component sensitivity or importance measures as future work.
future_work_unstated: Further work could test the proposed sampling methods against field damage and restoration records and quantify uncertainty in network topology, component fragilities, and earthquake location. It could also incorporate operational demand, component dependencies, and network-wide service consequences into reliability estimates and decision-making.

summary: Repeated train loading deforms railway track, and maintenance through tamping only partly restores its geometry. The paper models this non-monotonic degradation with a multivariate Wiener process that represents correlations among several track geometry indicators and uncertain post-tamping conditions. The authors fit the model with hierarchical Bayesian estimation to inspection data from an 18-kilometre Queensland commuter track divided into 182 segments, using track recording vehicle measurements and identifying 73 tamping events. They test predictions against the last three inspections and compare the multivariate approach with separate single-indicator models. The multivariate model better covers test measurements and supports a condition-based inspection plan that saves some inspections while maintaining comparable simulated maintenance and failure outcomes.
key_results: For the multivariate model, 88.9% of test measurements were within the predictive credible zone and 5.3% were above it; the corresponding single-indicator model figures were 63.8% and 8%. The log-transformed version had 82.9% of test measurements in its credible zone, with 5.3% above it. Estimated correlations were about 0.8 between the two longitudinal indicators and about 0.6 between the two alignment indicators; longitudinal indicators triggered maintenance first in more than 80% of simulated cases. In 2,000 simulation repetitions, the condition-based policy saved approximately 2 to 3 track recording vehicle runs over 10 years, with the same number of simulated tampings and failures as the three-month inspection plan.
key_equations:
Multivariate degradation process: \[\mathbf{Z}_i(t)=\boldsymbol{\mu}_i t+\mathbf{L}_i\mathbf{B}(t),\quad \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_i=\mathbf{L}_i\mathbf{L}_i^{\mathsf{T}}\] Z_i(t) is the vector of geometry indicators for segment i at time t, mu_i is its drift vector, L_i is the covariance factor, B(t) is a vector of independent Brownian motions, and Sigma_i is the covariance matrix.

Inspection-to-inspection change: \[\Delta\mathbf{z}_{i,k}\sim\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu}_i\Delta t_{i,k},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_i\Delta t_{i,k})\] Delta z_i,k is the change in the indicator vector during inspection interval k for segment i, Delta t_i,k is the time elapsed in that interval, mu_i is the drift vector, Sigma_i is the covariance matrix, and N denotes a multivariate normal distribution.

Upper-bound failure probability: \[p_{\lim,i}=1-F_{i,3}(\mathbf{z}_{D1}-\mathbf{z}_{M3})\] p_lim,i is the upper-bound failure probability for segment i, F_i,3 is the cumulative distribution function for its three-month degradation change, and z_D1 and z_M3 are vectors of the D1 and M3 indicator thresholds.
limitations_stated: The model currently covers longitudinal level and alignment, but not other geometry indicators such as gauge, cant, and twist. It also excludes external influences such as speed, tonnage, soil conditions, and weather, for which the authors say additional data are needed.
limitations_unstated: The case study uses one 18-kilometre track, so the reported predictive performance and inspection savings may not transfer to other routes or operating environments. Tamping events are inferred from simultaneous drops in indicators and assigned to interval midpoints, so missed or incorrectly classified events may affect fitted maintenance effects and predictions.
future_work_stated: The authors propose adding environmental and operational factors to the degradation model. They also propose developing optimization models for inspection scheduling, routing, and tamping planning.
future_work_unstated: Validate the model prospectively and on multiple railway networks, including routes with different traffic, climate, and track structures. Assess sensitivity to tamping-event misclassification and compare the policy with cost- and risk-based decision methods once reliable operational cost and consequence data are available.

summary: Conventional likelihood-based and Bayesian estimates can be misleading when the observed test data depart slightly from the assumed model. The authors model nondestructive one-shot device lifetimes under accelerated testing with two independent competing causes and a two-parameter Lindley distribution. They replace the ordinary likelihood contribution with a density power divergence objective to form a robust posterior, estimate it using Hamiltonian Monte Carlo, and develop robust hypothesis tests and influence-function analyses. They evaluate the methods using simulated data and a cancer registry dataset containing 235 pancreatic cancer patients. Their main finding is that the robust estimators generally have lower bias under contamination than their conventional counterparts.
key_results: The simulations used 75 devices and 1,000 generated datasets; under contamination, the weighted robust Bayes estimator had the smallest bias among the estimation methods considered. In the real-data bootstrap results, the root mean square error for the first model parameter was 0.000533 for the weighted minimum density power divergence estimator at gamma 0.8, compared with 0.012516 for the maximum-likelihood estimate; for the robust Bayes estimate with a normal prior at gamma 0.6, it was 0.000401. The cancer-data goodness-of-fit test gave a statistic of 0.388285 and an approximate p-value of 0.528. For the tested parameter value, the reported empirical Bayes factors ranged from 23.51231 to 45.82246, which the authors interpret as strong support for the null hypothesis.
key_equations: Robust posterior: \[\pi_{\gamma}(\Lambda\mid x)=\frac{\exp\{B_{\gamma}(\Lambda)\}\pi(\Lambda)}{\int \exp\{B_{\gamma}(\Lambda)\}\pi(\Lambda)\,d\Lambda}\] Here, gamma is the robustness tuning parameter, Lambda is the vector of model parameters, x is the observed data, B is the divergence-based objective, and pi is the prior density.
limitations_stated: None stated.
limitations_unstated: The method assumes independent competing causes, but the paper does not validate that assumption with the cancer registry data. The cancer analysis groups patients by tumor size and treats that grouping as an accelerated stress level; it does not establish that this interpretation transfers to device testing or to other patient populations. Contamination performance is evaluated in simulation and by bootstrap analysis, but there is no validation on independent operational device data.
future_work_stated: The authors propose extending the model to step-stress testing and other lifetime distributions. They also propose studying dependent competing risks and missing causes of failure.
future_work_unstated: Further work could evaluate whether the cancer-data results replicate in other cohorts and assess additional patient covariates, such as treatment or comorbidities. For engineering use, the methods could also be connected to inspection or replacement decisions and tested on operational device data under realistic stress histories.

summary: The paper develops a way to measure how dependent uncertain inputs influence a system’s probability of failure, separating effects through the engineering model from effects through input dependence. It uses one set of failure samples from a rare-event estimation run, transforms those samples into independent standard-normal spaces using hierarchical Rosenblatt transformations, and estimates conditional densities with kernel density estimation. The method is tested on a nonlinear function, a short column, and a finite-element model of an offshore wind-turbine monopile foundation, all using simulated model evaluations. summary: The paper addresses a failure of standard improved cross entropy (iCE) sampling for network reliability problems with discrete component states: a category absent from an intermediate sample can receive zero probability in later samples. future_work_unstated: Future work could test BiCE against field data and assess how uncertainty in component probabilities and operating conditions affects failure estimates. summary: Stochastic outage simulations used to assess distribution-grid resilience can take up to 24 hours for a 54-bus system. summary: One-shot devices are tested only once, so the data record whether each device has failed by an inspection time rather than its exact failure time. Simulations show that the robust estimates and tests are less affected by contamination than likelihood-based methods, though they can be less efficient when the model is uncontaminated. The examples use electro-explosive devices and devices tested under temperature and electric-current stresses.
key_results: The simulation study used 1,000 runs and compared tuning-parameter values of 0, 0.2, 0.4, and 0.6; the authors report that positive values generally improve performance under contamination, while the likelihood estimator performs best on clean data. For reliability at the moderate-reliability setting with 80 devices per group, the 90% asymptotic interval had coverage 0.817 on clean data and 0.497 on contaminated data; the logit-transformed interval had coverage 0.901 and 0.996, respectively, at tuning parameter 0. For contaminated data, Wald-type tests with positive tuning parameters had more stable behavior than the classical Wald test, while the classical test had greater power on clean data. The authors also report that the logit and arsech reliability intervals generally outperformed the untransformed asymptotic interval in their simulations.

Weighted minimum DPD estimator: \[\hat\theta_\beta=\arg\min_{\theta\in\Theta}\sum_{i=1}^{I}\frac{K_i}{K}\sum_{r=1}^{2}\left[\pi_{ir}^{\beta+1}-\frac{\beta+1}{\beta}\hat p_{ir}\pi_{ir}^{\beta}\right]\] The estimated parameter vector theta at positive tuning parameter beta minimizes the weighted discrepancy across I conditions and two outcomes; K_i is the group size, K is the total size, pi_ir is the model probability, and p_hat_ir is the observed proportion.

Asymptotic covariance of the estimator: \[\Sigma_\beta(\theta)=J_\beta(\theta)^{-1}K_\beta(\theta)J_\beta(\theta)^{-1}\] Sigma_beta is the asymptotic covariance matrix for the estimator at parameter vector theta, and J_beta and K_beta are the sensitivity and variability matrices defined for the weighted divergence estimator.

Reliability under the lognormal model: \[R(t;x_i,\theta)=1-\Phi\!\left(\frac{\ln(t)-\mu_i}{\sigma_i}\right)\] R is the probability of surviving beyond time t at stress condition i, Phi is the standard normal cumulative distribution function, x_i denotes that condition's stress values, theta is the parameter vector, and mu_i and sigma_i are its lognormal parameters.
limitations_stated: The authors state that their study considers only a binary outcome: failure or success at inspection. They also note an unavoidable loss of efficiency for the robust methods compared with likelihood-based inference when the model is correctly specified.
limitations_unstated: The method assumes independent observations and a specified lognormal lifetime model, while the real-data illustrations are two existing designed-test datasets rather than field-life validation. future_work_stated: The authors propose extending the analysis to competing risks, where devices can fail from multiple possible causes.
future_work_unstated: Future studies could validate the stress relationships and robust estimates with field data and include operating covariates that vary over time or across units. summary: The paper develops a method for comparing the reliability of products from multiple production lines when testing is stopped after a set number of failures and some surviving units are removed during the test. key_results: For the real jute-fiber example, maximum likelihood estimates of the reliability parameter were 0.017 for the 10 mm gauge-length data and 0.134 for the 20 mm data; the authors' comparison therefore implies higher reliability for the first set under their transformation. The Weibull-Gamma fit checks gave Kolmogorov-Smirnov distances of 0.105828 and 0.149029, with reported p-values of 0.855287 and 0.473037, respectively. In the simulated example, the approximate expected failure counts were 8.13025 and 1.86975 for the two lines, compared with observed counts of 7 and 3; for the real-data example, the corresponding approximations were 3.83187 and 16.1681, compared with observed counts of 8 and 12. The real-data maximum likelihood and Bayesian point estimates were close; for example, the two Bayesian reliability-parameter estimates were 0.017 and 0.1302.

Weibull-Gamma reliability function: \[R_h(t)=\left[1+\left(\frac{t}{\alpha_h}\right)^{\theta_h}\right]^{-\beta_h}\] R_h(t) is the probability of survival beyond time t for production line h; alpha_h is its scale parameter, theta_h its shape parameter, and beta_h its reliability parameter.

Joint progressive censoring likelihood: \[L\propto\prod_{i=1}^{r}\prod_{h=1}^{k} f_h(\zeta_i)^{\delta_i(h)}\,\bar F_h(\zeta_i)^{s_i(h)}\] L is the likelihood, i indexes the r observed failures, h indexes the k production lines, f_h is line h's density, zeta_i is failure time i, delta_i(h) indicates whether that failure came from line h, Fbar_h is its survival function, and s_i(h) is the number of units withdrawn from line h at that failure time.
limitations_stated: The authors note that the model is parametric and recommend its use with real data that fit the Weibull-Gamma distribution well, assessed using the p-value and Kolmogorov-Smirnov distance. They also state that the model gives more reliable results when the selected sample size is relatively large.
limitations_unstated: The real-data illustration uses jute-fiber breaking strengths at only two gauge lengths, rather than field lifetimes of manufactured products, so its relevance to other products and operating conditions is not established. future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be validation using field failure data across products, production sites, and operating conditions, with checks for dependence between units and for competing failure mechanisms. summary: Estimating failure in hybrid industrial systems is difficult because failures are rare and simulating each trajectory can require costly physical calculations. The paper models such systems as piecewise deterministic Markov processes and develops adaptive importance sampling guided by approximations to the probability of eventual failure. It proposes three importance-function families based on component failures, minimal path sets, and minimal cut sets, and adapts their parameters with cross-entropy optimization while recycling simulated trajectories. The method is evaluated on simulated series and parallel systems and on a simplified spent fuel pool model based on a nuclear-industry system. The minimal-path-set version performs best in the reported spent fuel pool experiments, including for an estimated failure probability on the order of 10 to the minus 7 using fewer than 10,000 trajectories.
key_results: For the standard spent fuel pool case, the minimal-path-set method estimated a failure probability of 1.99 × 10 to the minus 5 using 10,000 trajectories, with an estimated standard deviation of 2.01 × 10 to the minus 5. The crude Monte Carlo estimate using 10,000,000 trajectories was 1.77 × 10 to the minus 5, with an estimated standard deviation of 4.21 × 10 to the minus 3; the authors report variance reduction exceeding a factor of 10,000 for the best method on their examples. In the extreme spent fuel pool case, the minimal-path-set method estimated 3.83 × 10 to the minus 7 using 10,000 trajectories, with a 95% confidence interval from 3.58 × 10 to the minus 7 to 4.08 × 10 to the minus 7. In the series and parallel examples, adaptive importance sampling generally produced confidence intervals comparable in length to crude Monte Carlo intervals based on 10,000 times as many trajectories.

Minimal-path-set importance function: \[U_{\theta}^{(\mathrm{MPS})}(z)=\exp\left[\left(\sum_{i=1}^{d_{\mathrm{MPS}}}\theta_i\,\mathbf{1}_{\{\beta^{(\mathrm{MPS})}(z)\ge i\}}\right)^2\right]\] The minimal-path-set importance function U at state z is the exponential of the squared sum of parameter theta i times an indicator that the number beta of damaged minimal path sets is at least i, with d MPS denoting the total number of minimal path sets.

Recycled importance sampling estimate: \[\widehat P_{N_L}=\frac{1}{N_L}\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\sum_{k=1}^{n_\ell}\mathbf{1}_{\{Z_k^{(\ell)}\in D\}}\frac{\pi_0(Z_k^{(\ell)})}{q_{\theta^{(\ell)}}(Z_k^{(\ell)})}\] The estimated failure probability is the weighted average over all trajectories, where L is the number of iterations, n ell is the number simulated at iteration ell, Z k ell is a trajectory, D is the failure set, pi zero is its original density, q theta ell is the sampling density used, and N L is the total number of trajectories.
limitations_stated: The authors note that listing all minimal path sets or minimal cut sets is an NP-hard problem and can become impractical for very large systems. future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to test the method with field-informed component rates and independent validation against operational or engineering benchmark data. summary: The paper proposes a condition-based aircraft-engine maintenance method that estimates engine hazard from sensor measurements and chooses a maintenance threshold to balance safety and cost. It combines a Cox proportional-hazards model with repeated sampling and numerical threshold optimization. The evaluation uses simulated turbofan data from the National Aeronautics and Space Administration, generated with Commercial Modular Aero-Propulsion System Simulation, including four benchmark partitions. The method treats preventive restoration and replacement after failure as fixed-cost alternatives, and estimates the failure probability associated with a chosen threshold. The authors report lower maintenance costs than a generic strategy, while showing that the cost-minimizing choice can leave substantial failure risk, particularly in one partition.
key_results: For the combined dataset, the cost-minimizing threshold was 9.0, the estimated failure probability was 0.28, and the estimated maintenance cost was about 76 million US dollars, a 37% reduction against the stated baseline. Across the four partitions, optimal thresholds were 17.5, 10, 22, and 9, and the corresponding estimated failure probabilities were 0.28, 0.15, 0.22, and 0.55. The authors report cost reductions of 40%–50% for the partition-specific strategies and about 13% greater savings than with a generic strategy. They caution that the high failure probability for FD004 makes its cost-minimizing threshold risky, so decision-makers could lower the threshold to reduce risk at additional cost.
key_equations:
Cox proportional-hazards model: \[h(t|x)=h_0(t)\exp\!\left(\beta^{\mathsf T}(x-\bar{x})\right)\] Here h(t|x) is the hazard at time t given measurements x, h₀(t) is the baseline hazard, β is the fitted coefficient vector, and x̄ is the training-data mean of the measurements.

Maintenance cost for a threshold: \[\mathrm{TotalCost}(\lambda)=C_1\sum_{i=1}^{n} I\!\left(\max_t\log\hat{h}(x_{it})\ge\lambda\right)+C_2\sum_{i=1}^{n} I\!\left(\max_t\log\hat{h}(x_{it})<\lambda\right)\] Here λ is the threshold, C₁ is the performance-restoration cost, C₂ is the replacement cost after failure, n is the number of engines, i indexes engines, I is an indicator, t ranges over observed times, and ĥ(xᵢₜ) is the estimated partial hazard for engine i at time t.

Cost-minimizing threshold: \[\lambda^*=\arg\min_{\lambda}\mathrm{TotalCost}(\lambda)\] Here λ* is the selected threshold, λ is a candidate threshold, and TotalCost is the maintenance cost calculated for that candidate.
limitations_stated: The authors note that airlines may find it difficult in practice to classify engines by failure mode and operating conditions, which complicates use of partition-specific strategies. They also report noisy hazard estimates and high estimated failure risk for FD004, and assume fixed costs across engines and time while noting that variable costs could be accommodated.
limitations_unstated: The evaluation uses simulated benchmark data rather than field records, so the reported savings and failure probabilities may not transfer to operating fleets. The method also treats engine trajectories as separate observations and relies on a proportional-hazards model; the paper does not test sensitivity to dependence between engines or violations of that model assumption.
future_work_stated: The authors propose using more advanced machine-learning methods and artificial intelligence to support more complex maintenance strategies. They also describe extending the framework to other intelligent, safety-critical transportation systems.
future_work_unstated: Future evaluation could test the approach on censored, in-service engine records and assess calibration of the estimated failure probabilities under real operating conditions. The method could also incorporate changing operating conditions, additional failure mechanisms, interactions among engines or aircraft systems, and explicit decisions that trade maintenance cost against a specified safety target.

summary: The paper addresses the problem of forecasting damage and remaining useful life in structural health monitoring (SHM), where future conditions and damage progression are uncertain. It proposes a time-series generative adversarial network (TimeGAN) for population-based structural health monitoring (PBSHM), which uses a structure’s observed history to generate possible future damage paths without limiting dependencies to only the most recent state. The method is tested on simulated data from a homogeneous population of 1000 spring-mass structures, with damage represented by decreasing spring stiffness and failure defined using a natural-frequency threshold. The monitored frequency response functions are reduced using principal component analysis (PCA) before training. In this simulation, the generated lifetime distribution and the reported score for predicting actual lifetimes were better than those from a simple population-lifetime baseline.
key_results: The first three principal components retained 96% of the variance in the simulated frequency response function (FRF) data, and the Kullback-Leibler divergence between real and generated total-lifetime distributions was reported as 0.25. On a separate simulated testing population generated using the same assumptions, the mean probability density assigned to the real lifetime was 0.058 with the proposed method, compared with 0.037 for the baseline that used the population lifetime distribution directly. The paper reports these results as evidence of more confident predictions, but it does not report a point-estimation error or a calibrated failure probability.
key_equations:
Simulated stiffness degradation: \[k_{2}^{t+1}=k_{2}^{t}-\left(k_n+\mathcal{N}(0,0.1k_n)\right)\] Here k2 is the stiffness of spring 2, t is the time step, kn is the structure-specific nominal degradation step, and N denotes the Gaussian random variation in the decrease.

Generation of potential future outcomes: \[x_{1:T_f}^{k}=r\left(g\left(z_{1:T_f}^{k}\right)\right)\] Here x is generated damage-sensitive data for sample k through final time step Tf, z is its noise sequence, g is the generator, and r maps the generator output back to the time-series space.

Average lifetime-density score: \[P=\frac{1}{n_{test}}\sum_{i=1}^{n_{test}}p(T_i)\] Here P is the average score, n_test is the number of testing time steps, p(Ti) is the density assigned to the real lifetime, and Ti is the real lifetime for test structure i.
limitations_stated: The authors acknowledge that their simulated data may not resemble a realistic situation. They also note that there is no generally established validation process for generative adversarial networks and evaluate training using the total-lifetime distribution.
limitations_unstated: The training and testing populations use the same simulated damage rules and parameter distributions, so the reported test does not establish performance on field measurements or under shifted operating conditions. The analysis also reduces the frequency response data to three principal components and uses a failure threshold selected by human examination, so performance may depend on information discarded by the reduction and on the chosen threshold.
future_work_stated: None stated.
future_work_unstated: Evaluate the method using field data from structures with measured damage and varying loads and environmental conditions, and test how well its lifetime distributions are calibrated. Further work could also cover other damage mechanisms, multiple interacting failure modes, and system-level decisions such as maintenance actions.

scope_reason: It develops uncertainty propagation for Boolean functions and demonstrates it on a pressure-tank fault tree, directly addressing engineered-system failure probabilities.
