glossary: p-box = Probability box: a range of possible probability distributions.|u, v = The probabilities of the two input events.|rho = The Pearson correlation coefficient describing dependence between the two events.|C_rho = The correlated conjunction function, which gives the joint probability that both events occur.|W, M = The lower and upper Frechet bounds for the joint probability of two events.
summary: Assuming independence between events can give an incomplete or misleading assessment of system failure when the events are dependent or their probabilities are uncertain. The paper presents a correlated Boolean conjunction that uses Pearson correlation while respecting the Frechet bounds, and uses it to propagate precise probabilities, intervals, and probability boxes through Boolean functions. The method distinguishes dependence between the events from dependence between uncertain probability inputs. It is illustrated with a pressure-tank fault tree using specified component probability intervals and probability boxes, rather than observed field data. The results show that relaxing dependence assumptions can substantially widen the range of possible system failure outcomes.
key_results: For the illustrative interval case, the system failure probability is between 2.950 times 10 to the power of -5 and 4.053 times 10 to the power of -5 under independence, between 2.949 times 10 to the power of -5 and 6.551 times 10 to the power of -5 under mixed dependence, and between 2.499 times 10 to the power of -5 and 1.905 times 10 to the power of -4 when dependence is unknown. In the probability-box case, the probability that system failure is no more than 10 to the power of -4 is between 0.969 and 1 under independence, between 0.88 and 1 under mixed dependence, and between 0 and 1 under unknown dependence. These comparisons demonstrate that reducing dependence assumptions broadens the reliability assessment; they are numerical illustrations, not estimates validated against field observations.
key_equations: Correlated conjunction: \[C_\rho(u,v)=\min\{M(u,v),\max[W(u,v),uv+\rho\sqrt{u(1-u)v(1-v)}]\},\quad W(u,v)=\max(u+v-1,0),\quad M(u,v)=\min(u,v)\] Here C_rho is the joint probability for the conjunction, u and v are the two event probabilities, rho is their Pearson correlation, W is the lower Frechet bound, and M is the upper Frechet bound.
limitations_stated: The authors state that they provide no proof that the proposed function satisfies the two-increasing condition required for it to be a copula. They note that the main results require only that the operator be non-decreasing.
limitations_unstated: The pressure-tank example uses specified component probabilities and dependence scenarios, not measured field data, so it does not establish how accurately the method represents a real system. The method treats dependence at successive Boolean operations; pairwise correlation choices alone may not establish a globally consistent joint dependence structure for a larger fault tree.
future_work_stated: None stated.
future_work_unstated: The method could be tested against field reliability data and fault trees with documented common-cause failures to assess whether its dependence bounds are informative in practice. Further work could also address globally consistent dependence across larger systems and incorporate operating conditions or component covariates into the probability inputs.

summary: The paper develops a lifetime model for censored data when two failure modes can be dependent, addressing the limitations of using independent failure times or a model with constant failure rates. It constructs a bivariate Weibull model with separate shape parameters and develops likelihood-based and Bayesian parameter estimation, along with methods to predict future failures. The methods are assessed using simulated data with sample sizes of 100, 200, and 400 and censoring levels of 0%, about 20%, and about 40%. The real-data example uses failure times and failure modes for 30 devices, including 8 units still operating at 300 thousand cycles. The methods give broadly reasonable estimates and similar future-failure predictions, but intervals for the shared-shock shape parameter can have poor coverage under censoring.
key_results: In the simulations with about 40% censoring and sample size 400, coverage of the nominal 95% intervals for the shared-shock shape parameter was 0.239 for likelihood-based intervals and 0.266 for Bayesian intervals; at about 20% censoring, the corresponding coverage was 0.532 and 0.509. Coverage for the other parameters was generally closer to the nominal level, and relative estimation errors tended to decrease as sample size increased. For the device data, estimated mean time to failure was 210.27 thousand cycles using likelihood estimation and 219.68 thousand cycles using Bayesian estimation. For the eight units still operating at 300 thousand cycles, the predicted total failures by 330 thousand cycles were 1.40 by the frequentist method and 1.59 by the Bayesian method; by 500 thousand cycles, the predictions were 6.37 and 6.42, respectively.
key_equations:
Survival of the first failure: \[S_T(t)=\exp\{-\lambda(t^{\alpha_0}+t^{\alpha_1}+t^{\alpha_2})\}\] T is the time of the first failure from either mode, S_T(t) is its survival probability through time t, alpha0, alpha1, and alpha2 are shape parameters, and lambda is the scale parameter.

Likelihood for censored and mode-identified observations: \[L(\theta)\propto\prod_{i\in I_0}f_0(t_i)\prod_{i\in I_1}[-\partial_x S_1(x,y)]_{x=y=t_i}\prod_{i\in I_2}[-\partial_y S_2(x,y)]_{x=y=t_i}\prod_{i\in I_c}S_0(t_i)\] L is the likelihood, theta is the vector of model parameters, I0, I1, and I2 identify tied failures and failures from modes 1 and 2, Ic identifies censored units, ti is an observed time, f0 is the tie density, and S0, S1, and S2 are the applicable survival functions whose derivatives give the mode-specific failure contributions.

Probability and count of future failures: \[\rho=1-\frac{S_T(R+\delta)}{S_T(R)},\qquad M\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(n^*,\rho),\qquad E(M)=n^*\rho\] rho is the conditional probability of failure in the interval after study end time R and of length delta, S_T is the survival probability of the first failure, M is the future failure count among n* surviving units, and E(M) is its expected value.
limitations_stated: The authors report that intervals for the shared-shock shape parameter have poor coverage with censored data, and that the problem worsens as censoring increases; they attribute this to persistent estimation bias. They also state that extending the distinct-shape model to more than two failure modes is not straightforward because singular distributions complicate the analysis.
limitations_unstated: The likelihood and future-count model treat units as independent, and the count prediction uses a common failure probability for the surviving units; the paper does not test sensitivity to dependence between units or differing unit histories. The real-data illustration contains only 30 devices from one example, and the future predictions extend beyond the observed censoring time without validation against later field outcomes.
future_work_stated: The authors propose extending the approach to a multivariable setting with more than two competing failure modes, while recognizing that a distinct-shape Weibull extension will require further development.
future_work_unstated: Further work could incorporate unit-level covariates and changing operating conditions, then assess whether the inferred dependence and predictions remain reliable under those conditions. Independent validation on larger field datasets and evaluation of how prediction intervals support maintenance decisions would also be useful.

summary: The paper addresses the trade-off between preventive maintenance expense and the costs of machine failures and overhauls when maintenance does not restore a machine to a like-new state. It models how maintenance frequency affects the numbers of overhauls and failures, using machine and contract characteristics to estimate outcomes for maintenance levels that were not actually observed. The authors use a causal machine-learning approach to estimate those outcomes from historical contracts, then select the frequency that minimizes estimated total cost for each machine. The data comprise more than 4,000 real full-service maintenance contracts, but the evaluation uses semi-synthetic outcomes generated from those contracts. In that evaluation, the individualized causal policy has lower outcome-prediction error and lower estimated cost than the supervised and non-individualized policies compared.
key_results: Across five runs, the causal model’s mean integrated square error was 7.71 ± 0.60 for overhauls and 14.16 ± 1.68 for failures, compared with 10.25 ± 1.33 and 18.27 ± 3.65 for the supervised model. The individualized causal policy’s policy error was 2.40 ± 0.46, compared with 4.36 ± 1.25 for the individualized supervised policy and 8.77 ± 1.07 for the non-individualized causal policy. Its policy cost ratio was 1.07 ± 0.01, compared with 1.11 ± 0.02 and 1.24 ± 0.04, respectively; a ratio of 1 represents the ideal policy. In experiments with increasing selection bias, the causal approach remained comparatively stable, while the supervised approach’s outcome and policy performance degraded.
key_equations:
Estimated cost per running period: \[C_i(t)=c_t t+c_o o_i(t)+c_f f_i(t)\] C_i is the total cost for machine i at maintenance frequency t; c_t, c_o, and c_f are the unit costs of preventive maintenance, overhauls, and failures; o_i(t) and f_i(t) are the predicted overhaul and failure counts per running period.

Cost-minimizing maintenance frequency: \[t_i^*=\arg\min_{t\in T} C_i(t)\] t_i* is machine i’s cost-minimizing maintenance frequency, t is a candidate frequency, T is the set of available frequencies, and C_i(t) is the estimated cost at that frequency.
limitations_stated: The authors state that causal estimation depends on consistency, overlap, and unconfoundedness. They note that overlap can fail when machines receiving different maintenance frequencies do not have comparable characteristics, and that unconfoundedness cannot be tested directly; unobserved factors affecting both maintenance assignment and outcomes could therefore bias estimates.
limitations_unstated: The unobserved counterfactual outcomes are evaluated using outcomes generated from a specified semi-synthetic setup, so the reported results do not establish performance on genuinely observed counterfactuals or in a prospective field deployment. The framework also optimizes one maintenance type and one frequency per contract, which does not represent changing machine condition or sequences of interventions over time.
future_work_stated: The authors propose studying multiple intervention types, intensities, and costs; more complex costs, including stochastic costs or costs predicted from machine or maintenance characteristics; and more flexible maintenance timing and intervention sequences. They also suggest integrating prediction more closely with the decision step using predict-and-optimize or cost-sensitive methods.
future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be a prospective field evaluation that tracks realized costs and failures under the prescribed schedules, alongside checks of overlap and sensitivity to hidden confounding. The approach could also be extended to incorporate time-varying condition measurements and competing failure mechanisms, then optimize maintenance decisions at the system level rather than for individual contracts alone.

summary: The paper gives guidance for choosing prior distributions when fitting parametric lifetime models to reliability data, especially when only a few failures are observed. It explains how censoring affects prior construction and develops Independence Jeffreys priors for common censoring situations, alongside recommendations for weakly informative and partially informative priors. The methods are illustrated with bearing-cage field data and current-status rocket-motor data, and evaluated using simulated Weibull and lognormal data. In the examples, priors informed by engineering knowledge made failure-probability estimates more precise than minimally informative priors. In simulations, the Independence Jeffreys prior generally had coverage closer to the nominal level than a flat prior when information was limited.
key_results: For the bearing-cage data, the partially informative prior gave a 95% credible interval of 0.15 to 0.92 for failure probability at 8,000 hours, while the noninformative prior gave 0.03 to 0.99992. For the rocket-motor data, the corresponding intervals for failure probability at 20 years were 0.008 to 0.16 with a partially informative prior and 0.007 to 0.98 with a weakly or noninformative prior; the estimated Weibull shape was 3.4 rather than 5.9 under the latter prior and 8.126 by maximum likelihood. The simulation used 5,000 data sets per factor combination and assessed 95% intervals; for both Weibull and lognormal models, coverage was close to the nominal 0.95 level when the expected number of failures was at least 35. The Independence Jeffreys prior usually performed as well as or better than the flat prior, with a clearer improvement when the expected failure proportion was 0.01; these are coverage comparisons, not prediction-error or cost results.
key_equations:
Weibull lifetime distribution: \[F(t;\eta,\beta)=1-\exp\left[-\left(\frac{t}{\eta}\right)^\beta\right]\] F is the probability of failure by time t, eta is the Weibull scale parameter, and beta is the Weibull shape parameter.

Type 1 censoring Independence Jeffreys prior: \[\pi(y_p,\tau)\propto\sqrt{f_{11}\{f_{11}[\Phi^{-1}(p_r)]^2-2f_{12}\Phi^{-1}(p_r)+f_{22}\}}\] Pi is the joint prior density, y_p is the logarithm of the selected lifetime quantile, tau is the logarithm of the distribution scale parameter sigma, p_r is the selected quantile probability, Phi inverse is the inverse standard distribution function, and f11, f12, and f22 are scaled Fisher information matrix elements for the censoring model.

Bayesian posterior: \[\pi(\theta\mid\mathrm{DATA})\propto L(\mathrm{DATA}\mid\theta)\pi(\theta)\] Pi of theta given the data is the posterior density, L is the likelihood of the data given parameters theta, and pi of theta is the prior density.
limitations_stated: The authors report that noninformative priors can yield improper or poorly behaved posteriors with very few failures; their numerical experiments found practical sampling difficulties with two failures and occasional extreme values even with three. They note that analytical reference priors for Type 1 censoring are difficult to obtain, and their main guidance focuses on single log-location-scale distributions. Their implementation also encountered long run times and sampler difficulties for some Independence Jeffreys prior fits.
limitations_unstated: The field examples are limited to two cases and do not provide independent validation across products, failure mechanisms, or operating environments. The modeling framework assumes independent observations and noninformative censoring, so dependent failures or censoring related to unobserved failure risk could undermine the results. The simulation evaluates specified Weibull and lognormal models under Type 1 censoring, and therefore does not establish coverage under model misspecification or the more complex censoring patterns of all field settings.
future_work_stated: The authors propose extending the prior methods to accelerated test models with Type 1 censoring and to other reliability data, including degradation, fatigue stress-life, and recurrent-event data. They also call for implementing default noninformative and partially informative priors in widely available software, with options for sensitivity analysis.
future_work_unstated: Future work could test the recommended priors prospectively on larger, independent field datasets and quantify how robust the conclusions are to alternative lifetime distributions and informative censoring. Extensions could incorporate covariates and changing operating conditions, competing failure mechanisms, and system-level dependence, then connect posterior reliability estimates to maintenance or redesign decisions.

summary: The paper addresses identifying which rolling-element bearings need attention by classifying their current degradation stage, rather than predicting when to service an entire machine. It proposes automatically labeling bearing lifetime observations with k-means clustering in an AutoEncoder-derived low-dimensional representation, then training a multi-input neural network using vibration data in both time and frequency domains. The data come from 17 bearings tested under accelerated conditions in the public FEMTO Bearing dataset, with six bearings used for training and 11 for testing. The authors report that automatic labels generally resemble manual labels, although distinguishing the earliest degradation stage is difficult. Their results favor AutoEncoder-based labels over principal component analysis labels for classifier accuracy and for producing more actionable fault-detection timing.
key_results: The automatic labeling results broadly agreed with manual segmentation, but both approaches had difficulty with stage 1; the authors note that manual separation of healthy operation from stage 1 can be arbitrary. The classifier trained on AutoEncoder-based labels reached higher training accuracy in fewer epochs than the classifier trained on principal component analysis labels; a classifier trained on random four-class labels achieved about 25% training accuracy. For bearing 1-6, the AutoEncoder-label classifier detected a fault with 4.6% of healthy lifetime remaining and 93.2% of total lifetime remaining, compared with 97.2% and 32.2% for the principal-component-label classifier. Across the test set, the authors report that AutoEncoder-based predictions overlap less with other stages and are more consistent with their conservative maintenance objective; the comparison uses generated labels rather than independent ground-truth stage labels.
key_equations: AutoEncoder reconstruction loss: \[\mathcal{L}_{MAE}(\theta)=\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=0}^{T}|X_t-\hat{X}_t|\] L_MAE is the mean absolute reconstruction loss, theta is the AutoEncoder weights, T is the final time index, t is a time index, X_t is the frequency-domain signal at t, and X-hat_t is its reconstruction.
limitations_stated: The authors state that the method assumes access to a training set of representative bearings, and it is unknown whether zero-shot use across different bearings is possible. They also say that the applicable scope of a degradation-stage model and the practical availability of cheap, reliable vibration measurements in regulated production remain unresolved.
limitations_unstated: The experiments use a small accelerated laboratory benchmark, not bearings monitored in pharmaceutical production, so performance under routine loads, sensor installations, and operating variation is not established. Test predictions are assessed against automatically generated clustering labels rather than independent expert-verified ground truth, and the classifier treats observations individually before smoothing predictions, so its accuracy as a temporal state estimator is uncertain.
future_work_stated: The authors propose investigating whether zero-shot learning can extend the method to bearings not represented in training, and otherwise characterizing the scope of each degradation-stage model. They also identify determining how to obtain vibration measurements reliably and cheaply in production, using either permanently embedded sensors or sensors applied before scheduled maintenance, as an open question.
future_work_unstated: Future studies could test transfer across bearing fault modes, loads, speeds, and sensor placements, and validate stage labels through independent inspections and field data. They could also evaluate uncertainty-aware, temporally constrained predictions and compare replacement decisions under different costs of early replacement and missed faults.

summary: The paper addresses time-dependent reliability analysis for nonlinear dynamical systems, where response changes over time and failure probability cannot be captured by a single time-independent calculation. It trains an encoder, a linear Koopman operator, and a decoder together so that system states can be advanced in time and first threshold-crossing times can be estimated. Separate architectures handle uncertainty in initial conditions and uncertainty in system parameters, and Monte Carlo simulation on the trained surrogate is used to estimate failure-time distributions. The evaluation uses simulated outputs from a Duffing oscillator, a chaotic Lorenz system, and two-dimensional Burgers’ equation. The reported examples show close agreement with Monte Carlo benchmarks and generally better failure-time distributions than autoregressive neural-network comparators.
key_results: For the Duffing oscillator with random initial conditions, the estimated failure probability was 0.0351 versus 0.0389 from Monte Carlo simulation, and the reported reliability-index error was 2.67%. With random Duffing system parameters, the values were 0.307 versus 0.295 and the reported error was 6.4%. For the Lorenz system, the reported errors were 1.25% for random initial conditions and 3.7% for random system parameters; the corresponding estimated failure probabilities were 0.167 versus 0.170 and 0.212 versus 0.203. For Burgers’ equation, the estimated first-passage-time distributions closely matched the Monte Carlo results for the illustrated limit states, while the autoregressive convolutional network showed poorer agreement.
key_equations:
Linear evolution in learned Koopman coordinates: \[\psi(X_{k+1})=K\psi(X_k)\] Psi maps the state X at discrete time step k into latent coordinates, and K advances those coordinates to the next time step.

Weighted training loss: \[\mathcal{L}=\lambda_1\mathcal{L}_1+\lambda_2\mathcal{L}_2+\lambda_3\mathcal{L}_3\] The total loss L is the weighted sum of reconstruction loss L1, latent-dynamics loss L2, and next-state prediction loss L3, with lambda1, lambda2, and lambda3 as their weights.

Failure probability over the analysis interval: \[P_f=P\left(\tau\in[t_0,t_s]\right)\] P_f is the probability that the first threshold-crossing time tau, measured by probability operator P, falls between the start time t_0 and end time t_s.
limitations_stated: The authors state that uncertainty in initial conditions and uncertainty in system parameters are studied separately rather than together. They note that the framework can be extended to handle both at the same time, and state no other explicit limitations.
limitations_unstated: The evaluation uses simulated examples only, so agreement with simulation benchmarks does not establish accuracy for measured structural or infrastructure data. Out-of-distribution tests vary the sampled ranges and distributions within the examples, but do not establish performance far beyond those tested cases or under other failure mechanisms. The paper does not report computational-cost comparisons or quantify uncertainty in the learned surrogate’s predictions.
future_work_stated: The authors propose extending the framework to cases where uncertainty in initial conditions and system parameters occurs together.
future_work_unstated: The method could be tested on field measurements and on structures with multiple interacting failure mechanisms and changing operating or environmental conditions. Further work could also quantify surrogate prediction uncertainty and connect first-passage estimates to system-level decisions, including inspection or maintenance planning.

summary: The paper addresses the difficulty of estimating software reliability when testing records are organized by test case rather than by time between failures. It models the chance of detecting a bug as increasing with the bug’s latent eventual size, and uses a Bayesian generalized linear mixed model (GLMM) to estimate the number and sizes of bugs as well as software reliability. The method uses pass-fail detection records from testing phases and predicts how many additional phases may be needed to meet a chosen reliability target. The authors evaluate it with simulated data and two empirical software testing data sets, one commercial and one from mission software. They report satisfactory parameter estimation in simulations and show that estimates of required testing effort vary substantially with test volume and application data.
key_results: Across four simulation scenarios, coverage of the 95% credible intervals was 0.92 to 0.96 for the number of bugs and 0.90 to 0.96 for the detection parameter; the reported mean coefficients of variation for bug count ranged from 0.05 to 0.10. For the commercial data, the estimated bug count was 348, with a 95% credible interval of 317 to 382, and the remaining eventual bug size after four phases was estimated as 703, with an interval of 457 to 1006. With 3,000 test cases per future phase, the commercial application reached the target reliability of 0.95 at phase 16; the authors estimate about 36,000 future test cases would be needed. For the mission software, the estimated total was 94 bugs, with an interval of 94 to 95, and reliability was reported as 0.995 after eight phases at a remaining-size threshold of 25; the discussion later describes it as approximately 0.998.
key_equations:
Bug detection probability: \[p_i=1-(1-r)^{S_i}\] Here p_i is the probability of detecting bug i with one input, r is the shared probability of detection per passage through the bug, and S_i is the bug's eventual size.

Phase detection outcomes: \[y_{ij}\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(T_j,p_i z_i)\] Here y_ij is the number of detections for bug i in phase j, T_j is the number of inputs in that phase, p_i is the bug's detection probability, and z_i indicates whether the bug is present.

Remaining eventual bug size: \[B_j=\sum_{i=1}^{M}S_i z_i(1-u_{ij})\] Here B_j is the undetected eventual bug size after phase j, M is the upper bound on potential bugs, S_i is bug i's size, z_i indicates whether it is present, and u_ij indicates whether it has been detected by phase j.

Reliability at phase j: \[\gamma_j(\epsilon)=P(B_j\leq\epsilon\mid Y)\] Here gamma_j is reliability after phase j, epsilon is the allowed remaining-size threshold, B_j is the remaining eventual bug size, and Y is the observed testing data.
limitations_stated: The authors characterize parameter estimates as moderately robust and recommend conducting a prior sensitivity study before applying the model. They do not state other specific limitations.
limitations_unstated: The model assumes distinct independent bugs and a shared detection parameter, so dependencies among bugs or differences in detectability beyond bug size may not be represented. Predictions of additional testing phases depend on assumed future test-case counts, and the evaluation does not establish predictive performance on post-release field failures.
future_work_stated: The authors do not propose a specific future research task. They note that the modelling approach may also apply to problems such as hydrocarbon exploration.
future_work_unstated: Future work could incorporate software, mission, and operating-condition covariates, as well as dependencies among bugs and additional failure mechanisms. Prospective validation against field failures and integration with release decisions or system-level reliability assessments would test whether the predicted stopping phase is useful in practice.

summary: The paper studies how to allocate active redundant components in coherent systems made up of different, dependent component types. The system reliability is represented using a survival signature and a specified copula model for dependence. The authors optimize two mean cost rates: one for renewal and refreshment at system failure, and one for replacement at failure or at a chosen age, whichever comes first. They also derive corresponding formulas for series-parallel systems. The evaluation is theoretical and uses numerical examples with assumed lifetime distributions, cost values, and copulas rather than observed lifetime data; the optimal allocation varies with the costs, system structure, and dependence model.
key_results: For the six-component example with Gumbel-Hougaard dependence parameter alpha equal to 2, the failure-time criterion is minimized at v1 equal to 2 and v2 equal to 0, with cost rate 4.99041; the age-replacement criterion is minimized at v1 equal to 1 and v2 equal to 0, with cost rate 7.77258. Under independence in that example, the respective minima are 6.48197 at v1 equal to 3 and v2 equal to 0, and 8.48716 at v1 equal to 1 and v2 equal to 0. For the eight-component independent example, the best allocation for both criteria is v1 equal to 0, v2 equal to 1, and v3 equal to 0; the reported minima are 37.4142 and 28.9959, with the latter obtained at replacement age tau equal to 0.375. In the series-parallel example, the failure-time criterion is minimized at component counts (2, 3, 2), with cost rate 7.4068, while the age-replacement criterion is minimized at (2, 2, 2), with cost rate 12.2278.
key_equations:

Mean cost rate under age-based replacement: \[\mathrm{Cost}_2(\mathbf v)=\frac{M_1(\mathbf v)P(T_R\leq\tau)+M_2(\mathbf v)P(T_R>\tau)}{E[\min(\tau,T_R)]}\] Cost2 is the age-based mean cost rate; M1 is the average renewal cost when failure occurs by age tau; M2 is the average renewal cost when the system survives past tau; P denotes probability; E denotes expectation; tau is the predetermined replacement age; and T_R is system lifetime with redundancy.
limitations_stated: The authors note that they assume each original component and its added redundant components are independent and identically distributed within the parallel subsystem, which can restrict practical applicability. They also identify the more general case of dependent, nonexchangeable components within a group as beyond the present treatment.
limitations_unstated: The numerical examples use specified distributions, dependence copulas, and costs; the paper does not validate the resulting allocations against observed field lifetimes or maintenance outcomes. The method also assumes that the dependence structure and lifetime distributions are known, so the effects of parameter-estimation uncertainty on the recommended allocation are not assessed.
future_work_stated: The authors propose studying dependence within each component group beyond exchangeability. They also identify cold- and warm-standby redundancy allocation for coherent systems as future research.
future_work_unstated: A practical extension would estimate lifetime distributions, copula dependence, and maintenance costs from field data, then test whether the selected allocations remain effective under parameter uncertainty and changing operating conditions. Further work could examine multiple failure mechanisms, system-level resource or service constraints, and scalable optimization for larger systems.

summary: This paper develops a Bayesian accelerated life testing model for predicting product reliability under normal-use conditions from tests conducted at higher stress levels. It combines a Weibull lifetime distribution with a generalised Eyring time transformation function, allowing temperature and a non-thermal stressor to be modelled together. The authors formulate likelihoods that accommodate complete data and two types of right censoring, and present several prior choices with posterior sampling methods. They apply the models to laboratory failure-time data for electronics epoxy packaging tested under temperature and relative humidity stress. Models using diffuse priors give similar fit and reliability estimates, while more concentrated subjective priors can substantially change the predictions.
key_results: For the electronics test data, the deviance information criterion (DIC) was 228.2 for both GEW2,1 and GEW4, compared with 228.4 for GEW1 and GEW2,2, and 228.3 for GEW3; these diffuse-prior models had similar results. At 2,000 hours and the stated use stresses, predicted reliability was 0.179376 for GEW1 and 0.193196 for GEW2,1. Subjective-prior models produced higher predictions at that time: 0.369133 for GEW2,3, 0.586761 for GEW2,4, and 0.946555 for GEW2,5. The authors report that the increasingly concentrated priors pull posterior parameter estimates toward the prior values and caution against priors with very small variance.
key_equations:
Generalised Eyring stress relationship: \[\lambda(T,S)=T\exp\left(-\theta_1-\frac{\theta_2}{T}-\theta_3V(S)-\frac{\theta_4V(S)}{T}\right)\] Lambda is the stress-dependent Weibull rate, T is temperature, S is the non-thermal stress, V(S) is its specified transformation, and theta1 through theta4 are unknown model parameters.

Weibull reliability: \[R(t\mid T,S,\theta,\beta)=\exp\left[-\lambda(T,S)t^\beta\right]\] R is reliability at time t and stresses T and S, lambda is the stress-dependent Weibull rate, theta denotes the four Eyring parameters, and beta is the Weibull shape parameter.

Posterior predictive reliability estimate: \[R(t\mid x)\approx\frac{1}{M}\sum_{m=1}^{M}R\left(t\mid\theta_1^{(m)},\theta_2^{(m)},\theta_3^{(m)},\theta_4^{(m)},\beta^{(m)}\right)\] R(t given x) is predicted reliability at use time t given observed data x, M is the number of posterior draws, m indexes each draw, and the superscripted parameters are values sampled from the posterior.
limitations_stated: The authors do not identify specific limitations of the model or application. They do caution that gamma priors with very small variance can dominate the posterior and should be used carefully.
limitations_unstated: The application uses one laboratory electronics data set, and the paper does not validate the use-condition predictions against field failures or an independent test set. The model assumes a Weibull shape parameter that is unchanged across stress conditions and relies on the chosen generalised Eyring relationship to extrapolate from accelerated tests to use conditions. The paper gives no assessment of how sensitive that extrapolation is to alternative stress-response forms or to dependence among tested items.
future_work_stated: The authors propose no specific future-work directions.
future_work_unstated: Further studies could validate the predicted reliability using field data or independent tests at use conditions, and compare alternative stress-response forms and failure mechanisms. They could also examine additional covariates and operating conditions, dependence among components in a system, and how reliability predictions support testing or maintenance decisions.

summary: The paper addresses the problem that multiple sensor signals may track degradation, but no single signal provides a suitable degradation index. It builds a monotone index from the cumulative exposure of sensor signals, using flexible nonlinear effects and selecting sensors with an adaptive group penalty. The model uses both observed failure times and right-censored service times, and is designed to favor avoiding missed failures. The authors evaluate it using simulated data and NASA jet-engine sensor data. Their method has the lowest reported average total classification error among the methods compared on the jet-engine data.
key_results: In simulations with 10 sensors, five of them having no effect, and sample sizes from 50 to 300, the proposed method had the smallest total error for almost all scenarios and generally removed more irrelevant sensors than the linear-effect comparison. In the jet-engine analysis, the data contained 200 units, with 100 failures and 100 censored units; the authors used 16 sensors and repeated stratified training and test splits 50 times. The proposed method's average false-negative rate was 0.030, false-positive rate was 0.026, and total error rate was 0.057. The corresponding total error rates were 0.104 for the existing health-index method, 0.645 for the linear-effect method, and 0.080 for the method without variable selection.

Cumulative-exposure degradation index: \[u(t)=\int_0^t h\!\left(\sum_{j=1}^p f_j[x_j(s);\beta_j]\right)\,ds\] Here, u(t) is the index at time t, s is time within the accumulated history, h is the positive transformation, j indexes the p sensors, f_j is the effect function for sensor j, x_j(s) is its observed signal, and beta_j contains its coefficients.

limitations_stated: The authors report that when the number of units increases, the method becomes less able to exclude sensors with no effect, even as it retains more useful sensors. They also note that the additive sensor-effect specification may not represent more complex relationships among sensors.
limitations_unstated: The real-data evaluation is limited to one NASA jet-engine dataset and repeated splits of its 200 units, so performance on other equipment or independent field populations is not established. The model relies on a specified threshold and failure-time distribution, and the paper does not report a sensitivity analysis for these choices or quantify computational time for the numerical optimization.
future_work_stated: The authors propose allowing interactions among sensor effects, improving variable selection through an adaptive group elastic-net penalty, and incorporating the number of units into the variable-selection penalty.
future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be external validation on field data from other systems and operating conditions, including an assessment of how stable the selected sensors and failure classifications are. Future evaluations could also connect false-positive and false-negative classifications to system-level consequences and decision costs, rather than relying only on classification error rates.

summary: This paper develops a test of whether time to failure is independent of the cause of failure in competing-risks data with two causes. The authors construct a U-statistic estimate of a measure of dependence and use jackknife empirical likelihood to form the test. The method is derived for independent, identically distributed observations with fully observed failure times and causes. The authors evaluate it using Monte Carlo simulations and four real-data examples. They report that the test has type I error close to the intended level and can have greater power than the comparison test, particularly for stronger dependence.
key_results: In simulations with 10,000 replications and sample sizes from 20 to 100, the reported type I error for the proposed test was close to the nominal level; for example, at sample size 100 and significance level 0.05, it was 0.0502 and 0.0486 for the two parameter combinations, compared with 0.0508 and 0.0502 for the Dewan et al. test. At dependence parameter a = 1.9 and sample size 100, power at level 0.05 was 0.9532 versus 0.8924 for the comparison test under one parameter combination, and 0.9827 versus 0.9551 under the other. In the four real-data examples, the authors report test statistics of 0.4827, 0.1491, 6.0764, and 20.2296; they report accepting independence for the first three and rejecting it for the tire data. The reported acceptance of independence for the mouse data accompanies a statistic of 6.0764, but the paper does not explain this result in relation to its stated chi-square testing rule.

Equivalent probability contrast: \[\Delta=P(T_1>T_2,J_1=1,J_2=2)-P(T_1>T_2,J_1=2,J_2=1)\] Delta is the departure measure, T sub 1 and T sub 2 are two failure times, and J sub 1 and J sub 2 are their respective causes; the probability difference compares the two stated orderings of times and causes.

Null distribution of the test statistic: \[-2l(0)\xrightarrow{d}\chi^2_1\] l of zero is the JEL log-likelihood ratio evaluated when the departure measure is zero, and the test statistic converges in distribution to a chi-square distribution with one degree of freedom under the null hypothesis.
limitations_stated: The proposed procedure does not incorporate right-censored observations. The authors say that a JEL method for censored observations is being studied and will be reported separately.
limitations_unstated: The simulations use a particular family of two-cause distributions based on exponential failure times, so performance under other lifetime distributions, dependence patterns, and more than two causes is not established. The real-data examples also exclude censored observations or combine causes, and the paper provides no field-data validation of the method for reliability applications.
future_work_stated: The authors propose developing a JEL ratio test that incorporates censored observations. They also propose developing a JEL ratio test for equality of cumulative incidence functions.
future_work_unstated: Future work could assess the test with more than two competing causes, broader dependence structures, and covariates or changing operating conditions. It could also validate the method on field reliability data with censoring and evaluate how test results support system-level risk and maintenance decisions.

summary: The paper develops optimal measurement-time plans for accelerated degradation testing of highly reliable products. It models degradation with a linear mixed-effects model, allowing units to vary in their degradation paths, and defines failure as the path reaching a threshold. The design objective is to improve estimation of quantiles of the failure-time distribution under normal-use conditions, especially the median. The authors derive plans for both repeated measurements on the same units and destructive testing, where each unit is measured only once. Numerical illustrations show that carefully chosen measurement times can estimate the median more efficiently than standard evenly spaced plans.
key_results: For the repeated-measurement example, an adjusted plan using six measurements at times 0.00, 0.05, 0.10, 0.90, 0.95, and 1.00 achieved 98.70% efficiency relative to the locally optimal approximate plan. In the destructive-testing example, the median failure time was 1.583 on the standardized time scale, and the optimal joint design assigned proportions 0.22, 0.73, 0.01, and 0.04 to the four stress-time combinations. The authors report that the optimal design is more sensitive to misspecification of the ratio of endpoint standard deviations than to misspecification of the median failure time. A six-time-point evenly spaced design performed substantially worse throughout the illustrated comparison, while a two-endpoint design was preferable only for larger median failure times.
key_equations:
Median failure time for straight-line degradation: \[t_{0.5}=\frac{y_0-\delta_1}{\delta_2}\] Here t_{0.5} is the median failure time, y_0 is the failure threshold, delta_1 is the aggregate degradation intercept, and delta_2 is its slope.

Optimal destructive-test allocation at the final time: \[\pi^*=\frac{t_{0.5}\sigma(1)}{t_{0.5}\sigma(1)+(t_{0.5}-1)\sigma(0)}\] Here pi^* is the optimal allocation proportion at standardized time 1, t_{0.5} is the median failure time, sigma(1) is the measurement standard deviation at time 1, and sigma(0) is the measurement standard deviation at time 0.
limitations_stated: The authors do not provide a separate limitations section. They note that some designs are local to nominal parameter values and that design efficiency can be affected by misspecification, particularly of the variance parameters.
limitations_unstated: The method depends on a linear degradation structure, normally distributed random effects, and the stated structure linking stress and time; performance may differ when these assumptions do not hold. The examples are numerical rather than validations against field degradation data, and the median is extrapolated beyond the standardized experimental interval, so the accuracy of that extrapolation is not empirically established here.
future_work_stated: None stated.
future_work_unstated: Further work could test the designs on field degradation data and examine nonlinear degradation paths, non-normal unit variation, and unit-specific stress effects. It could also compare robust or decision-based plans that account for uncertainty in nominal parameters and for system-level reliability consequences.

summary: The paper addresses the computational burden of assessing how a system's reliability changes over time and the difficulty of incorporating observations into conventional calculations. It models system condition as probabilities across states of a continuous-time Markov process and trains neural networks to satisfy both the transition equations and initial conditions. A generative adversarial approach is also proposed to represent uncertainty and incorporate inspection measurements. The method is demonstrated on a simulated, four-state dual-processor computing system, including synthetic inspection data; no field measurements are used. The examples show agreement with numerical and Monte Carlo benchmarks and report substantially shorter computation times for the proposed approach.
key_results: For the baseline example, neural-network state-probability and reliability curves closely matched the differential-equation solver and Monte Carlo simulation, and the reported root-mean-square errors were described as small without a specific summary value. A replicate of the proposed method took 17.9 seconds, compared with 283.4 seconds for a Monte Carlo replicate. For uncertainty in the initial condition, the paper reports 625.9 seconds for training and sampling versus around 4 hours for the Monte Carlo procedure, describing the proposed method as 24 times more computationally efficient. In the synthetic inspection-data example, updated reliability curves followed the assumed better or worse performance relative to the baseline, but this demonstration was heuristic rather than validation against real observations.
key_equations:
Forward state-probability model: \[p'(t)=p(t)Q(t)\] Here p(t) is the vector of state probabilities, p'(t) is its time derivative, t is operational time, and Q(t) is the transition-rate matrix.

Physics-informed neural-network loss: \[L(\theta)=\|N_\theta(0)-s_0\|_2^2+\frac{\lambda}{N_c}\sum_{i=1}^{N_c}\|N_\theta(t_i)Q(t_i)-\frac{dN_\theta(t_i)}{dt}\|_2^2\] Here L(theta) is the loss, theta denotes network parameters, N_theta estimates state probabilities, s_0 is the initial probability vector, lambda weights the transition residual, N_c is the number of collocation points, t_i is the time at point i, Q(t_i) is the transition-rate matrix there, and the norm measures each residual vector.

System reliability: \[R(t)=\sum_{j\in U}p_j(t)\] Here R(t) is reliability at time t, U is the set of states considered reliable, j is a state index, and p_j(t) is the probability of state j at time t.
limitations_stated: The authors state that robust network architecture and training configuration remain open research issues and that their results could be improved through further tuning. They also note that adversarial-network training is difficult, with the physics-informed version made more challenging by its composite generator loss. The example incorporating observations during service life is explicitly presented as a heuristic demonstration using synthetic measurements.
limitations_unstated: The demonstrations use one simulated four-state system with specified transition behavior; they do not establish performance on field systems or real inspection records. The uncertainty examples focus on uncertain initial conditions and synthetic measurements, rather than uncertainty in transition rates or other model assumptions. The reported computational comparisons come from a single desktop setup, so runtime advantages may differ for other systems and implementations.
future_work_stated: The authors propose Bayesian deep learning and deep ensemble learning for improved uncertainty quantification, and meta-learning and multi-task learning to facilitate training. They also propose network configurations for non-Markovian reliability problems, using physics-informed learning to discover reliability patterns, and a systematic framework for integrating measurements with other mathematical models.
future_work_unstated: Future studies could validate the approach using real inspection and maintenance records, including noisy or incomplete measurements, and test it on systems with different failure mechanisms and operating conditions. They could also evaluate how component dependencies and system-level structure affect predictions, and assess whether reliability updates support practical maintenance or risk decisions.

summary: Lithium-ion cells lose capacity as they age, and manufacturing and test-condition differences cause degradation to vary from cell to cell. The paper asks how many cells need to be tested to estimate this population variability with a stable fit. It models capacity over time with simple linear curves and a linear-plus-exponential curve, then uses a hierarchical Bayesian method to estimate variation in model parameters across cells. The analysis uses five laboratory ageing datasets of commercial cylindrical cells, including publicly available data and experiments by the authors. The main finding is that stable population-variability estimates required an average of 9, 11, or 13 cells for models with one, two, or three parameters, respectively.
key_results: Across the datasets and model-parameter combinations, the estimated mean sample sizes for a stable population-variability fit were 9 cells for one-parameter models, 11 for two-parameter models, and 13 for three-parameter models. Stability was defined using a 10% threshold relative to the fitted stable trend in uncertainty, and estimates were based on 1,000 repeated random subsamples at each tested size. The hierarchical Bayesian estimates and direct subsample-distribution estimates approached similar results at larger subsample sizes, but the direct method appeared artificially confident for small subsamples. In most cases estimates stabilized with fewer than 20 cells; the paper notes that 20 were required when the sample parameter distribution was not Gaussian.
key_equations:

Their approach assumes Gaussian population distributions and no correlations between parameters; they found the no-correlation assumption questionable in two cases and did not test multimodal populations. They also lacked sufficient data to test the effects of usage variability separately from manufacturing variability or to estimate variability for more complex physics-based models.
limitations_unstated: The five datasets cover a limited set of cell types and test conditions, so the estimated sample counts may not transfer to other chemistries, operating conditions, or failure mechanisms. The stability criterion is based on a chosen 10% threshold and repeated subsampling of the available datasets, rather than independent field-data validation or a stated target for parameter-estimation accuracy.
future_work_stated: The authors propose testing the findings with larger and more varied datasets, examining correlated parameters and alternative population distributions, and quantifying use variability alongside manufacturing variability. They also suggest studying more complex physics-based models, including through synthetic data to investigate parameter identifiability.
future_work_unstated: Future studies could validate the proposed sample counts on field-operated cells and explicitly test whether conclusions change under calendar ageing, temperature variation, or other degradation mechanisms. They could also connect population estimates to pack-level reliability and use the uncertainty estimates to choose test sample sizes according to a specified engineering decision or cost.

summary: This paper develops optimal designs for accelerated degradation testing of systems with two degradation components. It models each component's degradation increments using a Gamma process, with stress affecting the degradation rate, and uses copulas to represent dependence between components. For independent components, the design minimizes the estimated variance of a system lifetime quantile; for dependent components, it uses determinant-based information criteria and also examines a simplified binary-outcome model. The authors derive the designs theoretically and illustrate them with numerical calculations, without using empirical product data. The examples show how the optimal stress settings and allocation of test units depend on the assumed model and estimation objective.
key_results: For the independent-component example, the optimal marginal designs use stress endpoints 0 and 1, allocating weights 0.79 and 0.21 for component one and 0.91 and 0.09 for component two. For dependent continuous measurements, the Frank copula example gives a six-point design with equal weights of 0.166, while the Gaussian copula example uses the same six points with reported weights 0.20, 0.20, 0.16, 0.16, 0.18, and 0.09. In the single-measurement binary example, the determinant-based designs use the four corners of the stress region, with reported weights from 0.22 to 0.28 across the two copulas. The binary example's variance-focused designs use four points and have reported weights 0.09, 0.18, 0.46, and 0.27 for the Frank copula, and 0.11, 0.22, 0.39, and 0.28 for the Gaussian copula; the sensitivity plots indicate good efficiency relative to the comparison designs, but the paper reports no numerical accuracy or failure-rate validation on observed data.
key_equations:
Stress-dependent Gamma rate: \[\gamma_l(x_l)=\exp(\beta_{1l}+\beta_{2l}x_l)\] The Gamma shape rate gamma for component l is the exponential of its intercept beta one, slope beta two, and stress level x.

Copula model for dependent increments: \[F(y_1,y_2)=C\bigl(F_1(y_1),F_2(y_2)\bigr)\] The joint distribution F of the two increment values y one and y two combines their marginal distributions F one and F two through copula C.

Variance-focused design criterion: \[c^{\mathsf T}M(\xi)^{-1}c\] The criterion is the asymptotic variance expression, where c is the target gradient, M is the design's information matrix, and xi denotes the design.

Joint binary failure probability: \[P_{11}=1-F_1(z_{10})-F_2(z_{20})+C\bigl(F_1(z_{10}),F_2(z_{20})\bigr)\] The probability P eleven that both components exceed their thresholds is calculated from the marginal distributions F one and F two at thresholds z ten and z twenty, with dependence represented by C.
limitations_stated: The authors explain that an arbitrary copula does not necessarily produce a bivariate process with independent increments, so the dependent continuous model is restricted to increments observed at fixed times. They also state that calculating the information matrix for repeated copula-based measurements is difficult, and therefore use a single measurement for the binary-outcome design. They note the difficulty of defining a continuous system failure-time variable under dependent failure modes, which motivates use of a determinant-based criterion for the dependent continuous models.
limitations_unstated: The results are numerical illustrations under nominal parameter values rather than validation using degradation data from real products, so the practical accuracy of the selected designs is not established. The designs assume constant stress within each unit, a common measurement schedule, and the specified Gamma marginal and copula forms; performance under heterogeneous units, changing operating conditions, or misspecified dependence may differ.
future_work_stated: The authors propose extending the results to other marginal degradation models, including Wiener processes, inverse Gaussian processes, and nonlinear mixed-effects degradation models.
future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to validate the design recommendations using field or laboratory degradation data and assess robustness when the copula or marginal process is misspecified. Further work could incorporate unit-level covariates, varying operating conditions, additional failure mechanisms, and system-level reliability objectives into the design criteria.

summary: The paper presents an autoregressive partially hidden Markov model for equipment health assessment and remaining useful life prediction. The model represents measurements with state-dependent autoregressive dynamics and uses hidden Markov states to represent changes in the equipment's condition. Its main extension is a likelihood-based learning procedure that incorporates uncertain or partial prior information about those hidden states. The authors test it using health indicators and associated remaining useful life values from the simulated CMAPSS turbofan benchmark, training on 100 engines and testing on 15. On that test subset, the approach has error similar to one comparator but worse timeliness than another; the authors describe the results as encouraging but preliminary.
key_results: On the 15 test instances, the proposed model's overall timeliness score was 36.32 and its reported error was 10.86%; the paper calls this error mean average percentage error in the text, although the table labels the column mean absolute error. RULCLIPPER scored 23.30 for timeliness and 10.08% for error, while SWELM scored 77.57 and 15.58%, respectively; lower values are preferred. Averaging the proposed model and comparator predictions produced a reported timeliness score of 21.8 and error of 9.26%. The authors also report about 80% accuracy within an interval extending 13 below to 10 above the true remaining useful life, with a false-positive rate around 67%, corresponding to early predictions.

limitations_stated: The authors say that more experiments are needed to validate the approach. They also note that they did not optimize the number of hidden states or autoregressive regressors, and that an objective criterion for choosing those parameters relative to the prior remains to be developed. They caution that the comparison with RULCLIPPER cannot be generalized from the reported instances.
limitations_unstated: The quantitative comparison uses only 15 test engines from CMAPSS dataset 1, which has one operating condition and one fault mode, so it does not establish performance across the benchmark's broader operating conditions or fault modes. future_work_stated: The authors propose further experiments to validate the method and say that they are improving it to include uncertain future operating conditions in the hidden-state structure. future_work_unstated: Evaluate the method on field run-to-failure and censored fleet data, with multiple fault mechanisms and changing operating conditions, to test whether the simulated-data results transfer to service. summary: The paper addresses how to choose a Type-II progressive censoring scheme when the number of feasible schemes makes exhaustive search impractical. It proposes a probabilistic search that generates candidate schemes and accepts or rejects them according to an objective criterion, such as uncertainty in estimated lifetime quantiles or test cost. The authors illustrate the method with a Weibull lifetime model and compare it with exhaustive search and variable neighborhood search. Their evaluation consists of numerical examples, not field data. The proposed method generally finds schemes with criterion values close to those of the comparison methods, but it does not guarantee that the exact optimum is found.
key_results: For the exhaustive-search comparisons at sample-size and failure-count pairs of (10, 5), (15, 5), and (20, 5), reported relative efficiencies range from 0.9990 to 0.9998. The proposed method did not always return the exact exhaustive-search optimum, although its reported criterion values were very close. For the larger cases compared with variable neighborhood search, the reported relative efficiency is 1 for every case shown. The authors say cost-criterion efficiencies were also close to 1, but do not report their numerical values.

limitations_unstated: The numerical study uses a Weibull model and a limited set of example configurations, with no validation using field or experimental lifetime data. summary: The paper compares methods for predicting remaining useful life (RUL) while also estimating uncertainty, since an inaccurate or overconfident prediction can lead to poor maintenance decisions. It evaluates scalable Gaussian process approaches, including deep Gaussian processes (DGPs) and Deep Sigma Point Processes (DSPPs), alongside Monte Carlo dropout (MCD) and a feedforward neural network. The evaluation uses NASA's New Commercial Modular Aero-Propulsion System Simulation (N-CMAPSS) aircraft-engine data, with six training units and three held-out test units. The authors report that DSPP and MCD provide useful uncertainty estimates, which grow for early-life predictions and for a test unit with flight conditions unlike the training data. DSPP has the strongest probabilistic results overall, while MCD has the lowest point-prediction error.
key_results: On the test data, DSPP achieved the best negative log-likelihood (NLL) at 3.10, compared with 3.24 for DGP, 3.50 for stochastic variational Gaussian process (SVGP), and 4.26 for MCD. MCD had the lowest root mean squared error (RMSE), 7.31 cycles; DSPP and DGP had 7.38 and 7.37, respectively, while SVGP had 8.70 and the feedforward neural network had 7.71. DSPP and MCD both scored 0.56 on the alpha-lambda metric, and DSPP had the highest probabilistic alpha-lambda score at 0.53, compared with 0.48 for MCD, 0.46 for DGP, and 0.36 for SVGP. The authors also report that uncertainty decreased as engines approached end of life and was higher for the test unit with shifted operating conditions.

limitations_stated: The authors identify that their methods do not explicitly capture temporal correlations in the time-series data. They note that incorporating such correlations is relatively straightforward for the neural-network approach but not straightforward for the Gaussian-process methods.
limitations_unstated: The test evaluation covers only three held-out engines, with data from six training engines, so the results may not generalize to a broad operational fleet. future_work_unstated: Further work could test these predictors on operational aircraft-engine data and across more engines, flight profiles, and failure modes. summary: The paper studies how to estimate failure rates when products can fail from either of two competing causes and test records are incomplete because of censoring. It models the two independent latent lifetimes with exponential distributions and uses an improved adaptive type-II progressive censoring scheme with warning and maximum-time thresholds. The authors derive classical and Bayesian estimates and intervals, and propose criteria for choosing among censoring plans. They evaluate the methods in simulations and with laboratory jute-fiber breaking-strength data, where failure causes correspond to two gauge lengths. Their results favor Bayesian estimates with informative priors for estimation accuracy, while the preferred interval method depends on whether interval length or coverage is prioritized.
key_results: The simulation study used 10,000 generated samples, with sample sizes of 30 or 40, effective failure counts of 10 or 15, and true rate pairs of (0.6, 0.8) and (1, 1.5). For sample size 30, 10 effective failures, and censoring scheme I with rates (0.6, 0.8), informative-prior Bayesian estimates under squared error loss had mean squared errors of 0.012 and 0.027 for the two causes, compared with 0.051 and 0.129 for the maximum likelihood estimates. In that same setting, the highest posterior density interval lengths were 0.413 and 0.686, compared with asymptotic interval lengths of 1.214 and 1.489; the paper reports that bootstrap-t intervals generally had coverage closer to the nominal 95% level. In the jute-fiber example, censoring scheme I was preferred to scheme II by all three proposed optimality criteria, and the authors report that the highest posterior density intervals were shorter than the asymptotic and bootstrap intervals.

limitations_unstated: The model assumes independent exponential latent lifetimes for the two causes, so it may not represent dependent causes or failure rates that change over time. summary: The paper addresses weak generalization and unquantified prediction uncertainty in deep-learning approaches to remaining useful life (RUL) estimation. It combines a stochastic Wiener degradation process with a deep neural network (DNN) that learns future degradation trajectories and updates the drift as new measurements arrive. A long short-term memory and convolutional neural network combination (LSTM-CNN) predicts the trajectories, while the model represents both random noise and drift uncertainty. The authors test the method on the four C-MAPSS turbofan-engine benchmark subsets, each built from 21 sensor signals, training on FD002 and applying the model to the other subsets without retraining. The adaptive method has lower reported RUL prediction errors than the compared non-adaptive DNN and Wiener-process approaches, and its interpolation procedure calculates RUL distributions faster than the tested particle-filter implementation.
key_results: On FD002, the adaptive DNN achieved an RMSE of 16.25, compared with 17.71 for the non-adaptive DNN, 43.22 for the adaptive Wiener model, and 45.62 for the non-adaptive Wiener model; its reported PICP was 99.45 and MPIW was 81.27. When applied without retraining, its RMSE was 22.44 on FD001, 32.74 on FD003, and 21.12 on FD004, lower than the other reported methods on each subset. The authors report that their interpolation approximation produced a smooth RUL distribution with 20 interpolation lines and ran in 0.011 seconds, compared with 0.592 seconds for a particle filter with 1,000 particles in their numerical illustration. On the separate linear-process illustration, the particle filter with 1,000 particles produced a distribution close to the interpolation method's result.

limitations_stated: The authors do not give a dedicated limitations section for their proposed method. They state that analytical RUL distributions for complex nonlinear trajectories are generally intractable, which is why they introduce an approximation procedure.

future_work_unstated: Further work could incorporate operating conditions and component covariates directly, and model competing failure mechanisms and dependence among components at the system level. summary: The paper develops a framework to estimate the value of long-term structural health monitoring (SHM) for maintenance decisions on deteriorating bridges. It models the monitoring process from simulated acceleration measurements through output-only operational modal analysis (OMA) and Bayesian model updating (BMU), then uses updated deterioration estimates to revise structural failure probabilities. The deterioration is represented by a power law and tested in simulated two-span bridge cases involving scour at a support or corrosion at two locations. Annual synthetic monitoring data are generated from a finite-element model, and the decision rule triggers one repair when the estimated hazard exceeds a chosen threshold. The authors find that monitoring can reduce expected life-cycle costs, but its value varies by deterioration case and repair-cost ratio.
key_results: For the scour case, the reported value of information was 32,843, 42,270, and 4,815 for repair-to-failure cost ratios of 10⁻¹, 10⁻², and 10⁻³, respectively; the corresponding partial-perfect-information values were 35,013, 42,717, and 4,918. For corrosion, the value of information was 0, 1,458, and 108 at the same respective cost ratios, compared with partial-perfect-information values of 132, 2,871, and 497. Thus the corrosion monitoring achieved 51% and 22% of the partial-perfect-information value at ratios 10⁻² and 10⁻³, while the scour results were close to that upper benchmark. In the sensor-placement study, 24 sensors yielded a value of information of 4,614, or 60% of the partial-perfect-information value; 12 sensors yielded 2,711, or 35%.

limitations_stated: The authors note that the decision model permits only a single repair action and does not account for varying environmental effects such as temperature. limitations_unstated: The evaluation uses simulated bridge data with a model that is also used for inference, so it does not establish performance under model mismatch or real sensor and field conditions. summary: This paper develops experimental designs for accelerated degradation tests in which the degradation paths are described by linear mixed-effects models. It models repeated degradation measurements, unit-to-unit variation, and measurement error, and defines soft failure as a unit's mean degradation path reaching a threshold under normal use. The design objective is to minimize the asymptotic variance of an estimated failure-time quantile, with measurement times fixed for the main results. The authors derive stress designs for models with one or more stress variables and illustrate them using virtual parameter values rather than observed field data. Their main finding is that the stress allocation can be chosen as a c-optimal design for extrapolating the mean response to normal use, and this choice is optimal for every nondegenerate failure-time quantile in the fixed-time setting.
key_results: For the single-stress illustration, with normal-use stress −0.056, the optimal allocation puts 0.95 of units at the lowest stress and 0.05 at the highest stress. The uniform design on those two endpoints has efficiency 0.55, so the paper reports that it would require 81% more units to match the optimal design's accuracy. In the two-stress illustration, the optimal allocations across the four stress combinations are 0.58, 0.17, 0.19, and 0.06; the uniform design has efficiency 0.61 and requires 64% more units for equivalent accuracy. For the separate two-stress model without stress interaction, the uniform design has efficiency 0.49 relative to an optimal design and requires more than twice as many units for equivalent accuracy.

Repeated-measures degradation model: \[Y_{ij}=(f_1(x_i)\otimes f_2(t_j))^T\beta+f_2(t_j)^T\gamma_i+\epsilon_{ij}\] Y_ij is degradation for unit i at time t_j, x_i is its stress setting, f_1 and f_2 are the stress and time regression functions, beta is the aggregate parameter vector, gamma_i is the unit-specific random effect, and epsilon_ij is measurement error.

Asymptotic variance of a failure-time quantile estimator: \[\operatorname{aVar}(\widehat{t}_\alpha)=c^T M_\theta^{-1}c\] The asymptotic variance of the estimated quantile t_alpha is determined by c, the gradient of that quantile with respect to the model parameters, and M_theta, the information matrix for those parameters.

Stress-design criterion: \[\min_{\xi}\ c_1^T M_1(\xi)^{-1}c_1\] The design xi is selected to minimize the extrapolation criterion, where c_1 is the stress-regression vector at normal use and M_1(xi) is the information matrix for the stress model under that design.
limitations_stated: The authors note that the independent optimization of stress and time designs relies on their model assumptions, including complete interactions between stress and time and random effects associated with time but not stress. They state that design construction becomes more complicated when these assumptions do not hold, such as when interactions are absent or stress variables have random effects.
limitations_unstated: The illustrations use virtual parameter values rather than field measurements, so they do not establish that the proposed designs perform as expected for real products or under model misspecification. The analysis also depends on normal random effects and measurement errors, independent units, and extrapolating the specified degradation relationship to normal-use conditions; finite-sample performance is not demonstrated.
future_work_stated: The authors propose studying how departures from their assumptions affect optimal designs and developing designs robust to misspecified nominal parameters, including maximin-efficient and Bayesian designs. They also propose criteria for simultaneous estimation of multiple characteristics of the failure-time distribution.
future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be validation with field degradation data and finite-sample simulations that include realistic measurement schedules and departures from normality or independence. Further work could also examine additional failure mechanisms, varying operating conditions, and how the designs support system-level reliability decisions.

The data come from laboratory cycling experiments in the Ames Prognostics Center of Excellence randomized battery-use dataset; 11 cells were retained for analysis. The authors trained on one exhausted cell per group and tested predictions on other cells in that group. The regressions predicted capacity competitively with a deep learning comparator while using few parameters, allowing feature interpretation, and requiring substantially less training time.

summary: The paper develops a method for planning inspections and maintenance of deteriorating structural systems when component damage is interdependent and inspection information changes what is known about the system. The method searches over simple rule-based plans to minimize expected discounted life-cycle cost, then re-optimizes the plan after inspection results become available. It combines a Bayesian network representation of system reliability with Monte Carlo sampling and numerical optimization. The numerical illustration models fatigue in a simulated offshore wind turbine support frame with 22 weld hotspots over a 40-year service life. The adaptive plan reduced expected remaining cost in the illustrated no-damage case, while the authors report more generally that adaptation produced cost reductions of about 5–10% in their numerical application.
key_results: For the initial plan, the selected inspection interval was 7 years, with 9 hotspots inspected per campaign, and the estimated expected total life-cycle cost was 20.1 cost units. Its reported cost breakdown was 13.0 for system failure, 3.3 for inspection campaigns, 3.0 for component inspections, and 0.8 for repairs. After the first campaign at year 7 found no damage, the re-optimized plan used a 9-year interval and retained 9 hotspots per campaign; its expected remaining cost was 15.9, compared with 16.9 for continuing the original plan under the same inspection information, a reported gain of 1.0. This is a numerical illustration rather than a comparison against a field-tested or exact globally optimal plan.

limitations_stated: The authors state that the heuristic search produces only an approximately optimal plan, since it searches within a chosen subset of possible strategies. limitations_unstated: The method is demonstrated on simulated data for one benchmark frame, not on field inspection records, so the reported performance does not establish real-world predictive or cost accuracy. summary: When only early failures are observed in a life test, predicting later failure times can be important, but predicting each time separately does not account for the relationship between the predictions. The paper develops best linear unbiased predictors (BLUPs) for two future order statistics at once, choosing their coefficients to minimize the determinant of their prediction variance-covariance matrix. It derives the method for location-scale lifetime distributions and discusses cases where joint predictors do not exist. The numerical illustration uses normal order statistics, and the real-data example uses the first five failure times from a previously published data set. In that example, joint prediction has a positive overall efficiency gain compared with separate predictions across all reported comparisons.
key_results: For the real-data comparisons, determinant efficiency ranges from 0.9737 to 0.9877, while trace efficiency ranges from 0.9937 to 0.9992. The reported overall efficiency gains range from 0.0116 to 0.0200, and are positive in every comparison. These results compare joint predictors with the separate marginal predictors of Kaminsky and Nelson. The paper reports efficiency measures rather than a prediction-error evaluation on held-out failure times.
key_equations: Joint predictor coefficient optimization: \[\min_{a,b}\det\begin{pmatrix}a^\top\Sigma a&a^\top\Sigma b\\b^\top\Sigma a&b^\top\Sigma b\end{pmatrix}\quad\text{subject to}\quad a^\top\mathbf{1}=b^\top\mathbf{1}=1,\;a^\top\alpha=\alpha_s,\;b^\top\alpha=\alpha_t\] The vectors a and b are the two predictor coefficient vectors, Sigma is the covariance matrix of the observed standardized order statistics, 1 is the all-ones vector, alpha is the vector of their expected standardized values, and alpha_s and alpha_t are the expected standardized values of the two target order statistics; the transpose operation forms row vectors, and det denotes the determinant.
limitations_stated: The authors establish that joint prediction of more than two order statistics does not exist for their location-scale setup. They also state that joint prediction does not exist when the parent distribution belongs to a scale family.
limitations_unstated: The real-data demonstration is limited to one previously published data set assumed to follow a normal distribution, so it does not establish performance across other lifetime distributions or operating conditions. The paper compares efficiency measures but does not validate predictions against withheld failure times or report prediction intervals, leaving practical uncertainty in the predicted failure times unquantified.
future_work_stated: The authors propose developing an optimal compound design for joint prediction that uses both trace efficiency and determinant efficiency.
future_work_unstated: Further work could test the method on additional field and laboratory data, including cases with different failure mechanisms and changing operating conditions. It could also develop decision-focused prediction intervals and assess how joint predictions affect system-level reliability decisions.
