summary: This paper addresses the loss of accuracy and convergence that can occur when cross-entropy (CE) importance sampling estimates a full Gaussian covariance matrix for high-dimensional failure problems. It proposes updating the covariance only along the direction of the estimated mean of inputs conditional on failure, while leaving variance in other directions close to its initial value. The authors also introduce an improved cross-entropy (iCE) version of this projection approach. They evaluate the methods using simulated standard-normal inputs and four computational test problems: a linear limit-state function, a modified Ackley function, a portfolio-loss model, and a parabolic failure domain. Across these examples, the projection methods often produce useful probability estimates at dimensions where the conventional methods fail to converge, without requiring gradient evaluations.
key_results: In the linear example at dimension 30, conventional CE and iCE had relative bias close to minus 100%, while CE-m* and iCE-m* had absolute relative bias below 1% and coefficients of variation of 4.6% and 2.6%, respectively. At dimension 300 in that example, iCE-m* had relative bias of minus 0.2% and a coefficient of variation of 7.3%; conventional CE and iCE did not converge. For the modified Ackley example at dimension 200, iCE-m* had relative bias of minus 0.5% and a coefficient of variation of 9.1%, while conventional CE and iCE did not converge. In the portfolio-loss example at dimension 250, CE-m* had relative bias of minus 5.9% and a coefficient of variation of 60%, whereas iCE-m* had relative bias of 1.0% and a coefficient of variation of 110%; both conventional methods failed to converge.
key_equations: Projected covariance update: \[\Sigma=(1+\epsilon)I+(\hat v-1)rr^\top\] Sigma is the updated covariance matrix, epsilon is the small numerical stabilizer, I is the identity matrix, v-hat is the estimated variance along the projection direction, and r is the unit vector in the estimated conditional-mean direction.
limitations_stated: The method is motivated for a unimodal failure domain; the authors note that the mean direction may not be the best direction for updating variance. In their narrower-parabola example, the method does not converge because the resulting distribution does not fit the failure domain. They also state that they do not yet fully understand why the full covariance update can collapse, or theoretically establish why their method avoids that problem.
limitations_unstated: The evaluation is limited to simulated benchmark problems, including a constructed finance example, and does not establish performance on field or engineering-system data. The method relies on Gaussian auxiliary distributions and a single estimated direction, so its effectiveness may be limited when failures are multimodal or when several directions strongly shape the failure region.
future_work_stated: The authors propose stronger theoretical justification for the method and further investigation of why estimating fewer covariance terms may prevent covariance shrinkage. They also propose studying alternative projection directions, including directions related to covariance eigenvalues, and extending the approach to multimodal problems by combining it with existing methods.
future_work_unstated: The method could be evaluated on field reliability data and on engineering models with measured covariates and changing operating conditions. Further work could also develop automated ways to detect when one projection direction is inadequate, and test how the resulting probability estimates support system-level reliability and maintenance decisions.

summary: The paper addresses forecasting failure rates when data are sparse, unevenly distributed across engine types and ages, and related through shared engine designs. It models each ship engine’s failure-rate curve over age with a Bayesian hierarchical spline, sharing information across ships, engine types, and an engine archetype. The data are operational failure-rate records for 99 Republic of Korea Navy combat ships, grouped into five engine types and covering approximately 31 years; warranty-repair records from shipyards were unavailable. The model is compared with Prophet and autoregressive integrated moving average forecasting. The authors report lower average prediction errors for the hierarchical spline in the overall comparison and in tests involving new ships and unseen engine types, with some exceptions for individual types.
key_results: Using root mean square error (RMSE), the overall ship-level comparison gave 0.9475 for the hierarchical spline, compared with 0.9553 for autoregressive integrated moving average and 1.0395 for Prophet. The authors suggest application could save several million dollars based on the current budget, but they do not report a quantified cost evaluation.

limitations_stated: The authors state that preventive repairs, which may change failure patterns, are not included. They report a few low values for energy Bayesian fraction of missing information and effective sample size, and say improving these sampling diagnostics could improve model fit. Only combat ships were used because combat and non-combat ships have substantial operational differences.
limitations_unstated: Unavailable shipyard warranty-repair records mean the early-age failure rates may be undercounted, so the curves and comparisons may not represent full-life failure behavior. The evaluation uses one navy’s data and does not establish performance on independent fleets or future chronological periods; some test groups are also small. The Gaussian observation model and dependence structure may not capture overdispersed failure counts or correlated failures across ships, and the paper does not evaluate uncertainty calibration or actual spare-parts costs.
future_work_stated: The authors propose incorporating preventive repairs and the probability of failure after such repairs. They also propose improving sampling diagnostics and including categorical information to represent differences between combat and non-combat ships, which could enable use of a larger dataset.
future_work_unstated: Future studies could include maintenance history, operating environment, ship mission, and exposure measures as predictors, while modeling dependence among ships that share equipment or operating conditions. Testing the approach on other fleets and with chronological holdouts, then connecting predictive uncertainty to spare-parts and maintenance decisions, would establish whether the reported accuracy gains translate into operational benefit.

summary: The paper addresses prediction of future failures when field data are sparse, heavily censored or truncated, or divided among heterogeneous subpopulations. It models failure times with parametric lifetime distributions and uses Bayesian hierarchical models to share information across related subpopulations. The method produces prediction intervals for future failure counts within one subpopulation or across a whole population, and can incorporate changing risk sets and covariates. The authors apply it to heat-exchanger tubes, hard drives, and warranty returns, and assess interval coverage using simulated data. Their main finding is that hierarchical Bayesian prediction can provide useful intervals with few observed failures, with better performance as information increases and particularly good coverage for upper bounds across multiple groups.
key_results: For the heat-exchanger example, the data covered 3 plants and 300 tubes, with 11 observed failures; the informative prior led to more conservative future-failure intervals, and its lower bound exceeded 30 tubes at year 10. For Product A, the proportional hazards model's 95% intervals for Cluster 1 covered the observed monthly return counts 19 times out of 24, compared with 15 times out of 24 for the cumulative damage model, and were narrower on average. In the hard-drive holdout analysis, the reported weekly 95% intervals for Drive-Models 6 and 23 covered the observed counts; predictions were updated for 26 weeks to reflect changing risk sets. The simulation used 300 data sets per factor combination and found that coverage was generally closer to nominal levels for upper bounds than lower bounds, while prediction performance improved with more observed failures.
key_equations:
Conditional probability of failure in the prediction interval: \[\rho_{ig}=\frac{F(t_{w,ig};\theta_g)-F(t_{c,ig};\theta_g)}{1-F(t_{c,ig};\theta_g)}\] Here rho with indices i and g is the probability of failure for unit i in subpopulation g, F is its modeled failure-time distribution, t_c is the observation time, t_w is the future prediction time, and theta_g is the lifetime-model parameter set for subpopulation g.

Posterior predictive distribution of the future failure count: \[J(y)=\int J(y;\theta)f(\theta\mid t)\,d\theta\] Here J(y) is the predictive probability that the future failure count is at most y, J(y;theta) is that probability at parameters theta, f(theta given t) is the posterior density of the parameters given observed data t, and integration averages over parameter uncertainty.

Monte Carlo estimate of the predictive distribution: \[J(y)\approx\frac{1}{B}\sum_{j=1}^{B}J(y;\theta_j^*)\] Here J(y) is the predictive cumulative distribution, B is the number of posterior draws, j indexes a draw, theta_j star is the jth draw from the joint posterior distribution, and J(y;theta_j star) is the predictive probability evaluated at that draw.
limitations_stated: The authors assume units are exchangeable within each subpopulation and note that this can miss important covariates or facility batch effects. They also report that some hard-drive predictions substantially underestimated failures, and that both warranty-return models underestimated returns in June and July, possibly because claims were reported late.
limitations_unstated: The lifetime models assume independent units conditional on their parameters, so dependence from shared environments or common production batches could make prediction intervals miscalibrated. The data-based checks cover selected operational and warranty datasets, but the paper does not report a prospective field validation of the method or a held-out validation for the heat-exchanger example; results may also depend on the selected parametric lifetime distributions.
future_work_stated: The authors propose adding drive-status and other time-varying covariates, including delayed warranty reporting, and modeling retirements when removal from service is not directly observed. They also suggest extending predictions from event counts to the costs of future events.
future_work_unstated: Further work could test sensitivity to dependence across units, alternative failure mechanisms, and departures from the assumed lifetime distributions, then validate the resulting intervals prospectively across more products and operating environments. It could also connect predicted counts to explicit engineering decisions, such as spare-parts levels or inspection timing, while accounting for the consequences of over- and under-prediction.

summary: The paper reviews how maintenance practice developed from reactive repairs and fixed-interval replacement to prediction, then proposes an intelligent maintenance framework. The authors report that the BRNN signals approaching failure more robustly than a standard recurrent neural network (RNN), but provide no numerical accuracy or cost measurements.

The study classifies whether failure is likely within the next 30 days and shows BRNN predictions for engines approaching failure, including predictive-distribution bands from the 10th to 90th and 25th to 75th percentiles. The authors report that the BRNN indicates approaching failures with high probability; compared with it, the standard RNN raises failure probabilities earlier for some engines and has greater spread, which could lead to more frequent maintenance. summary: The paper addresses the loss of useful historical sensor information in long sequences and the limitations of training a model only to predict remaining useful life (RUL). It proposes an attention-based sequence-to-sequence model that uses an encoder, a decoder, and a predictor, and trains them jointly to forecast the next sensor sequence and estimate RUL. Attention weights the encoder's sequence of hidden states, while the predictor combines encoder and decoder features. The authors evaluate the method on four simulated aircraft-engine benchmark subsets from the Commercial Modular Aero-Propulsion System Simulation (C-MAPSS) data, using 30-cycle sliding windows and capped RUL labels. The method performs better than the compared approaches on most reported metrics and subsets, with a similar root mean square error (RMSE) to the strongest comparison on one subset.
key_results: On FD001 through FD004, the proposed method reports RMSE values of 12.63, 14.65, 11.44, and 16.66, respectively; its corresponding Score values are 243, 876, 263, and 1,074. On FD004, the paper reports improvements over the second-best method of 8.3% in RMSE and 29.7% in Score. The ablation study finds that the full model, with both attention and sequence reconstruction, performs best across all four subsets on both metrics; combining encoder and decoder features also performs best among the feature sets tested.

summary: Data-driven models used in Prognostics and Health Management (PHM) can lose accuracy when equipment or operating conditions differ from the data on which they were trained, leading to fine-tuning or retraining. This review defines transfer learning (TL), classifies its types, and surveys its use in diagnostics and prognostics. The reviewed approaches transfer model parameters, data examples, or learned features, and may optimize models to reduce differences between source and target data. The authors review studies using images, sensor time series, laboratory and simulation data, and industrial data; this paper itself presents no new dataset or experiment. They conclude that TL could reduce dependence on scarce labeled failure data, but its PHM use is still limited and requires careful application.
key_results: The paper reports no new performance measurements or pooled comparison across methods. It notes that only two TL-related papers had appeared in the reliability engineering and systems safety journal it discusses. All identified inductive TL studies used images and convolutional neural networks, while the review found only one fully unsupervised TL study in PHM. The reviewed studies include examples of improved fault diagnosis with limited target labels and transfer of models from simulation or laboratory settings to real-world data, but the review gives no shared numerical accuracy or prediction-error result.

limitations_unstated: The review does not report a systematic search protocol or a quantitative synthesis, so the completeness of the surveyed studies and the strength of comparisons are difficult to assess. future_work_stated: The authors propose exploring transfer between more diverse tasks, including diagnosis across similar systems with different manufacturers and condition-monitoring configurations. future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to compare transfer methods on common benchmarks that include field data, changes in operating conditions, and explicitly documented failure and censoring information. Further studies could also test for negative transfer across multiple sources and connect predictions to system-level reliability and maintenance decisions.

summary: Conventional one-shot device methods often assume only one failure cause, and the likelihood-based estimator can be sensitive to anomalous test groups. This paper models survival and failures from two competing causes using exponential lifetimes whose rates depend on stress. It develops robust weighted density power divergence estimators, Wald-type tests, and a data-driven way to select the robustness tuning parameter. The robust methods perform better when a test group is contaminated, while the likelihood-based estimator is more efficient on clean data; the real-data analysis selects a tuning value of 0.37.
key_results: Across simulations with 5,000 repetitions, the likelihood-based estimator generally had the best efficiency on uncontaminated data, while estimators with a positive tuning parameter were more robust to contaminated test groups. That robustness came with some loss of efficiency on clean data, and the authors found that the tuning value selected by their procedure increased as contamination increased. In contaminated-data simulations, the likelihood-based Wald tests were the least robust; empirical test levels for all methods were far from the nominal 0.05 level, whereas larger sample sizes improved level accuracy for clean data. summary: The paper develops a sequential strategy for accelerated life testing (ALT) that chooses both material settings and stress levels to identify the material with the best mean lifetime at target conditions. It models log lifetime with a linear log-normal model and handles right-censored test results using approximate Bayesian parameter updates. The next test is selected using expected improvement (EI), which targets better material selection rather than only more precise coefficient estimates. The method is assessed in simulated examples and a copper-alloy wear-test case study based on historical laboratory data, with a Gaussian process used to create a pseudo-simulator for the case study. EI-based selection achieves the highest correct-selection probability in the comparisons; the approximate update becomes less effective when censoring is high.
key_results: The authors prove that the approximate coefficient estimates are consistent under their stated assumptions. Across synthetic experiments with 100 replications, EI-based approaches generally achieve higher correct-selection probabilities than full factorial designs and sequential Bayesian D-optimal designs; the advantage is especially clear in difficult settings, including six material alternatives. Synthetic censoring rates shown in the paper range from 9.3% to 39.4%, and the authors report that the approximate update can perform poorly when censoring is around 30%. In the copper-alloy case study, the three observation times of 200, 300, and 500 produce censoring rates of 45.1%, 34.7%, and 29.7%; the exact-update EI approach performs best overall, while the approximate-update EI approach is competitive at lower censoring.

Expected-improvement selection criterion: \[>\] The paper selects the next material and stress setting to maximize the expected increase in the best posterior mean lifetime at the target stress levels; the expectation is over the predictive distribution for the next observation.
limitations_stated: The authors state that observation times are assumed to be fixed, although choosing them based on accumulated results could be more practical, especially under an experiment deadline. future_work_stated: The authors propose choosing each test unit’s observation time based on the results already collected, including accounting for deadlines. The double exponential model reports the same values except for mean error −0.035, so the two methods perform very similarly on this dataset. For the 48-cell dataset, the authors report that training-set size has little effect on prediction accuracy; using one complete battery alongside censored records also gives reasonable predictions, whereas censoring without a complete battery makes prediction below the censoring threshold unstable.

summary: The paper presents a data-driven method for estimating the remaining useful life (RUL) of aircraft engines from sensor histories. summary: The paper develops a goodness-of-fit test for checking whether right-censored time-to-failure data follow a specified distribution. Censoring can make ordinary empirical-distribution tests unreliable, while log-rank tests may lose power when hazards change over time. The method transforms observed times using the hypothesized distribution, spreads the contribution of censored observations over the range of possible failure times, and compares the resulting distribution with a uniform distribution using the maximum mean discrepancy. The test generally detects time-varying alternatives more effectively than the comparison tests while remaining close to the log-rank test for proportional hazards.
key_results: The simulations used 2,000 independent repetitions per experiment; at a sample size of 200, the three kernel-test variants generally produced type-I error rates near the nominal 5% level, including under 30% and 50% censoring. For periodic hazards with parameter pair (3, 1), sample size 200, and the reported censoring setting, power at the 5% level was about 89.8% for the kernel variants, compared with 31.7% for the Pearson test, 5.0% and 11.4% for the two log-rank tests, and 31.5% for the combined log-rank test. For proportional hazards, the authors report that the method is competitive with the classical log-rank test at sample size 30 and that their performances are nearly equal at sample size 100. Some comparisons at sample size 30 require caution: Pearson and combined log-rank tests sometimes had incorrect type-I error levels, making their reported power potentially over-optimistic.

Kernel test statistic: \[\operatorname{MMD}^2(F_{\mathrm{unif}},\widetilde F)=\frac{1}{n^2}\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{j=1}^n J((U_i,\Delta_i),(U_j,\Delta_j))\] The squared maximum mean discrepancy between the uniform distribution F_unif and the estimate F̃ is the average of pairwise contributions J for transformed observations (U_i, Δ_i), over a sample of size n.

limitations_unstated: The evaluation is entirely simulation-based, so performance on real industrial life-test or field data is not established. future_work_stated: The authors propose investigating better kernel choices to improve test power, including adapting ideas that choose features to maximize power. They also identify extending adaptive, linear-time test statistics to this setting as a direction of interest.
future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be validation on industrial field data with realistic censoring and operating-condition variation, including assessment of how sensitive calibration is to informative censoring. The results show estimates comparable to reference simulations and to active Kriging, using substantially fewer evaluations than direct simulation in the examples. The frame case also shows that the method can provide useful uncertainty bounds when the competing active Kriging analysis does not converge within its evaluation budget.

summary: The paper develops inference for two competing failure causes when data are collected using generalized progressive hybrid censoring, which combines a time limit, a target number of failures, and planned removals. It assumes the cause-specific lifetimes are independent exponential distributions with different mean lifetimes. If no failures from a cause are observed, its maximum likelihood estimate does not exist; when only a few failures occur for a cause, a finite exact confidence interval may also be unavailable. The authors derive maximum likelihood and Bayesian estimates and confidence or credible intervals, and assess them with simulated data and a radiation-exposed mouse data set. In the simulations, the Bayesian estimates generally have lower bias and mean squared error than the maximum likelihood estimates, while bootstrap confidence intervals are presented as a practical alternative to exact intervals.
key_results: In 5,000 simulation replications per setting, with mean lifetimes of 1 and 1.3, sample sizes of 20 or 30, and three removal schemes, the authors report that estimation bias and mean squared error generally decrease as sample size and effective sample size increase. For sample size 20, target failure count 14, and the third removal scheme, the mean squared error for cause 1 was 0.200; the exact and bootstrap interval lengths were 2.173 and 2.082, with coverage of 96% and 94%, respectively. For cause 2 under the same setting, the mean squared error was 0.482; the exact interval was unavailable in 25 replications, while exact and bootstrap interval coverage was 96% and 95%. In the mouse data example, there were 7 failures from cause 1 and 18 from cause 2; the estimated mean lifetimes were 4,137.429 and 1,609. For cause 1, the reported exact, bootstrap, and highest posterior density interval endpoints were 2,017.686 to 10,397.358, 2,061.129 to 12,220.355, and 1,715.194 to 7,480.241; for cause 2, they were 1,018.497 to 2,790.006, 976.663 to 2,749.781, and 939.656 to 2,363.621.

Maximum likelihood estimate for cause 1: \[\widehat{\theta}_1=\frac{W}{D_1}\] Here the estimated mean lifetime for cause 1 is W divided by D 1, where W is total weighted exposure time and D 1 is the observed number of cause 1 failures; the estimate exists only when D 1 is greater than zero.
limitations_stated: The authors state that exact confidence intervals may not exist when the observed number of failures from a cause is very low, usually 1 or 2 in their simulations. They also could not prove analytically the monotonicity needed to construct those intervals, and the analysis is restricted to two independent exponential failure causes.
limitations_unstated: The model assumes independent cause-specific exponential lifetimes, so it does not represent dependence between causes or changing failure rates over time. The single mouse example is illustrative rather than an independent validation on operational field data, and the paper does not assess how conclusions change under misspecified lifetime distributions or other operating conditions.
future_work_stated: The authors propose developing exact inference for competing risks using the spline approach and extending the model to Weibull cause-specific lifetimes. They describe the latter as work in progress.
future_work_unstated: Future studies could evaluate the methods on independent field reliability data and assess robustness when failure rates are not constant or latent causes are dependent. summary: This paper studies how to estimate rare failure probabilities when engineering simulations are expensive and have many uncertain inputs. The authors model the simulation response with a canonical low-rank approximation (LRA), built from sums of products of univariate polynomial functions, and compare it with sparse polynomial chaos expansions (PCE). They test the methods on four simulated examples: a beam, a truss, a heat-conduction model with a spatially varying coefficient, and a frame, with input dimensions from 5 to 53. The surrogate models are built from relatively small experimental designs and then sampled computationally to estimate response distributions and failure probabilities. Across these examples, LRA generally estimates extreme response probabilities more accurately than sparse PCE when the experimental design is small relative to the input dimension, while also providing a broader probabilistic description of the response.
key_results: For the beam example, with 30 original-model evaluations, LRA estimated a reliability index of 4.32 for the largest threshold, compared with the analytical value of 4.25, a relative error smaller than 2%; sparse PCE did not estimate the corresponding failure probability at that design size. For the truss, with 50 evaluations, LRA estimated failure probabilities down to 4.73 × 10^-6, against an importance-sampling reference of 3.90 × 10^-6, and its reliability-index differences from reference were no more than 3%. For the heat-conduction model, LRA with 500 evaluations gave failure probabilities of 3.22 × 10^-4 and 7.35 × 10^-5 for the two highest temperature thresholds studied; the authors could not afford reference evaluations of the original model at those thresholds. For the frame, LRA’s reliability-index error stayed below 5% with 500 evaluations and below 4% with 1,000, while sparse PCE errors at the largest threshold exceeded 10% and 5%, respectively. The authors also report that the number of unknowns in LRA grows linearly with input dimension, unlike the full polynomial expansion, and that the surrogate can be reused for different thresholds without further evaluations of the original model.

limitations_unstated: The evidence comes from four simulated examples, including finite-element models, rather than field measurements or operational failure data, so performance in real infrastructure settings is not established. summary: Random failure events make the Net Present Value (NPV) of a maintenance strategy uncertain, while repeatedly running the VME simulator across all possible strategies is computationally expensive. The paper models the simulator’s full NPV distribution by emulating its quantile functions, representing them with selected basis functions and Gaussian process metamodels. It tests the approach on a toy simulator and on simulated maintenance decisions for four identical systems at different power plants, using replacement dates and a spare-system recovery date as inputs. Directly optimizing the metamodel can select a poor strategy, so the authors introduce an adaptive search method called Quantile Function Expected Improvement (QFEI). In the VME study, QFEI found a strategy close to the best one in the tested search set with 50 additional simulator evaluations, although the assessment is limited to simulated data and a restricted candidate set.
key_results: For the toy problem, QFEI found the exact maximizing strategy in 22 of 30 trials; in the other 8 trials it found the reported near-optimal alternative. For the VME case, optimizing the median directly from the metamodel performed poorly: the true maximum was 0.82, while the metamodel maximum was 0.42, with a reported relative error of 5.4%. For the 40th quantile in the VME study, the best value in the search set was -1.72, compared with -1.95 in the initial design; after 50 QFEI iterations, the selected strategy had a value of -1.74. Across 50 repetitions with different initial designs, the selected strategy was always among the five best points in the tested set.

limitations_stated: The authors describe the work as a first attempt and state that the QFEI algorithm has no guarantee of convergence. Their application uses a restricted candidate set rather than the full input space, and they say that further testing is needed.
limitations_unstated: The method is evaluated using simulator-generated outputs rather than observed plant or maintenance data, so its practical accuracy for real operating fleets is not established. The tested maintenance inputs are a small set of discrete dates for four identical systems, which gives limited evidence about different assets, dependencies among plants, or changing operating conditions.
future_work_stated: The authors propose varying the number of Monte Carlo runs, replacing the random initial sample with a space-filling design, and improving computation so the method can handle larger candidate sets and more inputs. They also propose optimizing multiple quantiles, accounting for uncertainty in estimated model parameters, applying the method to more complex cases, and studying robust optimization with environmental inputs treated as uncertainty.
future_work_unstated: Future studies could validate the predicted quantiles and selected strategies against field maintenance, failure, and cost records, including uncertainty in those records. They could also test correlated system failures and changing operating conditions, and assess how the optimized decisions perform for the fleet as a whole rather than for the tested systems and candidate dates.

summary: This paper develops truncated-life-test acceptance plans for lots whose unit lifetimes follow an inverse Weibull distribution. The comparable single plan requires 51 units and allows 11 failures, so the reported double plan uses fewer units on average. In the ball-bearing example, 40 groups of 10 units are used, for a total of 400 units. For the insulating-fluid data, the inverse Weibull fit has an estimated shape parameter of 1.05411 and scale parameter of 32.3524; the authors use a shape value of 1.05 to construct example plans.

Group-plan lot acceptance probability: \[P_a(p)=\left[\sum_{i=0}^{c}\binom{r}{i}p^i(1-p)^{r-i}\right]^g\] Here Pa is the probability of accepting the lot, p is the unit failure probability, r is the number of units per group, c is the maximum failures allowed in a group, g is the number of groups, and i counts failures within a group.

limitations_unstated: The plans rely on a fixed inverse Weibull shape parameter, but the paper’s practical example estimates that parameter from only 11 historical breakdown times and does not propagate its estimation uncertainty through the design. future_work_unstated: Future studies could test the plans with larger, independent data sets and prospective field-lot decisions, while accounting for uncertainty in the fitted shape parameter. summary: This paper derives reliability expressions for coherent systems that can fail when a specified active component fails and are equipped with one general standby component. The standby begins in a cold state, switches to a warm state after a fixed time, and may be activated when the system fails; its condition after warm operation is represented through a virtual-age model. The authors consider perfect switching, switching that can fail, and a random warm-up period. Their results use independent, identically distributed active-component lifetimes and an independent standby lifetime, and are theoretical rather than estimated from lifetime data. A numerical illustration shows the reliability of one example system with and without standby protection, but the paper does not report numerical accuracy or quantified reliability gains.
key_results: The authors derive reliability formulas for general coherent systems using the system signature, and give a more explicit formula for a k-out-of-n system. They also show how imperfect switching changes the reliability contribution from the standby: it is multiplied by the probability that switching succeeds. For their three-component illustration, the system signature is (1/3, 2/3, 0); the plotted example uses exponential component distributions with rate 2, warm-environment and virtual-age functions equal to time divided by 2, and fixed switching times of 0 and 0.5. In that illustration, the plotted reliability with standby is higher than without standby, but no numerical improvement value is reported.

limitations_unstated: The derivations assume independent, identically distributed active-component lifetimes and an independent standby lifetime, so they do not address common-cause failures or dependence among components. summary: The paper proposes a model for residual lifetime when units have different, randomly varying ages. It forms a weighted average of the baseline unit’s residual lifetime distributions over the random ages. The model is intended for settings such as populations of used devices and components that remain alive after a system failure. They show that some aging properties are preserved by the model, while certain positive aging properties need not be preserved.

summary: The paper presents a Bayesian nonparametric method for estimating reliability in systems made from components arranged in series or parallel. Component or subsystem failure-time data, including right-censored observations, are used to build and update beta-Stacy process models, which are combined by matching their first two moments. The method can combine information from components, subsystems, and the full system, while avoiding Markov chain Monte Carlo for its main posterior calculations. It is evaluated using simulated aircraft-propulsion data and an industrial example involving a six-component product; the industrial data are obfuscated. In simulation, the method is less accurate than a correctly specified parametric model but more accurate and less biased than the misspecified parametric model, and the authors report substantially faster computation.
key_results: Across 30 simulated data sets, each with 30 observations from each component, subsystem, and full system and approximately 15% right censoring, the method's mean absolute error was 0.0311 and average bias was 0.0021. The correctly specified parametric model had mean absolute error 0.0179 and average bias 0.0048; the misspecified parametric model had mean absolute error 0.0391 and average bias 0.0280. The authors report that the nonparametric posterior took under 2 seconds, compared with about 45 minutes for 10,000 Markov chain Monte Carlo draws for the parametric models. In the industrial example, analysis of the six-component series system took approximately 1.88 seconds; its posterior mean lifetime was 716.7, median was 330.0, and 95th percentile was 2849.0.
key_equations:

limitations_stated: The model assumes that components are independent; violations can reduce accuracy. It does not handle interval-censored data, and the authors note that doing so would incur substantial computational cost because they know of no conjugate model for that data type.
limitations_unstated: The system-level process created by combining components is approximated as a beta-Stacy process by matching only its first two moments, so the approximation may not preserve other features of the system lifetime distribution. The industrial example does not provide direct validation on unmodified field data: the data are proprietary and disguised, and the analyzed component data were generated from fitted Weibull distributions.
future_work_stated: The authors propose exploring copula models to account for dependence among components. They also propose extending the method to interval-censored reliability data, while noting the likely computational cost.
future_work_unstated: Further work could test the method on independently reported, unmodified field data and assess how well its uncertainty intervals are calibrated, especially in the lifetime tail. summary: Sales dates for unreturned products are often unknown when manufacturers sell through retailers, so field failure records may omit both sales lag and lifetime. The paper models the joint distributions of sales lag and product lifetime while accounting for a warranty limit and the end of the observation period. It proposes a stochastic expectation-maximization method that imputes missing values and updates the distribution parameters. The method is evaluated using simulations and three real field datasets, including furnace, automobile-component, and telecommunications data. The authors find that it can estimate parameters in settings where direct likelihood maximization is unstable, while very high missing-data rates can still make lifetime estimates unreliable.
key_results: Across simulations with 5,000 replications, the proposed method estimated parameters for dependent and independent sales lag and lifetime models, and estimates were generally more accurate with longer warranty periods. In a comparison with Ghosh’s imputation method, the proposed method had smaller biases and root mean square errors in many tested settings and required less computation; for the furnace data it took 12.28 seconds, compared with 72.12 seconds for that method. With 2,000 units, direct maximization failed to converge when more than 80% of data were missing; at a 94.7% missing rate, increasing the batch size to 20,000 reduced the reported relative root mean square errors for the sales-lag rate, lifetime scale, and lifetime shape estimates from 32.2%, 26.1%, and 18.2% to 15.1%, 13.2%, and 6.0%. In the automobile example, 66 claims were observed among 589 units, and the fitted lognormal sales-lag and Weibull lifetime model had an Akaike information criterion of 1165.0. For the telecommunications data, 98.6% of units were missing and the lifetime parameter traces were unstable, which the authors interpret as possible evidence of insufficient information or estimation breakdown.

limitations_stated: The authors report that when missingness is extremely high, such as 97% in their simulation, the root mean square error for a lifetime parameter becomes large and the method may break down. In the telecommunications example, the lifetime parameter traces were very unstable, suggesting large estimation bias or variance, insufficient information, or possible breakdown.
limitations_unstated: The core likelihood assumes that failures within warranty are reported without delay and that the units share the specified parametric model; departures from these assumptions could bias the estimates. Although the paper demonstrates the method on real datasets, the examples do not provide independent ground-truth parameter values against which to assess real-world estimation accuracy, and the telecommunications lifetime results show how weakly identified parameters can remain despite extensive computation.

summary: The paper extends Bayesian estimation for a general failure-rate model in which the failure rate can represent several lifetime patterns. It estimates the model's two nonnegative parameters while allowing them to be dependent through a Farlie-Gumbel-Morgenstern joint prior. The authors derive estimators under squared error, linex, and entropy loss using type-II right-censored failure-time data, with the shape parameter and prior marginal distributions treated as known. They evaluate the method using simulated data generated with Markov chain Monte Carlo and report estimator summaries, variances, and empirical Bayes risks. The simulations show that results depend on the assumed parameter dependence and loss function, but the paper does not establish accuracy on field data or compare estimates with known true parameter values.
key_results: The simulation tables report estimates for varying sample sizes, censoring counts, model parameters, and loss-function settings, rather than estimation errors against known parameter values. For sample size 50 and 15 observed failures, the reported squared-error empirical Bayes risk falls from 4.320078 at rho equal to 0 to 3.628694 at rho equal to 0.5. At those same settings, linex risk falls from 123.9033 to 36.62481, while entropy risk changes from 0.3094569 to 0.3146239. The authors also report that estimator variances generally decrease as sample size increases, and that the linex estimates depend on their loss-shape parameters.
key_equations:

Dependent joint prior: \[h(a,b)=f(a)g(b)+\rho f(a)g(b)[1-2F(a)][1-2G(b)]\] Here h is the joint density of a and b, f and g are their marginal densities, F and G are the corresponding distribution functions, and rho is the known dependence parameter.

Bayes estimators under the three loss functions: \[\hat{x}_{SE}=E[x\mid t],\qquad \hat{x}_{L}=-c^{-1}\log E[e^{-cx}\mid t],\qquad \hat{x}_{E}=\{E[x^{-1}\mid t]\}^{-1},\quad x\in\{a,b\}\] Here x is either parameter a or b, t denotes the observed censored data, E is posterior expectation, c is the linex loss parameter, and the subscripts SE, L, and E identify squared-error, linex, and entropy loss estimators, respectively.
limitations_stated: None stated.
limitations_unstated: The analysis assumes a known shape parameter, known exponential marginal prior distributions, a known dependence parameter, and statistically independent unit failure times; results may be sensitive when these assumptions do not hold. Evaluation is simulation-only and does not test performance against field data or report estimation errors against known true parameter values. The treatment is limited to type-II censoring and does not assess other failure mechanisms or operating-condition effects.
future_work_stated: None stated.
future_work_unstated: Future work could estimate the shape and prior dependence parameters rather than fixing them, and test robustness to alternative prior distributions, failure mechanisms, and operating conditions. The estimators should also be evaluated with field data and compared using parameter-error measures and reliability decisions for systems of multiple components.

summary: The paper develops a step-stress accelerated degradation test in which all test units move to a higher stress level when a scheduled measurement shows that at least one unit has crossed a chosen degradation threshold. It models degradation with a gamma process and relates the process rate to stress using an Arrhenius relationship. The design jointly selects the threshold, number of units, measurement interval, and number of measurements to estimate a chosen lifetime quantile precisely within a cost budget. The authors illustrate the method using published carbon-film resistor information and use simulated data to examine the stability of parameter estimates. In their illustration, the optimal design uses 13 units, 52 time units between measurements, and 7 measurements for all considered quantiles.
key_results: For the carbon-film resistor illustration, the optimal design was 13 units, a measurement interval of 52 time units, and 7 measurements, with total experiment time of 1456 hours. For the median lifetime quantile, the optimal threshold was 0.0502 and the minimum coefficient of variation was 0.1300; the estimated median was 336650.3. Across probability levels from 0.1 to 0.9, estimated quantiles ranged from 292795.6 to 387073.5, and the minimum coefficient of variation declined from 0.1389 to 0.1218. A simulation with 10,000 iterations was used to assess parameter-estimate stability under selected designs, and the authors reported stability for small departures from the optimal plan.
key_equations:
Gamma degradation increments: \[\Delta L(t\mid S_j)\sim \operatorname{Ga}(\alpha_j\Delta t,\beta)\] The degradation increment ΔL over time increment Δt at stress level S_j has a gamma distribution with shape α_j times Δt and scale β.

Stress-rate relationship: \[\alpha_j=\exp\left(a+\frac{b}{273+S_j}\right)\] The gamma-process rate α_j at stress level S_j is determined by parameters a and b through the exponential relationship shown, with 273 as the constant used by the authors.

Experimental cost: \[TC(n,f,M)=C_{op}fM+C_{mea}nM+C_{it}n\] Total cost TC is operating cost per unit time C_op times measurement interval f times number of measurements M, plus measurement cost C_mea times number of units n times M, plus item cost C_it times n.

Quantile-estimation design objective: \[\min_{n,f,M,\omega_1}\operatorname{Avar}(\hat{\xi}_p)\quad\text{subject to}\quad TC(n,f,M)\leq C_b\] The design minimizes the asymptotic variance Avar of the estimated lifetime quantile ξ_p over the number of units n, measurement interval f, number of measurements M, and threshold ω_1, subject to total cost TC not exceeding budget C_b.
limitations_stated: The authors state that the optimized design depends on initial parameter estimates, but report that their algorithm is robust to departures from those estimates. They also note that the estimates are stable for small departures from the optimized test plan.
limitations_unstated: The threshold-crossing time probabilities are approximated, and the model assumes independent gamma-process increments with a shared scale parameter; the paper does not quantify how violations of these assumptions affect the design. The resistor example uses parameter estimates from earlier work and simulated validation rather than a new field-data validation, so performance under real operating conditions remains untested.
future_work_stated: None stated.
future_work_unstated: Future work could test the design using field data and assess whether the stress-rate relationship remains reliable when accelerated conditions differ substantially from normal use. Extensions could also model unit-to-unit variation, additional degradation mechanisms and covariates, or system-level failure, and evaluate how design choices support reliability decisions beyond quantile estimation.

summary: This paper introduces a parametric lifetime model formed by combining a linear failure rate distribution with a power-series distribution for the number of components in a series system. It models the time to the first component failure and is intended to represent a wider range of hazard patterns than the basic linear failure rate model. The authors derive distributional properties and likelihood-based estimation procedures, including an expectation-maximization algorithm. They evaluate estimation through simulations and compare model fits on lifetimes of 40 leukemia patients. In that medical data example, the linear failure rate-geometric model fits better than the alternative models considered.
key_results: The simulation used 1,000 samples for each of 12 parameter settings, with sample sizes of 30, 70, 100, and 200. The authors report convergence in all simulated cases; standard errors decreased as sample size increased, and information-based standard errors were close to the simulated values for larger samples. For the 40-patient leukemia data, the linear failure rate-geometric model had a deviance of 604.0, Akaike information criterion of 610.0, and Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic of 0.0831 with p-value 0.9450. Its Akaike information criterion was lower than those reported for the generalized linear failure rate model (616.7), linear failure rate model (616.0), exponential-geometric model (611.5), Rayleigh-geometric model (611.1), Rayleigh model (614.0), and exponential model (644.9).
key_equations:
Cumulative distribution of the proposed lifetime family: \[F(x)=1-\frac{C\!\left(\theta\exp\left[-ax-\frac{b}{2}x^2\right]\right)}{C(\theta)}\] F is the cumulative distribution function, x is lifetime, a and b are the underlying rate parameters, theta is the power-series parameter, and C is the power-series normalizing function.

Density of the proposed lifetime family: \[f(x)=\frac{\theta(a+bx)\exp\left[-ax-\frac{b}{2}x^2\right]C'\!\left(\theta\exp\left[-ax-\frac{b}{2}x^2\right]\right)}{C(\theta)}\] f is the probability density, x is lifetime, a and b are the underlying rate parameters, theta is the power-series parameter, C is the power-series normalizing function, and C prime is its derivative.
limitations_stated: None stated.
limitations_unstated: The estimation procedure is presented for complete samples, and the paper does not demonstrate how the method handles right-censored or interval-censored lifetimes, which are common in reliability studies. The real-data check uses one medical cohort rather than operational equipment data, so fit performance under engineering failure mechanisms and changing operating conditions is not established.
future_work_stated: None stated.
future_work_unstated: Future work could evaluate the model with censored reliability data and field datasets from different equipment types, while checking whether the assumed component lifetimes and component count are appropriate. It could also extend the model to include operating-condition covariates or competing failure mechanisms and assess how estimates support maintenance or replacement decisions.

summary: The paper addresses the mismatch that can arise when laboratory accelerated life test results do not predict field failures well. It models unobserved differences in field operating environments as a gamma-distributed frailty, linking a laboratory Weibull lifetime model to a field failure-time distribution. The authors develop joint likelihood-based inference using laboratory and warranty-return data, and optimize accelerated test plans to estimate field lifetime quantiles or warranty failure probabilities. They evaluate the methods with simulations and data from Appliance B, including laboratory tests and field warranty records. Their analysis finds that accounting for environmental heterogeneity can improve field fit and produce test plans different from plans that assume uniform operating conditions.
key_results: For Appliance B, the laboratory data comprised 10 tested units, with 8 observed failures; the field data covered 4,708 units and 93 wear failures. For field data, the Burr-XII model fit better than the Weibull model by the Akaike information criterion, with values of 1,953.5 and 1,958.4, respectively. The test of a common Weibull shape parameter gave a ratio estimate of 0.585 and a probability value of 0.217; the likelihood-ratio test gave a probability value of 0.244, and neither test rejected the gamma frailty model. In the simulation, for one reported setting, the proposed test's estimated Type I error was 0.057 at a nominal level of 0.05, compared with 0.072 for the likelihood-ratio test; for the stated field-quantile planning example, the optimal plan was (0.338, 0.649), with an asymptotic standard deviation of 3.23, versus (0.419, 0.766) when heterogeneity was ignored.
key_equations: Marginal field failure-time distribution under gamma frailty: \[F_T(t)=1-\left[1+\frac{(t/\alpha)^\beta}{\mu}\right]^{-k}\] F_T is the field failure-time cumulative distribution, t is time, alpha and beta are the laboratory Weibull scale and shape parameters, and mu and k are the gamma frailty rate and shape parameters.
limitations_stated: The authors state that the shape-parameter ratio test is exact under complete or Type II censored data, but only approximately pivotal under Type I censoring. Their optimal-plan example also assumes that the new product vintage will encounter the same operating environments and environmental effects as the previous generation.
limitations_unstated: The single, unit-constant frailty compresses potentially different environmental factors into one random effect, so the model does not distinguish which conditions drive failures or represent within-unit changes over time. The paper does not establish that censoring is non-informative or assess the model on multiple independent field populations; the real-data illustration is limited to one product and one failure mode.
future_work_stated: None stated. The authors report that supplementary work develops inverse Gaussian and uniform frailty models and an inference procedure that considers those models alongside the gamma model, but they do not present these as future research directions.
future_work_unstated: Future studies could validate the approach across more products, failure modes, and field populations, and compare predicted failures with later warranty outcomes. They could also incorporate measured environmental and usage covariates, time-varying conditions, and dependence among components or units, then assess how these extensions change test planning and warranty decisions.

summary: The paper estimates stress-strength reliability using the generalized linear failure rate distribution (GLFRD), which can represent increasing, decreasing, or bathtub-shaped hazard rates. It models reliability as the probability that random stress is lower than random strength, so the complementary probability represents failure. The authors derive maximum likelihood and Bayesian estimators, confidence and credible intervals, and methods for progressively type-II censored samples. They evaluate the methods with simulations and breaking-strength data for jute fibers at two gauge lengths. In the reported simulations, estimation error generally decreases as sample sizes increase; the real-data reliability estimate is 0.5506.
key_results: In simulations with unknown common scale parameters, the maximum likelihood estimator (MLE) had mean squared errors (MSEs) of 0.0086 to 0.0093 at sample sizes 15 and 15, compared with 0.0025 to 0.0026 at sample sizes 50 and 50. The authors report that asymptotic interval coverage can be poor for small samples; for one reported case with sample sizes 15 and 15, coverage was 0.788, while the target was 95%. For a generated sample of size 20 from each distribution, the unknown-scale MLE was 0.6449 and the percentile bootstrap interval was 0.4777 to 0.7976; with known scales, the estimate was 0.7283 and the interval was 0.6064 to 0.8442. For the jute-fiber data, the complete-data MLE of reliability was 0.5506 with a 95% confidence interval of 0.4232 to 0.6717, and the Bayesian estimate was 0.5517 with a 95% credible interval of 0.4418 to 0.6544. Among three censoring schemes applied to those data, scheme 3 gave an estimate of 0.5298, which the authors report as closer to the complete-data estimate than the other two schemes.
key_equations: Reliability with common scale parameters: \[R=\frac{\alpha}{\alpha+\beta}\] R is the probability that stress is less than strength, alpha is the strength-distribution shape parameter, and beta is the stress-distribution shape parameter when both distributions share known scale parameters.
limitations_stated: For progressively type-II censored samples, the paper reports only maximum likelihood estimation and confidence intervals for the case with common, known scale parameters. The authors say Bayesian methods for the censored case require more sophisticated simulation and are work in progress.
limitations_unstated: The model assumes that stress and strength are independent and follow the selected parametric distribution, so dependence or a poorly fitting lifetime model could affect the reliability estimate. The real-data illustration uses one laboratory breaking-strength dataset, and the paper does not validate the approach on field reliability data or assess sensitivity to different failure mechanisms or operating conditions.
future_work_stated: The authors propose extending the censored-data analysis to Bayesian estimation using simulation methods. They also state that they are developing Bayesian approaches based on higher-order asymptotics, pseudo-likelihoods, and matching priors, intended to improve small-sample inference and reduce nuisance-parameter elicitation and computational integration.
future_work_unstated: Future work could test whether the independence assumption is appropriate when stress and strength share environmental or manufacturing influences, and could incorporate measured covariates and changing operating conditions. Validation on field data and evaluation of how reliability estimates inform component or system-level decisions would also strengthen the engineering usefulness of the methods.

summary: This paper develops a goodness-of-fit test of whether time-to-failure data follow an exponential distribution when some units are progressively removed from the test after failures. The method expresses the joint Rényi entropy of progressively Type-II censored failure times through a single integral involving the hazard function, then estimates that entropy from the observed data. The authors use the estimated entropy to construct a Rényi-Kullback-Leibler (R-KL) information test statistic and compare it with an existing Kullback-Leibler test. They evaluate the tests using simulated lifetime distributions with increasing, decreasing, and nonmonotone hazards, and illustrate the method with insulating-fluid breakdown data. In the reported simulations, the proposed test generally has higher power than the comparison test.
key_results: The authors estimated critical values and powers using 10,000 Monte Carlo simulations, and selected alpha equal to 0.4; the power comparisons use a 10% significance level. Across the reported simulation tables for sample sizes of 10, 20, and 30, the proposed test usually had greater power than the existing test against the tested Gamma, Weibull, Beta, and log-normal alternatives, though not in every individual comparison. For example, at sample size 20 with 10 observed failures and the scheme that removes 10 units after the first failure, the proposed and comparison tests had powers of 0.703 and 0.672 against the increasing-hazard Gamma alternative, and 0.231 and 0.039 against the decreasing-hazard Weibull alternative. For the insulating-fluid example, the proposed statistic was 0.2422 and the reported p-value was 0.9737, which the authors interpret as strong evidence consistent with exponentiality.
key_equations:
Joint entropy representation: \[H^{\alpha}_{1\cdots m:m:n}=-\log c+\frac{1}{1-\alpha}\sum_{j=1}^{m}\log\int f_{X_{j:m:n}}(x)h(x)^{\alpha-1}[1-F_{X_{j:m:n}}(x)]^{\alpha-1}\,dx\] Here H is the joint entropy, alpha is its order, c is the censoring-density normalizer, m is the observed failure count, j indexes those failures, and f, h, and F with the order-statistic subscripts are the density, hazard, and cumulative distribution function of the jth observed failure time.

Exponentiality test statistic: \[T^{\alpha}(w,n,m)=-\frac{H^{\alpha}(w,n,m)}{n}+\frac{m}{n}\left[\log\left(\frac{1}{m}\sum_{j=1}^{m}(R_j+1)X_{j:m:n}\right)+1\right]\] Here T is the test statistic, alpha is the Rényi order, w is the estimation window, n is the number of units tested, m is the observed failure count, H is the estimated entropy, j indexes failures, R_j is the removal count after failure j, and X_j:m:n is the corresponding failure time.

Exponential mean estimate: \[\hat{\theta}=\frac{1}{m}\sum_{j=1}^{m}(R_j+1)X_{j:m:n}\] Here theta is the exponential mean estimated by maximum likelihood, m is the observed failure count, j indexes failures, R_j is the removal count after failure j, and X_j:m:n is the corresponding failure time.
limitations_stated: The authors state that the test statistics have intractable sampling distributions, so they obtain percentage points by Monte Carlo simulation. They also select alpha by trial and error and identify development of an optimal method for choosing it as a possible improvement.
limitations_unstated: The power evidence is based on selected simulated alternatives and censoring schemes, with only one illustrative real-data example; it does not establish performance on broader field or production data. The method and comparisons rely on a common lifetime distribution for units and prespecified progressive removal schemes, and the paper does not assess sensitivity to departures from those conditions or the computational burden of repeatedly simulating critical values.
future_work_stated: The authors propose extending the approach to other censoring schemes and testing distributions beyond the exponential, naming Pareto, log-normal, and Weibull distributions. They also propose developing an optimality algorithm to choose alpha by maximizing power.
future_work_unstated: Further work could assess calibration and power using larger collections of field and laboratory life-test data, and test robustness to heterogeneous units and changing operating conditions. It could also extend the test to competing failure mechanisms and system-level reliability decisions, and compare the simulation cost with practical alternatives for obtaining critical values.

summary: Common-cause failures can make redundant systems less reliable, but data on joint failures are often sparse, and estimated failure rates can be very sensitive to prior choices, especially when some event counts are zero. The authors model uncertainty in the fractions of failures involving different numbers of components with sets of Dirichlet priors, and uncertainty in the total component failure rate with sets of Gamma priors. They combine these models to calculate lower and upper expectations for common-cause failure rates, using a Taylor approximation for the rate conversion and bounding its error. The paper illustrates the method with an example using 36 failure events for a four-component system and a separate fictional electrical network example. The method produces ranges rather than single estimates, allowing uncertainty about the analyst’s prior knowledge to be reflected in the results.
key_results: For the four-component example, the authors recommend an interval of 1 to 10 for the alpha-factor learning parameter; with 36 observations, the posterior expectation interval for the fraction of four-component failures is 0.00014 to 0.00109. In the fictional two-line network example, based on 11 observed events over 12 years per line, the estimated expected rate of double failures is 0.19 to 0.24 per year, and the rate of single failures is 0.318 to 0.373 per year. These are uncertainty bounds from the proposed approach, not results of a comparison against observed future failures or a competing method. The authors also report absolute approximation errors of 0.006 for the double-failure fraction and 0.003 for the single-failure fraction in this example.
key_equations:
Posterior lower and upper expectations for alpha factors: \[\underline{E}(\alpha_j\mid n,H)=\min_{(s,t)\in H}\frac{n_j+s t_j}{N+s},\quad \overline{E}(\alpha_j\mid n,H)=\max_{(s,t)\in H}\frac{n_j+s t_j}{N+s}\] The lower and upper expectations bound alpha sub j, the fraction for events with j failed components; n sub j is its observed count, N is the total event count, s and t are prior parameters with t sub j the prior expectation, and H is the allowed set of prior parameters.

Gamma posterior expectation for the marginal failure rate: \[E(q_t\mid M,T,u,v)=\frac{M+uv}{T+u}\] The expected total failure rate per component is based on q sub t; M is the observed number of failures, T is observation time, u is the learning parameter, and v is the prior expected rate.

Conversion from alpha factors to common-cause failure rates: \[g_j(\alpha)=\frac{j\alpha_j}{\binom{k-1}{j-1}\sum_{\ell=1}^{k}\ell\alpha_\ell},\quad q_j=g_j(\alpha)q_t\] The multiplier g sub j depends on the fraction alpha sub j, the component count k, the failure-count index j, and the sum over index ell; q sub j is the rate for events with j failed components, and q sub t is the total component failure rate.

Combined lower and upper expectations for failure rates: \[\underline{E}(q_j)=\underline{E}(g_j(\alpha))\,\underline{E}(q_t),\quad \overline{E}(q_j)=\overline{E}(g_j(\alpha))\,\overline{E}(q_t)\] The bounds for q sub j are formed from the corresponding bounds for the multiplier g sub j of the alpha factors and the marginal rate q sub t, under the paper’s assumption that the alpha factors and marginal rate are independent.
limitations_stated: The authors restrict the prior parameter sets to a particular convex form and note that other shapes might fit prior information or update better, but could be harder to elicit. They do not calculate imprecise credible intervals and expect that this would require an approximation procedure.
limitations_unstated: The model assumes exchangeable components, immediate repair, Poisson failures, and independence between the alpha factors and the marginal failure rate; these assumptions may not fit systems with unequal component health, delayed repair, or dependent failure processes. The network data are fictional and the method is not validated against field outcomes, so the reported bounds do not establish how well they predict operational failure rates.
future_work_stated: The authors propose studying more general shapes for sets of Dirichlet and Gamma priors, including their elicitation and updating properties. They also identify the calculation of imprecise credible intervals as an unresolved issue that may need an approximation procedure.
future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to test the approach on real utility or safety-system records and assess whether the reported bounds are calibrated against later failures. key_results: For the frame example, the model has 21 correlated uncertain inputs and is evaluated at displacement thresholds from 4 to 9 centimeters. A sparse polynomial chaos expansion used 450 finite-element runs and estimated reliability indices with less than 5 percent error up to a reference index of 4; the reported errors across all thresholds ranged from 0.9 to 6.2 percent. In the system reliability example, meta-model-based importance sampling used 40 model runs to build the surrogate and 200 more for correction, compared with 172,000 runs for crude Monte Carlo and 284,195 for subset simulation. Its estimated failure probability was 2.38 times 10 to the power of minus 3, with a coefficient of variation below 5 percent; the comparison estimates were 2.26 and 2.28 times 10 to the power of minus 3.

key_results: For the Modified Metropolis algorithm, the authors recommend tuning its acceptance rate to between 30% and 50%; in two 1,000-dimensional examples, optimal scaling reduced the coefficient of variation of estimates for a failure probability of 10^-6 to about 80% of that with the reference spread of 1. summary: The paper introduces the G1-Renewal Process, a model for recurrent failures in repairable systems whose failure rate can increase or decrease over time. It changes the scale of each successive inter-failure-time distribution according to a restoration parameter, allowing it to represent improvement after repair as well as deterioration. The authors derive the cumulative intensity function and maximum likelihood estimation for exponential and Weibull underlying distributions. They use numerical illustrations, Monte Carlo calculations, and a published set of 12 consecutive failure intervals. The example shows that the model can fit a curved cumulative failure pattern even with an exponential underlying distribution, but the paper does not report comparative prediction accuracy.
key_results: For the example data of 12 consecutive failure intervals, the estimated exponential scale parameter is 4.781 and the estimated restoration parameter is 0.232. The fitted cumulative intensity function is convex, rather than the linear pattern that might be expected from an ordinary exponential renewal model. The numerical illustrations show that positive and negative restoration parameters can represent improving and deteriorating processes with exponential and Weibull underlying distributions. The paper reports no prediction-error, estimation-accuracy, or comparative cost results.

summary: The paper studies degradation that is physically monotone but whose measurements may fluctuate or appear to improve because of noise or minor repairs. It models observed degradation as a gamma process plus an independent Brownian motion and estimates the model parameters using moments from degradation increments. The method is developed for independent items observed at potentially different, irregular times, with consistency and asymptotic normality established under stated sampling conditions. The authors evaluate it through simulations and two applications: a public National Institute of Standards and Technology dataset and heating-cable laboratory tests. Their results show improving estimates as the simulated sample size grows, while the heating-cable application has large parameter uncertainty and may fit poorly.
key_results: In simulations with parameters xi = 1, alpha = 0.02, and tau squared = 0.02, the reported empirical bias for xi decreased from 0.222 at 50 items to 0.0625 at 200 items; for alpha it decreased from 0.00555 to 0.00157, and for tau squared from 0.00621 to 0.000501. The study reports 1,000 repetitions and gives corresponding usable repetition counts of 937, 983, and 998 for sample sizes 50, 100, and 200. For the National Institute of Standards and Technology data at 65 degrees Celsius, the estimated tau squared was 0.0001, with a reported 95% confidence interval from 0 to 10.11; the authors say this result is consistent with a gamma-process model. For the heating-cable data, the 200 degrees Celsius estimate of tau squared was 0.03, with a 95% confidence interval from 0 to 2.81, and the authors note that large standard deviations make model choice difficult and may indicate poor fit; no competing-method comparison or reliability prediction is reported.

Moment-based parameter estimates: \[\hat\xi=\sqrt{2m^{(1)}/m^{(3)}},\quad\hat\alpha=m^{(1)}\hat\xi,\quad\hat\tau^2=m^{(2)}-\sqrt{m^{(1)}m^{(3)}/2}\] The hatted xi, alpha, and tau squared are parameter estimates; m^(1), m^(2), and m^(3) are empirical normalized increment moments.
limitations_stated: The authors report that the heating-cable data produce very large standard deviations, making it difficult to choose between the submodels and potentially indicating poor model fit. Under their stated results, consistency can be shown for one sampling case without establishing asymptotic normality, and neither property can be established for another case.
limitations_unstated: The model and asymptotic results rely on independent items and independent gamma-process and Brownian-motion components, as well as restrictive sampling conditions; the paper does not assess how violations affect estimates. Both real-data applications have only 15 items, and the reported intervals can be very wide, so the applications provide limited evidence about parameter stability or extrapolation to field conditions.
future_work_stated: The authors propose extending the model to include covariates, because the environment can influence degradation, and say this will be studied in a forthcoming paper.
future_work_unstated: Future work could test the method with larger field datasets and operating conditions beyond the laboratory examples, and assess how sensitive estimates are to the independence and sampling assumptions. It could also connect parameter estimates to failure-time or system-reliability predictions and maintenance decisions, which this paper does not develop.

summary: This review describes statistical models for failure and maintenance events in repairable systems. It explains perfect, minimal, and imperfect repair models, including models that represent a system’s condition through virtual age, and develops the trend-renewal process as a way to represent both renewal behavior and time trends. It also discusses unobserved differences between systems, observed covariates, trend tests, and models for different types of events such as failures and preventive maintenance. The discussion draws on published operational and medical examples, including aircraft air-conditioner failures and engine valve-seat replacements. The paper emphasizes model structure and likelihood construction rather than a new estimator or a comparative performance study.
key_results: The review illustrates its models using Proschan’s data on 17 aircraft air-conditioner systems: the estimated between-system heterogeneity variance is approximately 0.11, and a likelihood-ratio comparison reports a statistic of 5.28, a p-value of 0.022, and an estimated trend power parameter of 1.16. For the Aalen and Husebye recurrent-event data, the renewal distribution is reported as non-exponential; the comparison of a renewal model with a trend-renewal model gives a likelihood-ratio statistic of 4.18, a p-value of 0.041, and an estimated trend power parameter of 1.14. The review also describes valve-seat replacement data from 41 diesel engines, where the estimated replacement frequency appears fairly constant up to 550 days and then increases. These are illustrative findings from the reviewed datasets, not a head-to-head evaluation of competing methods.
key_equations: Trend-renewal process definition: \[\Lambda(T_i)-\Lambda(T_{i-1})\sim F,\quad i=1,2,\ldots\] Here Λ is the cumulative trend function, T_i and T_{i-1} are successive event times, i is the event index, ∼ means has the distribution, and F is the renewal distribution; the transformed interevent times are independent with distribution F.
limitations_stated: The author restricts the discussion to operation time and assumes the system is restarted immediately after a failure or maintenance action, so repair durations and topics such as availability are not covered. The paper also gives limited attention to statistical inference and notes that nonparametric estimation can be challenging in some models. In the models for multiple event types, covariates and heterogeneity are set aside to simplify the presentation.
limitations_unstated: The examples are analyses of previously published datasets rather than prospective validation on new field data, and the review does not establish how well the models predict future failures or maintenance needs. Its demonstrations rely on assumptions such as independent, identically distributed systems in some analyses, while the breadth of the model families may make selection and estimation difficult for practitioners with sparse event histories.
future_work_stated: The author identifies challenging nonparametric estimation problems as an area needing attention. The paper also points to model checking and goodness-of-fit procedures as important tools when choosing among models.
future_work_unstated: Further work could validate these models prospectively on field data and test their predictions across changing loads, environments, and maintenance policies. It could also connect event-process models to system-level reliability and maintenance decisions, including the costs and effects of repair downtime.

summary: This review addresses how to assess system reliability when full system tests are expensive, scarce, or unavailable. It describes Bayesian methods for combining component tests, system tests, degradation measurements, expert knowledge, and other data, and it covers lifetime and failure-count models as well as system representations. The examples use simulated data, component and system tests, and operational failure counts from 48 computers in a supercomputer. The authors also discuss allocating limited test budgets and represent systems with Bayesian networks and flowgraphs when standard series and parallel structures are inadequate. Their main conclusion is that combining different levels and sources of data can improve reliability assessment, especially when full system tests are limited, but substantial modeling and computational challenges remain.
key_results: In a simulated degradation example, the posterior estimate of the initial degradation level was 99.2, with a 90% posterior interval of 92.9 to 105.1; the estimated log-scale lifetime parameter was -1.00, with an interval of -1.21 to -0.76. For the same example, the estimated degradation noise standard deviation was 6.57, with an interval of 3.8 to 10.3, and the item-to-item standard deviation was 0.24, with an interval of 0.14 to 0.35. In the supercomputer example, the estimated reliability of a six-hour run increased with later start time, indicating reliability growth. In a test-allocation illustration with a budget of 2500 and system tests costing 30 compared with component tests costing 1 each, the selected allocation was 83 system tests, 10 tests of component 1, and no tests of component 2; its reported criterion was 0.160.
key_equations:
