Degradation-based lifetime: \[T_j=(\alpha-L)\beta_j\] The lifetime of item j is the time for its degradation to reach threshold L, given initial level alpha and item-specific time scaling factor beta_j.

Testing budget constraint: \[\sum_{i=1}^{3}TC_i n_i\le B\] The sum of the cost per test TC_i multiplied by the number of tests n_i at each level i must not exceed the total budget B.
limitations_stated: The authors state that further work is needed on eliciting system structure and component dependencies, statistical inference for richer system representations, and resource allocation for more complicated systems and data types. They also emphasize that large-system assessment and resource allocation can be computationally intensive, and that methods for reducing computation without sacrificing accuracy remain an open challenge.
limitations_unstated: The examples are illustrations rather than a consistent, systematic comparison of methods on a common validation set, so their results do not establish which approach performs best across settings. Several examples rely on specified component relationships or independence assumptions, while the review gives limited evidence on how robust results are when those assumptions are wrong or when models are extrapolated to operating conditions not represented in the data.
future_work_stated: The authors propose further research on expert elicitation of system structure and dependencies, statistical inference for Bayesian network and flowgraph representations, and resource allocation beyond simple binomial cases. They also call for work on computational approximations for large assessments and on designing accelerated degradation experiments, including the choice of test conditions, sample sizes, and inspection schedules.
future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to evaluate these data-combination approaches prospectively against held-out operational data and to compare their uncertainty calibration under common test scenarios. Further work could also examine how common-cause failures, changing operating conditions, and system-level decisions affect the reliability estimates and test-allocation recommendations.

summary: This paper develops a Bayesian semi-parametric model for bathtub-shaped failure rates, which decrease before a minimum point and increase afterward. The model represents the hazard using a random measure and a change point, and reduces its posterior calculations to two conditionally independent S-paths. The authors derive a closed-form posterior mean hazard estimator and provide iterative and importance-sampling procedures for computing it. They evaluate the procedures using simulated failure-time data with right censoring, and also illustrate a Bayesian test and an extension to covariates. In the simulations, the estimated hazards move closer to the generating hazards as sample size increases.
key_results: The theoretical result is that, conditional on the change point and observed data, the two S-paths are independent; the resulting posterior analysis is a Rao-Blackwellization of the partition-based approach. Simulations use total sample sizes of 500, 1,000, and 3,000, with censoring rates of about 15% and 20% for the two examples. The paper reports visually that estimates from both iterative and importance-sampling procedures tend toward the true hazard curves as sample size increases, and that changing the fixed change point among the tested values makes little difference. It reports no numerical estimation-error metric or quantitative comparison showing one proposed procedure is more accurate than another.

Conditional independence of the two paths: \[W(S^-,S^+\mid\theta,T)=W^-(S^-\mid\theta,T)W^+(S^+\mid\theta,T)\] Here W is the joint posterior probability of the two paths, W-minus and W-plus are their respective posterior probabilities, theta is the change point, and T is the observed data.

limitations_unstated: The model is limited to a bathtub shape with a single change point and monotone hazard behavior on each side, so it does not represent multiple turning points or other failure-rate shapes. summary: The paper addresses how AI coding agents can pass known tests without implementing all required behavior, and how repeated feedback can let them adapt to the tests they have seen. It proposes GTDD, where a separate testing agent generates cases after each candidate is committed, and verified failures are returned for repair and saved as regression tests. The authors model false acceptance on a fixed finite population and show how fresh, private random audits can control the chance of accepting a candidate whose failure rate is too high. They evaluate development policies on a stateful key-value store using a reference implementation and a fixed set of 2,000 generated traces. Policies that regenerated tests during repair had lower mean final failure rates than the policy that generated tests only once, but the study did not identify which feature of the policies caused the difference.
key_results: In the paired study of 30 blocks, the dynamic policy whose tester could inspect the candidate finished with a mean failure rate of 0.274, compared with 0.405 for the fixed-test language-model policy; the paired difference was minus 0.131, with a reported significance value of 0.0015. The dynamic policy without source access had a mean final failure rate of 0.279, and the comparison between the two dynamic policies showed no detectable difference. Neither dynamic policy had a detectable advantage over the property-based test baseline. In the paper’s numerical example with a population of 500 cases, a five percent tolerance, and a five percent error target, the exact audit size was 54 cases for one candidate and one requirement family, 108 cases for repository acceptance over 32 opportunities, and 131 cases for 160 simultaneous family conclusions.
key_equations: False acceptance bound for a zero-failure audit: \[q_{N,\rho}(n)=\frac{\binom{N-K_\rho}{n}}{\binom{N}{n}}\le (1-\rho)^n\] The population size N, the smallest failing-case count K sub rho above tolerance, the audit sample size n, the allowed failure-rate tolerance rho, and q, the upper bound on passing despite being above tolerance, define the finite-population result; the binomial coefficients count possible samples.

limitations_unstated: The empirical evidence comes from one key-value-store task, one coding and testing model, and a designed test population, so the results may not generalize to other software, models, or production workloads. summary: This paper adapts reliability engineering to artificial intelligence (AI) systems, arguing that average task accuracy does not show whether a system operates dependably and safely over time. It identifies failures at four levels, from technical components and operating loops to agent actions and multi-agent governance. The proposed program defines the system and operating conditions, analyzes failure modes, selects measures suited to the data, and uses testing, evaluation, verification, and validation (TEVV), monitoring, and a failure reporting, analysis, and corrective action system (FRACAS) to update evidence. The paper illustrates the approach with California autonomous-vehicle disengagement records, laboratory classifier testing, and simulated perception-module errors. Its main conclusion is that established reliability methods provide a useful foundation, but AI reliability claims need better field records, exposure measures, and safety controls, particularly for agents that act or change over time.
key_results: The California case analyzed 479 autonomous-vehicle disengagements from December 2017 through November 2019, using monthly mileage as exposure. The estimated monthly event-rate trend was negative for Cruise and Pony AI: their reported multiplicative changes in events per mile were 0.930 and 0.864, respectively, and their quasi-Poisson intervals excluded no change. Waymo’s estimated trend was negative, with a reported multiplier of 0.979, but was not distinguishable from zero after accounting for overdispersion; Zoox’s estimate was nearly flat, with a multiplier of 1.008. The laboratory classifier and simulated perception cases illustrate how reliability-growth and error-propagation models can be applied, but the paper does not report them as comparative evaluations of competing methods.
key_equations:
Manufacturer-month event-count model: \[N_{mt}\sim\operatorname{Poisson}\left(\exp(\alpha_m+\beta_m t)x_{mt}\right)\] N is the disengagement count for manufacturer m in month t, alpha is the manufacturer-specific intercept, beta is its monthly log-rate trend, and x is recorded mileage exposure.

Error propagation across modules: \[\lambda_m(t\mid H)=\lambda_m^0(t\mid H_m)+\sum_{n\ne m}\lambda_{m,n}^p(t\mid H_n)\] Lambda for module m at time t given event history H is the sum of its baseline intensity and intensities propagated from other modules n, with H_m and H_n denoting the respective module histories.
limitations_stated: The authors state that the California manufacturer-month analysis omits vehicle heterogeneity, that quasi-Poisson variance inflation does not explain the source of overdispersion, and that Zoox has short exposure, making its trend weakly identified. They note that disengagement is a human-gated surrogate that can miss hazardous behavior, and that agent field records with exposure and relevant system covariates are not yet available. They also state that detailed field-test data are difficult to obtain and are often held by industry.
limitations_unstated: The paper presents a broad engineering program rather than a single framework tested end to end, so the examples do not establish that adopting the program or its proposed controls reduces field failure rates. The California analysis aggregates by manufacturer and month, which limits assessment of within-month variation and confounding by changing routes, fleet composition, or operating conditions.
future_work_stated: The authors call for a field repository that links failures to exposure, operating context, system versions, tools, memory, policies, agent connections, reasoning traces, severity, and corrective actions. They also propose linking controlled tests with field data to support drift-aware reliability-growth and failure-propagation models, and encourage industry to share more granular field-test data. summary: Correlation-based degradation models represent dependence symmetrically, so they can suggest physically implausible combinations of performance paths and distort reliability or remaining useful life estimates. When U14 was unavailable, the proposed model's corresponding errors were 40.17, 25.21, and 19.05, while the independent model's were 80.42, 61.86, and 51.04. Bayesian fusion of degradation and causal predictions: \[m_{post}=\frac{v_c m_p+v_p m_c}{v_c+v_p},\qquad v_{post}=\frac{v_c v_p}{v_c+v_p}\] m_p and v_p are the prior mean and variance from the univariate degradation model, m_c and v_c are the mean and variance from the causal prediction, and m_post and v_post are the fused predictive mean and variance.

System reliability and remaining useful life: \[R(t)=\Pr\{M(t)>0\},\qquad T_{RUL}=\inf\{t>t_n:M(t)\leq 0\}\] R(t) is system reliability at time t, M(t) is the system performance margin, T_RUL is the first time the margin reaches zero or less after current time t_n, and Pr denotes probability.

future_work_unstated: Evaluate the method on field data and across C-MAPSS subsets with varied operating conditions, and test whether inferred causal structure remains valid under operating changes. summary: Structures can fail when uncertain loads, material properties, or degradation push their response beyond a specified safety limit. This review examines how structural reliability methods estimate failure probabilities for both static problems and systems whose responses change over time under random excitations. It describes analytical approximations, simulation and variance-reduction methods, splitting methods, and machine-learning tools that are used to reduce computational effort or find rare failures. The paper reviews methodological research rather than presenting a new dataset or experimental evaluation. Its central conclusion is that efficient estimation has advanced, but methods can still miss important failure regions, especially in high-dimensional problems with complex failure boundaries.
key_results: The review reports that direct simulation of a failure probability around 10^-6 may require approximately 10^8 samples to achieve a coefficient of variation of 10%, illustrating the cost of estimating rare failures. It also cites an experimental-testing study that estimated failure probabilities as low as 10^-5 with about 1,750 samples. For subset simulation, the review reports that an intermediate conditional probability near 0.2 minimizes the estimator's coefficient of variation in the cited analysis, while values from 0.1 to 0.3 performed similarly; 0.1 is commonly used. These are figures reported from work reviewed in the paper, not results from a new experiment conducted by the review authors.
key_equations:

Failure probability by splitting: \[P_F=\prod_{l=1}^{L}\mathbb{P}(F_l\mid F_{l-1})\] P_F is failure probability, the product runs over levels l from one to L, F_l is the failure region at level l, F_0 is the initial region, and P(F_l given F_{l-1}) is the conditional probability of reaching the next region.
limitations_stated: The authors state that the review is limited to methodological developments and does not address application-specific loads or degradation mechanisms, design-code calibration, structural optimization, or performance-based engineering. The review also identifies the possibility of missing important failure regions in high-dimensional problems with complex or discontinuous failure boundaries as a persistent challenge.
limitations_unstated: The paper does not describe a systematic literature-search and study-selection process, so readers cannot assess how comprehensively the reviewed work was identified or whether selection bias affected the coverage. future_work_stated: The authors identify the discovery of potentially important failure regions in high-dimensional spaces as an outstanding research challenge. future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to extend and validate these reliability methods for specific degradation processes, such as corrosion or fatigue, with changing environmental and operating conditions and with field observations. summary: The paper addresses hypothesis tests for lifetime data from cyclic-stress accelerated life tests when units are inspected only at fixed times and failures are recorded as interval counts. Classical tests can lose control of their significance level when a small number of counts are contaminated, because the interval probabilities jointly inform the model parameters. The authors model lifetimes with a log-normal distribution, a cumulative exposure assumption, and a log-linear relationship between stress and lifetime scale. They develop robust Wald-type and Rao-type tests based on the weighted minimum density power divergence estimator for simple and composite hypotheses. Simulations and an automotive air-conditioner evaporator test show that the robust tests better control significance under contamination, while giving up some power under clean data.
key_results: In simulations with 1,000 replications, sample sizes from 100 to 400, and contamination up to 0.10, the tests remained near the nominal 0.05 significance level under clean data. Under contamination, classical tests’ empirical significance levels rose rapidly, while larger tuning-parameter values kept the robust tests closer to nominal; clean-data power was highest for the classical tests, with a modest reduction for robust tests. In the evaporator example, the pilot-based full-parameter hypothesis was not rejected: at tuning value 0, the Wald and Rao statistics were 0.69 and 0.68, with p-values of 0.88 for both. The no-stress-effect hypothesis was strongly rejected at every tested tuning value: at tuning value 0, statistics were 95.75 for the Wald test and 50.14 for the Rao test, with reported p-values of 0.000; at tuning value 1.0, they were 71.76 and 48.98, also with reported p-values of 0.000. The hypothesis about the log-normal shape parameter was not rejected across the tested tuning values.

limitations_stated: The authors do not explicitly identify limitations of the proposed framework. They do note that their simulated contamination proportion is capped at 0.10 because larger contamination would change the underlying model rather than represent a small fraction of outlying observations.
limitations_unstated: The framework assumes log-normal lifetimes, a common shape parameter across stress conditions, cumulative exposure, and a log-linear stress-scale relationship; departures from these assumptions could affect test calibration and conclusions. future_work_stated: The authors propose extending the framework to other lifetime distributions and stress-life relationships. They also propose developing a data-driven procedure for selecting the tuning parameter beta.
future_work_unstated: Further work could assess robustness to alternative failure mechanisms, unit-level covariates, and stress profiles that vary between units or over time, and could test the method on independent field data. summary: Very small failure probabilities are difficult to estimate by ordinary simulation, especially when the failure region has multiple separated or curved parts. The paper proposes FAMIS, which trains a weighted mixture of normalizing-flow proposals to place samples in important failure regions, using a smooth failure surrogate, gradual tempering, defensive exploration, and component repulsion. It is tested on simulated multimodal targets and reliability problems with non-Gaussian inputs, nonlinear failure regions, and dimensions up to 300. Across these tests, the authors report accurate and stable estimates, including improved results over several comparison methods in selected high-dimensional examples.
key_results: In the two-dimensional truncated-tail tests, reported relative root mean-square errors varied from 0.002 to 0.510 depending on the event, batch size, and number of proposals; for the four-region product-tail event, using four proposals reduced the error to 0.014 at batch size 1,000, compared with 0.381 using two proposals. In the nonlinear benchmark at dimensions 100, 200, and 300, FAMIS had logarithmic error values of 0.060, 0.101, and 0.120, respectively, lower than the reported values for the other two methods in each case. On the funnel benchmark, its logarithmic errors were 0.005, 0.042, 0.075, and 0.048 at dimensions 2, 31, 51, and 101; at dimension 101, the paper reports that REIN failed. limitations_stated: The authors note that proposal performance depends on tuning the surrogate and tempering schedules, defensive sampling, the balance between the two fitting terms, and the number of mixture components. limitations_unstated: Evaluation is based on synthetic targets and benchmark reliability models; the paper does not validate the method against field measurements or an operational engineering system. summary: The paper studies interval estimation when several Weibull populations share a shape parameter but have different rate parameters. key_results: The simulation used 5,000 replications at a nominal 95% interval level, with 2 or 4 populations and sample sizes of 30, 50, and 100; exact coverage percentages are presented graphically rather than tabulated. summary: The paper addresses failure-probability estimation when expensive engineering models make direct Monte Carlo evaluation costly and conventional surrogate uncertainty can misclassify points near the failure boundary. It extends active Kriging Monte Carlo simulation (AK-MCS) by adding conformal prediction intervals to a Gaussian process surrogate, then uses those intervals to select new model evaluations and bound the estimated failure probability. The method is tested using simulated outputs from three analytic reliability benchmarks: two four-branch cases, a modified Rastrigin function, and a nonlinear oscillator. Across these tests, the more conservative conformal version generally estimates failure probability accurately and has empirical coverage near or above its nominal level. The authors recommend it when disconnected failure regions cannot be ruled out in advance.
key_results: The study used 50 replications, a Monte Carlo population of 10^4 points, an initial design of 20 points, and a nominal conformal level of 0.90. On the four-branch cases, the J-minmax-GP variant had relative errors of +0.9% and -5.8%, with 66 and 53 model calls; its terminal empirical coverage was 0.886 and 0.905. On the modified Rastrigin benchmark, the U-function underestimated the reference failure probability by 25.7% after 409 calls, while EFF and the two conformal variants had errors of +0.7%, +0.6%, and -0.3%, respectively, using 564, 525, and 541 calls. On the oscillator, EFF stopped after a median of 32 calls with a +5.5% error, while the conformal variants had errors of -1.5% using 99 and 105 calls; the J-minmax-GP terminal coverage was 0.905.
key_equations:
Conformal bounds on failure probability: \[\hat{P}_{f}^{+}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\mathbf{1}\{M_t(x_i)\leq 0\},\quad \hat{P}_{f}^{-}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\mathbf{1}\{m_t(x_i)\leq 0\}\] Here N is the Monte Carlo sample size, x_i is sample point i, t is the current iteration, M_t and m_t are the upper and lower conformal interval endpoints, and the indicator equals one when its condition is true.

Stopping rule: \[\hat{P}_{f}^{+}-\hat{P}_{f}^{-}\leq\epsilon_{\mathrm{stop}}\] The procedure stops when the upper estimated failure-probability bound minus the lower bound is no greater than the prescribed tolerance epsilon_stop.
limitations_stated: The authors note that the theoretical coverage guarantees are marginal rather than conditional on the specific training design, and that training-conditional coverage remains to be established. They also state that empirical coverage requires true responses at unevaluated sample points, so it is an offline diagnostic unavailable for a genuinely expensive black-box model unless a held-out evaluation set is used. The paper observes that adaptive sampling can cause feedback covariate shift, with coverage declining for the less conservative J+GP intervals in some experiments.
limitations_unstated: The evaluation covers only three analytic benchmark problems and does not validate the method on field data or an expensive real engineering model. future_work_unstated: Further work could test the method on field data and computationally expensive models, including reliability problems with time-varying loads, dependent inputs, or failure mechanisms beyond those in the benchmarks. summary: Classical performance-based earthquake engineering can miss cumulative damage and finite repair times because it treats damaging events as independent and assumes the structure renews immediately after each event. This paper models structural damage, collapse, and recovery together as a continuous-time Markov chain with state-dependent transition rates. It derives time-dependent collapse reliability and a resilience measure based on the time spent operational before collapse. The framework is illustrated with a three-state example and applied to computational models of a steel braced frame and a base-isolated frame using seismic hazard, fragility, and recovery-time inputs. The main finding is that recovery speed strongly affects resilience but has little effect on long-term reliability in the two case studies.
key_results: At a 50-year horizon, the braced frame has a reliability index of about 1, while the base-isolated system has an index of about 2.08. For the braced frame, the reported resilience index is 2.50 for short recovery and 1.49 for long recovery; for the base-isolated system, it is 4.16 and 3.15, respectively. Across the case studies, reliability changes little as the repair rate varies, whereas resilience improves with faster recovery. The spectral approximation of resilience agrees closely with the exact calculation, with reported discrepancies no greater than about 10 to the power of minus 2.

limitations_stated: The industrial applications assume time-invariant seismic hazard and exclude aftershock and foreshock sequences; a time-varying generator is outside the scope of the paper. The base-isolated system's fragility curves were not computed from a dedicated fragility analysis: the authors shifted the braced-frame curves using qualitative engineering judgment. limitations_unstated: The recovery model in the industrial applications allows only one repair transition, from the slightly damaged state to the undamaged state, and uses constant rates derived from median durations under an exponential holding-time assumption. future_work_stated: The authors propose extending the framework to time-varying generators for clustered seismicity, including aftershock sequences. future_work_unstated: Future studies could validate the transition rates and predicted outcomes against observed damage and recovery histories from earthquakes. They could also model multiple repair stages, operational dependencies, and uncertain repair resources, then use the resulting estimates to compare recovery and retrofit decisions.

summary: Small samples and right-censored observations can make conventional reliability confidence intervals for log–logistic lifetimes inaccurate. The paper proposes a method that combines least squares estimates with generalized pivotal quantities to construct confidence intervals for distribution parameters and reliability. For censored data, it uses Kaplan–Meier estimates to obtain plotting positions and fits the least squares regression to observed failures. The evaluation uses simulated log–logistic samples and operational failure-time datasets, including grinder and secondary reactor pump data. In the reported simulations, the new method generally gives coverage closer to the intended level than likelihood-based asymptotic intervals and parametric bootstrap intervals.
key_results: For complete-data simulations with sample sizes of 10 and 20, the method’s coverage was generally closer to the nominal levels of 0.90 and 0.95 than that of the maximum likelihood and parametric bootstrap approaches. With sample size 10 and censoring proportions of 20 percent and 50 percent, its coverage was generally higher than the comparison methods, although not in every scenario; for example, one 50 percent censoring scenario reported coverage of 0.940 for the proposed method and 0.945 for the bootstrap. In the grinder and secondary reactor pump examples, the proposed method’s reported 95 percent interval lengths were shorter than both alternatives at all three selected time points: grinder lengths ranged from 0.393 to 0.474, and pump lengths ranged from 0.278 to 0.340. The paper describes three real-data applications, but the supplied results provide interval tables for the grinder and pump datasets.

Log–logistic reliability: \[R(t;\alpha,\beta)=\left\{1+(t/\beta)^\alpha\right\}^{-1}\] R(t) is the probability of surviving beyond time t, alpha is the shape parameter, and beta is the scale parameter.

Generalized pivotal quantities for the parameters: \[G_s=\frac{\hat{s}}{\hat{s}(Z)},\quad G_\mu=\hat{\mu}-G_s\{\bar{Z}-\bar{x}\hat{s}(Z)\},\quad G_\alpha=1/G_s,\quad G_\beta=\exp(G_\mu)\] G_s, G_mu, G_alpha, and G_beta are pivotal quantities for scale, location, shape, and scale; s_hat and mu_hat are observed least squares estimates; s_hat(Z) is the least squares slope for the standard logistic sample Z; Z_bar is that sample’s mean; and x_bar is the mean plotting-position regressor.

Reliability generalized pivotal quantity: \[G_R(t)=\left\{1+\left(t/G_\beta\right)^{G_\alpha}\right\}^{-1}\] G_R(t) is the generalized pivotal quantity for reliability at time t, using the pivotal quantities G_beta for the distribution scale and G_alpha for the shape.
limitations_stated: The authors describe their simulation studies as limited. They report results for small samples with light or moderate censoring and say that further investigation is warranted.
limitations_unstated: The censored-data procedure estimates plotting positions with the Kaplan–Meier estimator and regresses over observed failures, but the paper does not establish how its performance changes under different censoring mechanisms or very high censoring. future_work_stated: The authors propose studying the method for other location–scale distributions. They also suggest investigating analysis of variance problems under log–logistic assumptions, including comparisons of reliability or mean survival time across groups.
future_work_unstated: Further work could evaluate the method under alternative censoring mechanisms, heavier censoring, and dependence between failure and censoring, and check the validity of the intervals when the lifetime distribution is misspecified. The paper provides no numerical RUL error, coverage, or quantified reduction in uncertainty, so the size of the improvement cannot be assessed from reported metrics. summary: The paper addresses the problem of choosing a nominal design that is least likely to fail when random perturbations affect its realized design. It develops Bayesian optimization strategies based on Thompson sampling and knowledge gradient, using a Gaussian process surrogate to learn the black-box performance function. Importance sampling is incorporated to target failure probabilities as small as 10^-6 to 10^-8, and quasi-Monte Carlo estimates are used in the approximations. The methods are tested on 12 synthetic problems, including randomly generated functions and standard test functions from 2 to 16 dimensions, with 30 runs per problem. The one-shot knowledge-gradient method is the strongest overall in these tests, while the discrete version degrades in higher dimensions and the proposed methods are computationally more expensive than some alternatives.
key_results: Across the 12 test problems, one-shot knowledge gradient for maximal reliability performs best or jointly best on 10 problems; the discrete version matches it in lower dimensions. On higher-dimensional problems, the discrete approximation is reported to be too coarse and slows convergence, while the one-shot method remains a top performer, sometimes jointly with the Thompson-sampling method. The tests cover extreme failure probabilities, including targets in the range 10^-6 to 10^-8, and a separate set of less-extreme cases; the authors report similar overall conclusions for both regimes. The one-shot method can take about 30–40 seconds to optimize its acquisition function in the slowest reported case using a graphics processing unit, whereas Thompson sampling is presented as a faster alternative when computation is not negligible relative to evaluation cost.
key_equations:

Logarithmic reliability objective: \[R_n(x)=-\log P_n(x)\] R_n(x) is the negative logarithm of P_n(x), the posterior expected failure probability after n observations, and x is the nominal design.
limitations_stated: The authors report that the discrete knowledge-gradient approximation is too coarse and harms convergence on higher-dimensional problems. They also note that the knowledge-gradient methods are computationally intensive, with the slowest reported acquisition optimization taking about 30–40 seconds on a graphics processing unit. Their experiments do not evaluate multiple limit-state functions.
limitations_unstated: The evaluation uses synthetic benchmark functions rather than field or manufacturing data, so performance on real processes is not established. The experiments mainly use a single threshold and additive perturbations with specified distributions; results may not carry over to uncertain or changing perturbation distributions, dependent operating conditions, or interacting failure mechanisms. The Gaussian process surrogate and numerical approximations may also be less dependable when the true response is poorly represented by that surrogate, especially when extrapolating into rare-failure regions.
future_work_stated: The authors propose evaluating the framework with multiple limit-state functions and with constrained versions of the problem. They also suggest testing other mappings between nominal design and perturbation, including multiplicative perturbations, and exploring adaptive importance sampling using kernel density estimation or Markov chain Monte Carlo.
future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be validation on real manufacturing or field data, including checks that estimated rare failure probabilities remain calibrated under changing operating conditions. Further work could model dependent perturbations and multiple interacting failure mechanisms, then extend the optimization to system-level reliability and explicit cost or risk decisions.

summary: The paper presents a surrogate model for predicting responses of nonlinear dynamical systems when repeated numerical simulations are costly. Its function-on-function nonlinear autoregressive model with exogenous inputs (F2NARX) predicts a response over a time window using features from excitation and response windows, with principal component analysis and sparse Gaussian process regression. The authors also use the unscented transform to propagate prediction uncertainty and guide active learning for first-passage failure probability estimation. They evaluate the approach on simulated data from a Bouc-Wen oscillator and a three-story steel frame under simulated seismic loading, including response histories generated with OpenSees. In these examples, the method achieves accurate predictions with far fewer training histories and substantially less prediction time than the compared methods.
key_results: For the steel-frame example, a model trained on 50 time histories predicted 10,000 responses in 37 seconds, with normalized mean squared error below 1 × 10⁻³; this was about 3,000 times faster than the finite-element model and more than two orders of magnitude faster than the compared functional NARX model. For the steel frame, F2NARX prediction was 63, 142, and 198 times faster than that comparator using 25, 50, and 100 training histories, respectively, while achieving lower prediction errors. The unscented-transform uncertainty estimates had errors of 8.65 × 10⁻³ for the oscillator and 1.09 × 10⁻³ for the steel frame, and ran in 2.58 × 10² and 9.35 × 10² seconds, respectively, versus Monte Carlo simulation times of 1.38 × 10⁵ and 2.13 × 10⁵ seconds. Active learning reduced the number of required training histories to about 15 for robust first-passage probability estimates; in the steel-frame example, its relative estimation error fell below 0.05 after about five added histories, whereas the non-active approach remained above 0.1 after 20 additions.
key_equations: Window-to-window response mapping: \[y^{+}=f(u^{+},u^{-},y^{-},\Theta)\] Here y-plus is the response function in the next time window, f is the learned mapping, u-plus is the excitation function in the current or next window, u-minus is the excitation function in the preceding window, y-minus is the response function in the preceding window, and Theta is the vector of uncertain system parameters.
limitations_stated: The authors note that a shared low-dimensional feature space may not represent strongly non-stationary excitation or response patterns well. limitations_unstated: Evaluation is limited to two simulated structural examples; the paper does not validate the model against field measurements or demonstrate performance across different structures and operating environments. future_work_stated: The authors propose studying different look-back and look-ahead window widths and developing ways to select them automatically, as well as using overlapping windows or continuity penalties where boundary smoothness matters. They also suggest more advanced feature extraction, more efficient rare-event simulation and active-learning strategies, improved stopping criteria, and extensions to multiple responses, large-scale responses, design optimization, control, and digital twins.
future_work_unstated: Evaluate the method on measured structural response histories and field seismic records, including comparisons across structures, sensor configurations, and operating conditions. summary: This paper compares a policy that replaces a failed unit with a same-age used unit against a policy that replaces it with a new unit. The conclusions depend on whether units tend to improve or worsen with age, expressed through ageing properties such as new-better-than-used and new-worse-than-used. summary: The paper studies how single-sided aluminized polyimide films (SAPFs) degrade during ground storage, an issue the authors say has received little attention compared with degradation in space. The measured performance indicator is the solar absorption ratio (SAR), which rises as the aluminum coating corrodes and peels. The authors model SAR degradation under temperature and relative humidity, including a temperature-driven transition from accelerating to inhibiting degradation, and estimate model parameters using a likelihood method with the TERIME optimization algorithm. They use laboratory measurements from 12 samples at each of eight temperature and humidity combinations, and use simulation to predict lifetime and reliability. The proposed model identifies the transition and predicts substantially lower storage reliability than a conventional model that assumes an unchanged degradation mechanism.
key_results: The estimated transition temperature is 63.75 °C, with a 90% confidence interval of 54.30–75.76 °C; the estimated temperature effect changes from positive below the transition to negative above it. On the full data, the proposed model has a root mean square error of 0.217 versus 0.219 for the conventional model, and its Akaike information criterion is 944.38 versus 947.72. Across eight held-out stress-level tests, average root mean square error is 0.202 for the proposed model and 0.207 for the conventional model; average Kullback-Leibler divergence and Cramér-von Mises distance are 1.76 and 11.74, versus 7.88 and 30.19. limitations_stated: The authors state that financial constraints limited the breadth of the experiments and the number of stress levels. limitations_unstated: The model is based on eight laboratory stress combinations, with 12 samples at each, and the paper does not validate its long-term predictions against field storage data. future_work_stated: The authors propose extending the method to other products with stress-induced mechanism transitions and investigating such transitions with non-Arrhenius models. future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to validate predicted degradation and reliability with longer-duration warehouse or logistics data, including samples from additional production batches. summary: This paper derives reliability expressions for a one-out-of-n cold standby system whose active components follow a Generalized Lindley distribution (GLD). It models component lifetimes as identically distributed and derives the distribution of their sum using a moment-generating-function approach. With a perfect switch, it gives a closed-form system reliability expression; with an imperfect switch, it gives a lower bound because exact calculations are described as difficult. The numerical illustration considers a 100-hour mission and systems with 2, 5, 10, and 20 components, using specified distribution parameters rather than measured lifetime data. In that illustration, imperfect switching reduces reliability relative to perfect switching, while adding components increases reliability, especially with a perfect switch.
key_results: The authors derive a closed-form reliability expression and a mean time to failure formula for the perfect-switch system, and a lower bound for the imperfect-switch system. The numerical illustration uses 2, 5, 10, and 20 components over a 100-hour mission; the plotted results show lower reliability with the imperfect switch and higher reliability as component count increases, particularly for the perfect switch. Sensitivity analysis identifies theta as having the greatest influence on reliability, while eta and gamma have the least influence. For the reported mean-time-to-failure sensitivity with respect to alpha, the values for 2, 5, 10, and 20 components are 3.4932, 8.7329, 17.4658, and 34.9317, respectively; the corresponding values for beta are 0.5068, 1.2671, 2.5342, and 5.0683.

limitations_stated: The authors state that exact reliability calculations for the imperfect-switch case become very difficult, so they derive a lower bound rather than an exact expression. They do not report a corresponding exact imperfect-switch result.
limitations_unstated: The analysis assumes identical component lifetime distributions and the usual cold-standby conditions, including healthy standby components and negligible switching time, so it does not represent heterogeneity or non-negligible transition delays. future_work_stated: The authors propose studying redundancy allocation. They plan to model a previously introduced system using different methods and maximize reliability subject to constraints on component cost, weight, and volume.

They evaluate the methods in simulations with several sample sizes, monitoring schedules, censoring schemes, and parameter settings, and apply them to survival data from 112 patients with plasma cell myeloma. For the same setting, the second-order coefficient’s mean squared errors were 0.0011, 0.0012, 0.0014, and 0.0014, respectively. In many simulated settings, the highest posterior density intervals had coverage near or above the nominal 95 percent; for example, their reported coverage for the Pearson coefficient was 0.987 in one setting with shape 0.75, rate 0.052, scheme I, sample size 50, and four examination points. limitations_stated: The authors state that their alternative maximum-likelihood algorithm does not work when the experiment has no observed failures. limitations_unstated: The simulation examines only two shape values, two rate values, two sample sizes, two monitoring schedules, and three censoring schemes, so performance beyond those settings is not established. future_work_stated: The authors suggest developing approximate and generalized confidence intervals using the least-squares estimates. scope_reason: The paper models software failures and estimates future failure-free operation probabilities for safety-critical software, directly addressing software reliability assessment.
reliability_topic_evidence: “This work extends robust Bayesian inference results and so-called conservative Bayesian inference methods.”
model_family_evidence: “Using a Bernoulli process to model the occurrence of software failures” (Abstract)
glossary: CBI = Conservative Bayesian inference, which selects the least favorable posterior probability among priors consistent with specified evidence.|pfd = Probability of failure on demand.|i.i.d. = Independent and identically distributed.|x_i, p_i, I_i, n = The parameter value chosen in interval i, the prior probability assigned to that interval, the interval itself, and the number of intervals.|m, k, r = The number of future demands, past successful demands, and past failed demands, respectively.|phi* = The smallest posterior predictive probability of correct operation over the specified future demands.|h, y*, y** = The fixed-point function and its two locations that determine the conservative solution.
summary: The paper derives a conservative Bayesian method for assessing on-demand software reliability when an assessor specifies only partial prior beliefs about the probability of failure on demand (pfd). It models demand outcomes as an independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) Bernoulli process and finds the least favorable posterior predictive probability that the software will operate correctly on future demands. The method uses prior probabilities assigned to intervals of possible failure probabilities and reduces the assessment to a finite optimization with a unique fixed-point solution. The authors illustrate the method numerically by comparing its required test demands with those obtained using a uniform prior. The paper is theoretical and uses no field or other empirical data.
key_results: The authors show that the conservative solution is determined by a unique fixed point and that its prior places probability mass at selected interval endpoints and fixed-point locations. In the table’s example with no observed failures, a uniform prior requires 4,602 demands for each of three future-reliability claims, while the conservative method with y2 equal to 10^-4 requires 46,861, 49,322, and 51,882 demands, respectively. With one observed failure, the corresponding uniform-prior requirements are 9,229, 9,450, and 9,681 demands, compared with 52,320, 54,417, and 56,634 under that conservative prior specification. The authors also find that the conservative-to-uniform testing gap is roughly an order of magnitude for the small failure counts shown, and that the conservative solution increases with observed successes and decreases with observed failures.
key_equations:
Conservative posterior predictive probability: \[\phi^*=\inf_{x_i\in I_i}\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}p_i x_i^r(1-x_i)^{m+k}}{\sum_{i=1}^{n}p_i x_i^r(1-x_i)^k}\] Here phi* is the least favorable posterior probability of surviving m future demands, x_i is the pfd value chosen in interval I_i, p_i is that interval’s specified prior probability, n is the number of intervals, r is the number of observed failures, and k is the number of observed successes.

Fixed-point function: \[h(x)=(1-x)^m\frac{r-x(m+k+r)}{r-x(k+r)}\] Here h is the function defining the fixed point, x is a candidate pfd value, m is the number of future demands, r is the number of observed failures, and k is the number of observed successes.

Fixed-point condition: \[h(y^{**})=\phi^*=h(y^*)\] Here h is the fixed-point function, y** and y* are its two relevant locations, and phi* is the conservative posterior predictive probability.
limitations_stated: The authors state that CBI still requires eliciting partial prior specifications, and that the best way to elicit them from diverse evidence and their sensitivity to evidence need further study. Their example concerns on-demand software; they expect analogous results for continuously operating software but note that continuous-operation effects may change the outcomes. They also note that demonstrating ultra-high reliability can require partial prior specifications that strongly influence the result.
limitations_unstated: The result depends on the i.i.d. Bernoulli demand model, while the paper itself notes that software outcomes can be correlated; the numerical illustrations do not validate the method under those departures. Because the evaluation uses constructed prior constraints rather than field data, it does not establish how reliable the interval probabilities or resulting demand requirements are in a real certification assessment.
future_work_stated: The authors propose studying imprecise prior specifications in which interval probabilities are ranges rather than fixed values, and extending the analysis to continuously operating software. They also propose proving convergence and characterizing the speed of the fixed-point iteration, broadening the optimization to multi-objective conservative assessments, and identifying cases where strongly influential partial prior specifications can be justified.
future_work_unstated: Future studies could test the method using operational records from safety-critical software and compare its predicted reliability with later observed performance. They could also extend the model to include relevant operating conditions or software versions, explicitly represent dependence between demands, and assess how component-level results combine into system-level reliability.

summary: The paper addresses nonuniform etched thickness and uncertainty in plasma etching, where wafer-to-wafer process settings and spatial variation affect whether the remaining oxide thickness meets its target. It models mean thickness and input-dependent spatial variability separately using a heteroscedastic Gaussian process, while also representing uncertainty from sparse training data. The model and reliability-based design optimization framework use 84 laboratory experimental input-output runs, each with thickness measured at nine wafer locations. The optimization searches for process settings that reduce thickness variance while meeting a specified probability-of-failure requirement. For the illustrated target, accounting for model uncertainty produced a design with a lower reported failure probability than optimization that considered only process variability, at the cost of a slightly higher variance.
key_results: Across 10 random training and test splits, the heteroscedastic Gaussian process had a mean-thickness root mean square error of 1.5749 ± 0.3249, identical to the standard Gaussian process, but its variance-prediction error was 0.4005 ± 0.1457 versus 17.1884 ± 4.1281 for the standard model. Its continuous ranked probability score was 1.1150 ± 0.1558 versus 1.3410 ± 0.1018, and its conditional negative log-likelihood was 1.3843 ± 0.1239 versus 2.4019 ± 0.0941. For a 240 nm target, ±2.4 nm tolerance, and 3.0% target failure probability, the aleatory-only design had variance 0.9136 nm² and failure probability 2.94%; the design accounting for aleatory and epistemic uncertainty had variance 0.9626 nm² and failure probability 0.71%. In the most stringent scenario, the aleatory-only method reported a design with 1.52% failure probability against a 1.5% target, whereas the method accounting for both uncertainty types found no feasible solution.
key_equations:
Input-dependent observation model: \[y(x)=g(x)+\epsilon(x),\qquad \epsilon(x)\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^2(x))\] The thickness observation y at process input x equals the latent mean function g plus spatial noise epsilon, whose normal distribution has zero mean and input-dependent standard deviation sigma.

Predictive variance decomposition: \[\operatorname{Var}(Y)=\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{Var}(Y\mid Z)]+\operatorname{Var}(\mathbb{E}[Y\mid Z])\] The total thickness variance Var(Y) is the expected variance conditional on surrogate uncertainty Z, representing aleatory uncertainty, plus the variance of the conditional mean, representing epistemic uncertainty.

Failure probability for the target range: \[P_f(Z)=\Pr\!\left(\left|\hat y(X,Z)+\epsilon-T\right|>\delta\right)\] The conditional failure probability Pf is the probability that predicted thickness y-hat, evaluated at random process inputs X and surrogate uncertainty Z and combined with spatial noise epsilon, differs from target thickness T by more than tolerance delta.

Robust process-parameter optimization: \[\min_{\mu_X}\operatorname{Var}[\hat y(X,\bar Z)]\quad\text{subject to}\quad\Pr\!\left(\left|\hat y(X,Z)-T\right|>\delta\right)\le P_{f,\mathrm{target}}\] The method selects process-input means muX to minimize predicted thickness variance at representative surrogate realization Z-bar, subject to the probability that thickness under random inputs X and surrogate uncertainty Z misses target T by more than tolerance delta being no greater than the target failure probability.
limitations_stated: The authors state that spatial variability was measured at only nine discrete wafer locations, which may not represent continuous wafer nonuniformity. They also state that experimental data provide high physical fidelity but are resource-intensive and make large-scale data acquisition and validation difficult.
limitations_unstated: The optimized settings are model predictions and were not validated by new etching experiments at the reported optima, so actual process performance there remains unconfirmed. Input fluctuations are represented as independent normal random variables using equipment specifications, and the analysis does not account for uncertainty in those distribution parameters; results may therefore depend on assumptions about input distributions and process variation. The surrogate is trained and tested on a sparse laboratory dataset within a limited process range, so reliability beyond that range and transfer to other tools, wafers, or production conditions are not established.
future_work_stated: The authors propose additional experiments covering a wider range of process parameters and more wafer measurement locations. They also propose combining experiments with simulation data through a multi-fidelity approach, and extending the method to model time-dependent etching using stochastic process modeling and time-variant reliability analysis.
future_work_unstated: A direct experimental confirmation of the optimized recipes, followed by validation across wafers, lots, and etching tools, would test whether the predicted reliability carries over to production. Future models could represent spatially structured wafer variation and include operating covariates such as chamber condition or material batch, then connect thickness reliability to system-level device yield and process-control decisions.

summary: Buried pipelines can experience excessive tensile or compressive strain when ground movement occurs, while directly simulating many uncertain cases can make reliability assessment computationally demanding. The authors develop a physics-informed neural network surrogate and combine it with Monte Carlo simulation to estimate strain-exceedance failure probabilities. The model represents pipeline response using governing beam equations and accounts for uncertain ground-movement magnitude, soil cohesion, friction angle, unit weight, and burial depth. It is evaluated in a simulated pipeline case study, including scenarios with and without internal pressure and temperature effects. The authors report substantially lower computation time than finite element and finite difference approaches, while finding that ground-movement magnitude is the most influential uncertain input.
key_results: For 100,000 simulated samples, the paper reports tensile failure probabilities of 86.12% without operational loads and 33.63% with them for case I; the corresponding compressive results are 90.32% and no observed failure. For case II, tensile failure probabilities are 12.07% without operational loads and 0.001% with them, while compressive failure probabilities are 0.024% and no observed failure. In the operational-load scenario, mean tensile strain demand is 1.92% with a standard deviation of 0.17%, compared with 2.25% and 0.22% without those loads; sensitivity indices identify ground-movement magnitude as the leading factor, at 85.57 and 82.85. For the reliability analysis, surrogate training takes 3.1 hours and sample evaluation a few seconds, compared with 138.9 hours for the finite element method, 55.5 hours for the finite difference method, 23.2 hours for the finite element method using six processors, and 3.3 hours for the optimized finite difference method.
key_equations:
Ground-movement strain: \[\varepsilon_{GM}(x,z)=u_x(x)+\frac{1}{2}w_x^2(x)-z w_{xx}(x)\] Ground-movement strain epsilon_GM at pipe position x and cross-section position z is calculated from the first derivative of axial displacement u, the first derivative of lateral displacement w, and the second derivative of w.

PINN training loss: \[\mathcal{L}_{total}(\theta)=\mathcal{L}_1(\theta)+\mathcal{L}_2(\theta)+\mathcal{L}_{BC}(\theta)\] The total loss L_total for network parameters theta is the sum of the residual losses L_1 and L_2 for the governing equations and the boundary-condition loss L_BC.

Strain limit state: \[g=\varepsilon_c-\varepsilon_d\] The limit state g is strain capacity epsilon_c minus predicted strain demand epsilon_d, with failure defined when g is zero or less.

Monte Carlo failure probability estimate: \[P_f\approx\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}I(g(\xi_i)\leq 0)\] Estimated failure probability P_f is the number of failed samples, counted by indicator I for each sample's limit state g at random-variable values xi_i, divided by the total number of samples N.
limitations_stated: None stated.
limitations_unstated: The demonstration uses one simulated pipeline geometry and a restricted scenario: horizontal ground movement crossing the pipeline at 90 degrees, fixed pipe ends, and specified ranges and distributions for the uncertain inputs. The paper reports no validation against field observations, and it does not establish whether the input uncertainties are dependent or how well the normal distributions represent real sites; very small estimated failure probabilities also receive limited direct validation beyond the finite simulation sample.
future_work_stated: None stated.
future_work_unstated: Future work could test the approach against field measurements and additional pipeline geometries, ground-movement patterns, and failure mechanisms such as weld rupture or local buckling. It could also represent dependence and spatial variation in soil and operating conditions, assess system-level pipeline consequences, and connect failure estimates to risk-informed inspection or mitigation decisions.

summary: The paper develops a model for a single-unit system that can operate at multiple degradation levels and experience internal failures and external shocks. It models repair and vacation times with phase-type distributions and represents events using a marked Markovian arrival process (MMAP). The repairperson’s vacation and return decisions depend probabilistically on the observed degradation level, while a critical level triggers preventive maintenance; corrective repair or unit replacement follows the corresponding failure. The authors derive transient and steady-state measures in continuous and discrete time, then optimize vacation settings using profit and availability objectives. A numerical illustration motivated by a precision aerospace milling machine shows a trade-off between profitability and availability.
key_results: In the numerical example, the balanced selection from the Pareto front has steady-state net profit of 0.0164 per unit time and availability of 0.9168. The profit-maximizing selection reaches 0.2734 profit per unit time and 0.9089 availability, while the availability-maximizing selection reaches 0.9187 availability but has a net profit of −0.1972 per unit time. The reported mean operational times before the first failure are 13.3705, 36.8556, and 61.0399 time units for the profit-maximizing, balanced, and availability-maximizing selections, respectively. The balanced selection begins to generate positive returns at time 2646.569, compared with time 155.7316 for the profit-maximizing selection.
key_equations:
Continuous-time stationary balance: \[\pi Q=0,\quad \pi \mathbf{1}=1\] The vector pi gives stationary state probabilities, Q is the continuous-time transition-rate matrix, and the vector 1 contains ones so that probabilities sum to one.

limitations_stated: The authors state that computational cost increases as the number of operational levels grows. They mention state grouping or removal, limiting the number of levels, fixing transitions with known phase-type distributions, or using stochastic simulation as possible ways to mitigate this.
limitations_unstated: The numerical illustration is not calibrated against observed field data, so the reported performance and optimization results do not establish how well the policy would work for an operating machine. The model assumes external shocks occur independently of system condition and does not report uncertainty in the input parameters or sensitivity of the selected policy to that uncertainty.
future_work_stated: None stated.
future_work_unstated: Estimate and validate the model parameters using field records, including observed degradation, shock events, repair durations, and costs, then test the policy on data not used for calibration. Extend the decision model to account for multiple machines competing for repairperson time and compare the resulting policies under varying operating conditions and failure mechanisms.

scope_reason: The paper develops a statistical method for estimating engineered-system reliability from component lifetimes, directly addressing system time-to-failure.

glossary: c = The shrinkage coefficient applied to the component reliability estimates.|h_phi = The function that combines component reliabilities according to the system structure.|K = The number of components in the system.|phi = The system structure function, which specifies how component states determine whether the system operates.|R_S = The reliability function of the system.|Rhat_j = The estimated reliability function of component j.|Rhat_S = The estimated reliability function of the system.|t = Time.
summary: The paper develops a nonparametric method to estimate the reliability of a system from right-censored component failure-time data. It raises each component’s product-limit reliability estimate to a common shrinkage coefficient, then combines the adjusted estimates using the known system structure. The coefficient is selected using an approximate risk calculation or a bootstrap, with performance assessed under a weighted Cramer-von Mises loss. The evaluation uses simulated component lifetimes from Weibull distributions and includes series, parallel, and series-parallel systems. Across the simulations, component-level estimates generally performed better than estimates based only on system failure times, while shrinkage offered further gains mainly in parallel systems with informative component data.
key_results: In 1,000 replications for a 3-component series-parallel system with sample size 15, estimated risk was 0.0713 for the system-level product-limit estimator and 0.0601 for the component-level plug-in estimator; analytical shrinkage reduced it to 0.0597, while bootstrap shrinkage yielded 0.0602. For a 5-component parallel system, the corresponding risks were 0.0714, 0.0508, 0.0500, and 0.0501, respectively. For a 5-component series system, the risks were 0.0700, 0.0700, 0.0703, and 0.0718, so shrinkage did not improve the component-level estimate in that setting. In the 5-component parallel simulations, reported risk-efficiency gains were 1.1756% at censoring parameter 0.1 and 1.46% with 15 components, relative to the component-level plug-in estimator.
key_equations: Shrinkage system reliability estimator: \[\widehat R_S(t;c)=h_\phi\left(\widehat R_1(t)^c,\ldots,\widehat R_K(t)^c\right)\] The estimated system reliability at time t is formed by applying the system structure function h_phi to the component reliability estimates Rhat_j at time t, each raised to the common coefficient c, for the K components.
limitations_stated: The authors note that the same observed data are used to estimate both component reliabilities and the shrinkage coefficient, which may cause optimistic bias in finite samples. Their study assumes that component failure or censoring times are observed; it does not address current-status data. The analytical method also relies on approximations based on asymptotic theory.
limitations_unstated: The evaluation is based on simulated Weibull lifetimes and a limited set of system structures, so performance with other lifetime patterns or real operating data is unknown. Component lifetimes are treated as independent, and the paper does not evaluate how dependence among components would affect the estimates. The bootstrap approach is described as more computationally intensive, but its computation time and scaling are not quantified.
future_work_stated: The authors propose extending the method to current-status data and studying more formal Bayesian or empirical Bayes approaches using nonparametric priors. They also identify evaluation under alternative loss functions and application to real-world reliability data as next steps.
future_work_unstated: Future studies could assess the method with dependent components, competing failure mechanisms, and changing operating conditions or component covariates. Field validation could also examine whether shrinkage improves system-level maintenance or design decisions, and report how computation scales for larger systems.

summary: Failures in railway track circuits can disrupt train operations, and early signal changes may be too subtle for visual inspection or simple thresholds to diagnose. The paper models received electrical signals with a deep neural network classifier that predicts which failure type an anomaly may develop into; it also describes uncertainty quantification and a possible time-to-failure estimator. The evaluation uses proprietary signals from laboratory failure experiments, with thousands of signal pulses generated from full profiles for 10 tested failure categories. The authors report high classification accuracy and an example in which their method identifies a failure type much earlier than a conventional approach. The study is based on laboratory experiments rather than validation on operational railway data.
key_results: The results section reports 99.33% overall classification accuracy across 10 failure categories, while the abstract reports 99.31%. In one example, the conventional method first classified the failure at 58.95% of the elapsed anomaly-to-critical-failure period, compared with 0.83% for the proposed method. At a stated 99% confidence level, the authors report sufficient coverage for every class and an average prediction-set size of 1.06 labels. These results come from laboratory-generated signals; the paper does not report operational field performance.
key_equations: Conformal prediction coverage: \[\Pr(Y\in\Gamma(X))\ge 1-\alpha\] P is probability, Y is the true failure-class label, Gamma is the set of predicted class labels, X is the input signal, and alpha is the acceptable error risk.
limitations_stated: The authors say that pulse-window length involves a trade-off: longer windows may improve accuracy and confidence but delay classification. They assume that the progression of laboratory-generated anomalies can be translated linearly to reality, while noting that field evolution rates may vary and require investigation and validation.
limitations_unstated: The experiments are laboratory-generated, and the paper does not establish performance on operational railway signals or across real sites and configurations. It does not describe how pulses from the same full signal profile were separated for model training and testing, so the independence of evaluation examples is unclear; this could make reported accuracy more optimistic than performance on new installations. The paper also does not report computational cost or evaluate the time-to-failure estimator.
future_work_stated: The authors propose investigating the trade-off between pulse-window length and classification earliness according to operational needs. They also plan to develop time-to-failure estimates, investigate failure evolution rates with field validation, and conduct an external audit of standards compliance.
future_work_unstated: Evaluate the classifier on independently collected operational data from multiple locations and configurations, with a clearly separated test set, to assess generalization beyond laboratory profiles. Study how predictions should trigger maintenance actions and how multiple track-circuit failures may affect railway operations at the system level.

summary: This paper develops an adaptive Bayesian reliability acceptance sampling plan using simple step-stress partial accelerated life testing for products with multiple competing failure causes. Units start at normal stress, and stress is raised at a preset time only if the number of early failures is below a chosen threshold; testing ends after a fixed number of failures. The method assumes independent exponential failure times for each cause, uses the cumulative exposure model, and accounts for sampling, test duration, salvage, rejection, and elevated-stress costs. The authors derive a Bayes decision rule and optimize sample size, failure count, early-failure threshold, and, when not fixed, stress-change time to minimize expected loss. They illustrate the method with numerical comparisons, simulated data, and laboratory life-test data for solar lighting devices with capacitor and controller failures.
key_results: In the numerical example, the adaptive plan had expected risk 35.964 compared with 36.582 for the conventional non-accelerated plan, a reported relative risk saving of 1.718%; the accelerated plan had the same risk as the adaptive plan in that scenario. Across the reported parameter scenarios, the largest relative risk saving over the non-accelerated plan was 2.526%. For the solar-device example with the stress-change time fixed at 5 hundred hours, the selected adaptive design used 7 units and stopped at 5 failures, with risk 77.126; the reported risks were 77.283 for the accelerated plan and 77.236 for the non-accelerated plan. The paper also reports that the fitted parametric reliability curves were close to the nonparametric curves for both failure causes and the whole unit in this dataset.
key_equations:
Survival under elevated stress: \[R(t)=\exp\{-\lambda_0\tau_1-\lambda_1(t-\tau_1)\},\quad t>\tau_1\] R(t) is unit survival probability at time t, lambda_0 and lambda_1 are the total failure rates across causes at normal and elevated stress, and tau_1 is the stress-change time.

Bayes lot decision: \[a_B(D')=\begin{cases}1,&\mathbb{E}[h(\lambda)\mid D']\le C_r,\\0,&\mathbb{E}[h(\lambda)\mid D']>C_r.\end{cases}\] a_B is the decision to accept or reject based on transformed data D', the conditional expectation is the posterior expected acceptance loss h of the baseline failure-rate vector lambda, and C_r is the lot-rejection cost.

Optimal design: \[q^*=\arg\min_q R_B(q,a_B)\] q is the sampling design, including sample size, target failure count, early-failure threshold, and stress-change time, and R_B is its expected Bayes risk under the Bayes decision rule a_B.
limitations_stated: The authors do not present a separate limitations section. They describe the current work as using the exponential lifetime distribution and identify extensions to other lifetime distributions, censoring schemes, and tests with more than two stress stages.
limitations_unstated: The model assumes independent exponential failure times for distinct causes and uses the cumulative exposure model to connect stress levels, so dependence between causes or stress-induced changes in failure mechanisms may not be represented. The real-data illustration is one solar-device test dataset, and the paper does not establish performance on field data or across a broad range of products and operating conditions.
future_work_stated: The authors propose extending the method to other lifetime distributions, alternative censoring schemes, and step-stress tests with more than two stages.
future_work_unstated: Further work could allow dependent competing causes and covariates or changing operating conditions that affect each cause differently. The plans could also be tested on field data and evaluated for system-level outcomes and practical lot-disposition decisions under uncertainty in costs and prior information.

summary: The paper addresses how to choose when to remove surviving units during a Type-II progressive-censoring life test. Exhaustive search becomes impractical as the number of possible censoring schemes grows, so the authors develop a genetic algorithm to search for a low-cost scheme. Their cost combines the number of failures, expected test duration, and imprecision of estimated lifetime quantiles. The numerical illustrations use a Weibull lifetime model and specified cost coefficients; the paper does not use field or experimental failure data. The authors report that their method finds better schemes than the comparison search methods in small examples and provides optimal or near-optimal solutions for larger examples.
key_results: For a Weibull model with shape 2, scale 1, 15 units, and 5 failures, the genetic algorithm found a cost of 107.0203, compared with 110.433 for variable neighborhood search. For 45 units and 15 failures with shape 0.5 and scale 1, the reported costs were 296.3334 for the genetic algorithm and 305.052 for variable neighborhood search. The authors also report solutions for tests with up to 65 units and 15 failures. In the tested sensitivity examples, the reported relative efficiencies were 1.0000 for the examined changes in model parameters or cost coefficients.

Feasible censoring schemes: \[\sum_{i=1}^{m}R_i=n-m,\qquad R_i\geq 0,\qquad R\in CS(n,m)\] Here n is the number of test units, m is the fixed number of failures, R_i is the number removed after failure i, i indexes the failures, and CS(n,m) is the set of admissible schemes; the removals sum to the units not observed to fail.

Cost-minimization design: \[\min_{R\in CS(n,m)}\xi(R)\] The method seeks the censoring scheme R in the admissible set CS(n,m) that minimizes cost xi, given the test size n and fixed failure count m.
limitations_stated: The authors do not give a formal limitations section. They note that the optimal scheme depends on the assumed lifetime-distribution parameters and cost coefficients, and describe their algorithm's solutions as optimal or near-optimal.
limitations_unstated: The numerical evaluation is limited to Weibull examples with specified parameter and cost values, so performance for other lifetime distributions and real field tests is not demonstrated. The algorithm is stochastic, but the paper gives limited detail about settings such as population size, random seeds, and stopping rules, which makes independent reproduction and assessment of solution stability difficult.
future_work_stated: The authors propose extending the algorithm to other variants of progressive censoring, with suitable adjustments, and state that this work will appear in future papers.
future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to test the method with field failure data and with lifetime distributions beyond the Weibull model, including settings with changing operating conditions or additional failure mechanisms. Further work could also quantify solution stability across repeated runs and evaluate how optimized censoring schemes affect decisions at the system level.

summary: The paper develops an adaptive Bayesian optimization (BO) method to reduce the cost of designing reliable solder joints. The method adaptively selects Gaussian process (GP) surrogate models and candidate designs while minimizing the nonlinear accumulated creep strain predicted by finite element method (FEM) simulations. The engineering example uses simulated results for a package on a printed circuit board under repeated temperature cycles from −40 to 125 °C. Sensitivity analysis reduces the five-parameter design problem to three parameters for the reported optimization runs. The adaptive methods improve the best-found strain and can reach comparable results with fewer expensive simulations than standard BO.
key_results: On the solder-joint case with coefficient of thermal expansion before glass transition (CTE1) set to 6 ppm/°C, the best adaptive result had 0.199% accumulated creep strain, 2.9% below the best standard BO result of 0.205% after 100 objective evaluations. With CTE1 set to 8.5 ppm/°C, the best adaptive result was 0.106%, compared with 0.107% for standard BO; the reported average improvement across iterations was 3.1%. The authors report that adaptive BO reached its optimized result with at least 50 fewer expensive objective evaluations than the worst-case standard BO scheme, out of the 100-evaluation budget. In synthetic tests on the six-dimensional Sphere and three-dimensional AlpineN2 objectives, adaptive methods generally improved on the worst-case standard BO reference, with results varying by objective and performance quartile.

limitations_unstated: The engineering evaluation is based on one simulated package and board setup, not physical test results or field failure data, and accumulated creep strain is a damage indicator rather than a measured lifetime or failure probability. summary: This tutorial explains how progressive wear or performance loss can lead to a soft failure when a measured characteristic crosses a chosen threshold. It introduces general path models and stochastic process models for describing degradation, estimating failure-time distributions, and predicting remaining useful life. The paper discusses repeated measurements on the same units and destructive tests that measure different units at different times, using laboratory and field examples such as lasers, coatings, adhesive bonds, metal fatigue, and road sections. future_work_stated: The authors identify multivariate and functional degradation data, sensor-based methods, and Bayesian and machine-learning approaches as active directions. future_work_unstated: Future studies could compare the reviewed models using shared field datasets, prespecified failure thresholds, and prospective prediction tests, including explicit evaluation of extrapolation from accelerated conditions.
