Transition probabilities from transition rates: \[P(t)=\exp(Qt)\] P(t) is the transition probability matrix at time t, Q is the transition rate matrix, and t is elapsed time or age.
limitations_stated: The authors state that their deterioration matrices are estimated without pooling across engine types and time regions, and propose partial pooling as a possible improvement. They also report that calibration diagnostics were not uniform for the maintenance probability from state 2 to state 1 and the deterioration rate from state 2 to state 3, indicating inference-computation problems for those parameters.
limitations_unstated: The model turns standardized annual failure counts into three discrete states, so it discards variation within each state and depends on the chosen cutoffs. Deterioration and maintenance may remain difficult to identify separately from these annual observations, and the test sets are internal random splits of the same fleet rather than independent field validation. Because the military data are scaled and the paper reports no maintenance-cost comparison, practical performance and policy value cannot be directly assessed from the reported results.
future_work_stated: The authors propose learning deterioration transitions hierarchically, with partial pooling across engine types and across the four time regions. They also propose incorporating prior knowledge about engine deterioration and operating patterns, and identify maintenance-policy recommendations as a direction for further research.
future_work_unstated: Future work could include operating hours, mission intensity, environment, and repair history as covariates, and distinguish different failure mechanisms rather than relying on a single three-state classification. It could also model interactions among ship systems and compare maintenance decisions using explicit reliability and cost objectives. Validation on an independent fleet or unscaled operational records would help establish how well the estimates transfer to practice.

summary: This paper compares Bayesian methods for choosing accelerated life testing models when their posterior distributions are too complex for closed-form calculation. It examines a generalized Eyring-Weibull model and a generalized Eyring-Birnbaum-Saunders model, and compares the deviance information criterion with several ways of estimating Bayes factors. The models describe how temperature and humidity stresses affect device lifetimes, with gamma priors on the model parameters. The application uses 21 complete failure times from an accelerated test of a device at different temperature and humidity combinations. The main finding is that model-selection conclusions vary by estimation method, although the deviance information criterion and posterior predictive comparisons generally give stronger support to the Birnbaum-Saunders model than to the Weibull model.
key_results: The lowest deviance information criterion was 248.9 for the generalized Eyring-Birnbaum-Saunders model with flat gamma priors, compared with 278.4 for the best-scoring generalized Eyring-Weibull model. In pairwise comparisons, the Laplace-Metropolis estimates strongly favored the generalized Eyring-Weibull model with subjective priors, while the harmonic mean estimates favored the Weibull model with flat priors and the posterior predictive estimates gave the strongest overall support to the Birnbaum-Saunders model with flat priors. The estimated log marginal likelihoods also differed across methods: the Laplace-Metropolis estimate was highest for the Weibull model with subjective priors at -145.1006, the harmonic mean estimate was highest for the Weibull model with flat priors at -141.5369, and the posterior predictive estimate was highest for the Birnbaum-Saunders model with flat priors at -136.8164. For model fitting, the authors used one chain per model, a burn-in of 50000 iterations, and 200000 posterior samples; they report Monte Carlo error below 5% of the sample standard deviation for every parameter.

Bayes factor: \[B_{ij}=\frac{f(x\mid m_i)}{f(x\mid m_j)}\] B sub ij compares models i and j; f of x given a model is that model's marginal likelihood; x is the observed data; and m sub i and m sub j denote the two models.

Posterior predictive density estimate: \[\widehat{f}_{PPD}(x\mid x,m_i)=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{t=1}^{N}f(x\mid\theta_{m_i}^{(t)},m_i)\] The estimated posterior predictive density for data x under model m sub i is the average of the likelihood across N posterior samples; t indexes a sample and theta is the sampled parameter vector.
limitations_stated: The authors state that the simple Monte Carlo marginal-likelihood estimator caused computational problems for some models and was therefore omitted from the application. They also note that the harmonic mean estimator can be unstable and have infinite variance, and that the Laplace-Metropolis estimator works well for symmetric distributions, whereas some posteriors in their application were skewed.
limitations_unstated: The application contains only 21 failure times from a small number of temperature-humidity combinations, so the comparison may not represent other products, stress ranges, or failure mechanisms. The paper does not validate lifetime extrapolations against field data, and its conclusions may depend strongly on the chosen gamma prior specifications and on the estimation method.
future_work_stated: None stated.
future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to test the comparison methods on larger experiments with more stress combinations and on field-lifetime data, including checks of extrapolation to normal operating conditions. summary: This review explains how reliability engineering can be applied to artificial intelligence systems, which may fail because of software, hardware, changing operating conditions, poor data, or model weaknesses. It organizes the work using the SMART framework and describes reliability measures, failure analysis, statistical assessment, and test planning. The authors connect traditional lifetime, degradation, and recurrent-event methods to artificial intelligence and propose modelling failures as events affected by external conditions and internal model properties. The paper draws on public autonomous-vehicle testing records and an incident database, alongside illustrative classification examples and reviewed studies. It concludes that existing approaches provide useful starting points, but data scarcity and the dependence of artificial intelligence performance on its operating environment make reliable assessment difficult.
key_results: This is a review and tutorial rather than a single new empirical comparison, so it does not report one overall estimation-accuracy or prediction-error score. Of 126 incidents listed in the artificial intelligence incident database, the authors identify 72 as reliability-related, and 29 of those involved death or injury. In the autonomous-vehicle illustration, a flexible spline model follows the observed cumulative disengagement counts for Waymo more closely than the less flexible parametric models; estimated event rates decline over time for Waymo, Cruise, and Pony AI, while Zoox's estimated rate remains approximately level. The paper also reports a separate simulation-to-track comparison from a cited study: 62.5% of unsafe simulated tests led to unsafe track behavior, while 93.3% of safe simulated tests led to safe track behavior.
key_equations:
Failure-event intensity framework: \[\lambda[t;x(t),z]=\sum_{j=1}^{k}\lambda_j[t;x(t)]p_j(z;\beta_j)\] The overall failure-event intensity lambda is the sum over event types j of each event's arrival intensity lambda_j, depending on external conditions x, multiplied by its probability p_j of causing failure, which depends on internal system properties z and coefficients beta_j; k is the number of event types.

Reliability over time: \[R(t;\theta)=\Pr(T>t)\] R is the probability that lifetime T exceeds time t, and theta denotes the parameters of the lifetime model.
limitations_stated: The authors say the paper is a general discussion with illustrations, not an exhaustive literature review. They identify limited public availability of reliability data and the cost and time required to collect field data as challenges, and note that the paper focuses on reliability rather than other aspects such as safety, trustworthiness, and security.
limitations_unstated: The paper does not report a systematic literature-search or selection procedure, so the coverage and reproducibility of its review are difficult to assess. Its proposed general failure-intensity framework is illustrative rather than validated as a common model across applications; the cited examples do not establish its predictive performance on independent field data or its sensitivity to dependence among repeated events.
future_work_stated: The authors propose building a repository of artificial intelligence reliability datasets and exploring Bayesian methods for reliability modelling. They also call for further modelling of accelerated tests, including linking accelerated test conditions to normal-use reliability.
future_work_unstated: Future studies could validate the proposed event framework prospectively on multiple field datasets, with explicit checks for dependence among events and changes in operating conditions. They could also connect component-level failures and failure causes to system-level reliability and use those estimates to guide test allocation and design decisions.

summary: Lumber can lose strength under sustained or repeated loading, so reliability estimates may degrade when load duration is not represented. The paper combines three duration-of-load models—the US model, the Canadian model, and a Gamma process model—using Bayesian model averaging to account for both parameter and model uncertainty. The models are fitted to laboratory time-to-failure data from western Hemlock lumber, including specimens that survived to the end of testing. The analysis simulates residential, snow, and wind loads and estimates failure over a 50-year period. The Canadian model receives most of the posterior model probability, and the combined estimates lie closer to its reliability estimates than to those from the Gamma process model.
key_results: Using equal prior probabilities for the three models, the approximate posterior probabilities are 0.00 for the US model, 0.88 for the Canadian model, and 0.12 for the Gamma process model. The Bayesian information criterion values are −5898, −6188, and −6184, respectively, with the US model's poorer fit explaining its negligible model probability. Across all four load scenarios, the combined 95% credible intervals contain the estimates from the individual models; reliability is higher under residential loads than under the other scenarios, and lower for snow in Quebec City than for snow in Vancouver.

summary: The paper addresses reliability-based design optimization (RBDO), where designs must meet probability-of-failure limits despite uncertainty in design variables and parameters. Existing efficient single-loop approaches based on the first-order reliability method (FORM) can give inaccurate failure probabilities when constraints are nonlinear, leading to designs that violate reliability requirements. The authors propose the response surface single-loop (RSSL) method, which fits quadratic models to constraints and estimates failure probabilities with closed-form higher-order formulas without searching for a most probable point (MPP). They evaluate it on mathematical examples and a simulated vehicle side-impact crashworthiness problem, using computational model outputs and Monte Carlo checks. The paper reports that RSSL generally achieves more accurate reliability results than the compared FORM-based methods while using substantially fewer function evaluations than nested reliability-optimization methods.
key_results: For the first mathematical benchmark, RSSL used 24 function evaluations, compared with 1,227 for the double-loop performance measure approach; its Monte Carlo reliability indices were 2.9725 and 3.0015 against a target of 3. For the vehicle crashworthiness problem with constant standard deviations and target reliability 0.9, the authors report that RSSL alone satisfied all probabilistic constraints; the reported objective was 24.801 kg, and RSSL used 41 function evaluations versus 3,324 for the double-loop performance measure approach and 26,984 for the double-loop reliability index approach. At target reliability 0.99865, RSSL again was reported as the only compared method satisfying all constraints, with objective 30.5009 kg. In the separate nonlinear example, FORM-based methods produced substantial errors; for the more demanding failure-probability target of 0.1350%, RSSL’s reported Monte Carlo probabilities were 0.1784% and 0.1346%, with the first constraint still exceeding the target.
key_equations:
Quadratic constraint surrogate: \[Q(z)=z^{T}Az+k^{T}z+c\] Q is the quadratic response-surface approximation of a constraint, z is its input vector, A is the quadratic coefficient matrix, k is the linear coefficient vector, c is the constant term, and T denotes transpose.

Failure-probability constraint: \[P_f=\Pr[Q(z)<0]\leq P_{f,\mathrm{all}}\] P_f is the estimated probability that the quadratic constraint Q evaluated at random inputs z is below zero, Pr means probability, and P_f,all is the allowed failure probability.
limitations_stated: The quadratic response surfaces are fitted around the deterministic solution, so errors can arise when active-constraint MPPs are far from that solution or the constraints are highly nonlinear between the solution and those points. The authors note that surrogate updates may be needed in such cases and that higher accuracy may require a more expensive sequential MPP-based approach.
limitations_unstated: The vehicle application relies on quadratic surrogate models fitted from 33 computational simulations, so reliability estimates depend on how well those surrogates represent the underlying crash model near relevant failure regions. The evaluation consists of benchmark examples and simulation-based checks rather than validation against observed field crash outcomes, and the rare-event checks can themselves require very large simulation runs.
future_work_stated: The authors suggest using an update scheme for the response-surface model when its local fit may be inadequate. They also propose developing a sequential MPP-based approach with a trust region and analytical sensitivities for higher-order failure probabilities when greater accuracy is needed.
future_work_unstated: The method could be validated against physical crash-test or field data, with explicit assessment of surrogate uncertainty and the effect of that uncertainty on failure-probability estimates. Further work could also test additional failure mechanisms and operating conditions, and examine system-level reliability and design decisions under uncertainty in multiple correlated constraints.

summary: The paper presents a preprocessing method for operational sensor data used to diagnose mechanical equipment. It addresses problems such as missing readings, irrelevant or redundant sensors, outliers, and the lack of health labels in real machinery data. The method combines engineers’ knowledge, statistical screening, preparation of data for model training, and labels derived from maintenance records and time before failures. It is demonstrated using operational data from an offshore vapor recovery unit and a copper mining crusher. The authors report that the resulting datasets supported strong diagnostic results for some classifiers, while performance differed between the two assets and models.
key_results: For the vapor recovery unit scrubber, the random forest and neural network each achieved a test F1-score of 0.99; the support vector machine and Bayesian neural network achieved 0.97 and 0.96. For the crusher, the random forest achieved a test F1-score of 0.95 and the neural network 0.91, while the support vector machine and Bayesian neural network achieved 0.97 and 0.70. In a comparison on the vapor recovery unit, balanced principal-component methods achieved test F1-scores of 0.98, compared with 0.99 for the proposed method’s best models; the unsupervised autoencoder achieved a test F1-score of 0.33 and classified all degraded test cases as healthy. The screening retained 66 informative features from 188 for the vapor recovery unit, and the authors report final feature counts equal to 50% of the original for the crusher.

limitations_stated: The method was developed for mechanical assets and was not tested on electrical systems, whose failures may develop much faster. It does not cover feature extraction from high-frequency signals, and selecting outlier thresholds and identifying unrelated sensors require manual input. The authors also note that the chosen degradation and transition windows may not match the component or failure mode and can cause label overlap or mislabeling.
limitations_unstated: The evaluation covers only two assets and one selected component in each, so the reported performance may not generalize to other equipment, sites, or failure mechanisms. Data points were randomly sampled for training and testing; because sensor records are time-dependent, nearby or temporally related observations may occur across splits and make test performance optimistic. The class balancing procedure also samples healthy observations down to the degraded sample count, so the results do not establish performance at the naturally occurring failure prevalence.
future_work_stated: The authors encourage researchers to explore further preprocessing tools and to report preprocessing steps in detail to improve transparency and replication. They also note that the health-label method could be adapted to remaining useful life labels when enough failure events are available.
future_work_unstated: Test the pipeline prospectively across additional operating sites and asset types, with time-separated evaluation and performance measures that account for rare failures. Extend the labels and features to multiple interacting components, additional operating conditions and covariates, and failure mechanisms beyond the mechanical cases studied. summary: The paper develops adaptive multi-fidelity Gaussian process reliability analysis (AMGPRA) to estimate failure probabilities when accurate but expensive models and cheaper, less accurate models are both available. The method uses a collective learning function (CLF) to select a point and the model source together, based on how much the point is expected to improve the surrogate across a set of candidates and relative to its evaluation cost. It models limit-state responses with a multi-fidelity Gaussian process, using model outputs from three mathematical examples and a transmission-tower engineering example. The examples use simulated or computational-model data rather than observed field failure data. Overall, the proposed approach achieves similar or better accuracy at lower evaluation cost than the compared methods in most mathematical examples, and it converges for the tower example where the comparison methods do not provide results.
key_results: For the multimodal example with two model fidelities, AMGPRA using the expected feasible function cost 12.58 and has an average relative error of 0.03 percent, compared with 13.31 and 0.06 percent for multi-fidelity efficient global reliability analysis (mfEGRA). With three fidelities in that example, the reported costs are 12.32 for AMGPRA and 12.87 for mfEGRA, with 0.02 percent average relative error for both. In the ten-dimensional example, AMGPRA costs 16.8 with zero percent average relative error, compared with 18.16 and 0.02 percent for mfEGRA. For the tower example, AMGPRA estimates failure probability as 2.46 times 10 to the minus 2 at cost 28.5, using an average of 18.1 high-fidelity and 25.6 low-fidelity training points; active learning reliability method combining Kriging and Monte Carlo simulation (AK-MCS) did not converge even with 300 high-fidelity training points, and mfEGRA did not function properly in this case.
key_equations: Cost-normalized collective learning function: \[\mathrm{CLF}(x,l)=\frac{1}{N_c c_l(x)}\sum_{i=1}^{N_c}\left[\ell_f(\mu_i,\sigma_i^2)-\ell_f(\mu_i,\sigma_{i|x,l}^2)\right]\] The collective learning function scores a candidate location x from information source l by averaging the reduction in core learning-function value across N_c candidate points and dividing by that source’s evaluation cost c_l(x); i indexes candidates, ell_f is the core learning function, mu_i is the current predicted mean, sigma_i squared is the current variance, and sigma_{i|x,l} squared is the hypothetical future variance after adding the candidate.
limitations_stated: The authors use only the expected feasible function and a modified version of the U learning function as cores for the collective learning function. They also state that the approach is limited on high-dimensional problems because of the general limitations of Gaussian process metamodels.
limitations_unstated: The main numerical comparisons use constructed mathematical models, and the tower application uses finite element outputs rather than field observations; therefore, performance on real operating data is not established. The tower result has no Monte Carlo reference estimate or successful comparison-method estimate, and the paper does not report uncertainty intervals for that failure-probability estimate.
future_work_stated: The authors propose investigating alternative, potentially more suitable learning functions as cores for the collective learning function. They also identify extending multi-fidelity reliability analysis to high-dimensional problems as an important future direction.
future_work_unstated: Further work could test the method against field observations or independent high-fidelity benchmarks for infrastructure systems, including uncertainty bounds on estimated failure probabilities. It could also study multiple failure mechanisms and operating conditions, and assess whether the method’s point-selection strategy supports system-level reliability or maintenance decisions.

summary: Battery health and end-of-life forecasting are difficult in off-grid solar systems because operating conditions vary, sensor data can be inaccurate or incomplete, and batteries cannot easily be taken offline for controlled tests. The authors model internal resistance as a function of operating conditions and time, then use that estimate together with usage-related stress factors to predict failure. They evaluate the approach on field measurements from 1,027 lead-acid batteries in sub-Saharan Africa, each observed for 400 to 760 days, and use a laboratory voltage test to support estimation of state of charge. The field dataset contains 620 million measurement rows, reduced to 39 million for modelling. The combined model reaches 73% balanced accuracy eight weeks before failure and 82% at the end-of-life point, outperforming the resistance-only benchmark.
key_results: Using resistance and its rate of change together with stress factors, the classifier achieved 82.4% balanced accuracy at the end-of-life point and 73.0% 56 days beforehand. The benchmark achieved 66.0% at the end-of-life point and 50.7% at 56 days, while the resistance-based model without stress factors achieved 77.3% and 63.1%, respectively. Stress factors alone achieved 70.7% at the end-of-life point and 66.4% at 56 days; their average across the tested prediction horizons was 68%. The resistance model produced smoother health trajectories than the benchmark by accounting for operating-condition effects.

limitations_stated: The authors acknowledge that repair records can mislabel batteries because repair depends on customer decisions, creating possible false positive and false negative failure labels. limitations_unstated: The data come from a selected group of batteries from one provider and one manufacturer, with healthy units sampled to create a roughly balanced dataset; the reported results may therefore not transfer directly to other products or populations. future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be prospective validation on independent deployments, with explicit treatment of batteries whose failure time is not observed and with checks of probability calibration. summary: The paper develops the record-based transmuted generalized linear exponential distribution, extending a generalized linear exponential lifetime model. The extension is intended to address the baseline model’s inability to fit decreasing or bathtub-shaped failure rates, while also accommodating increasing failure rates. The authors derive distributional properties and several parameter-estimation methods, and assess estimation using simulated samples and a real dataset of 50 failure times measured in weeks. In the real-data comparison, the proposed distribution fits better overall than the seven alternative lifetime distributions considered. The paper provides a theoretical and numerical illustration of a flexible lifetime model, rather than a maintenance or cost optimization method.
key_results: In simulations with 5,000 replicates and sample sizes of 20, 50, 100, and 200, the authors report generally small estimation biases and mean squared errors, although the results do not improve uniformly with increasing sample size. For the parameter setting alpha = 0.8, beta = 0.8, gamma = 1, and p = 0.7, the maximum-likelihood mean squared error for alpha decreases from 0.1665 at sample size 20 to 0.0784 at sample size 200. For the 50-observation failure-time dataset, the proposed model has the lowest reported negative twice log-likelihood, 258.2350, and the lowest Akaike information criterion, 266.2350, among the eight models. It also has the smallest reported Kolmogorov-Smirnov, Cramer-von Mises, and Anderson-Darling statistics, at 0.0869, 0.0503, and 0.2836, respectively; its corresponding reported p-values are 0.8698, 0.8768, and 0.9497.

limitations_stated: The authors state that their theorem does not determine the probability-density shape when beta is nonzero and gamma is between 0 and 1, or when beta is zero and gamma is between 0.5 and 1. future_work_stated: The authors encourage practical use of the proposed model in future applications, but they do not specify a particular research direction.
future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to validate the model on larger operational datasets, including censored observations, and compare its calibrated lifetime predictions with competing models. key_results: The simulation study used 10,000 samples, with sample sizes of 50, 150, and 250; the authors report that bias and mean squared error generally decreased as sample size, number of observed failures, or stress-change time increased. summary: Estimating structural failure probabilities can require many costly model evaluations, especially for rare failures and nonlinear or multiple failure regions. This paper surveys active-learning approaches and organizes them into a modular framework with a surrogate model, a reliability estimator, a learning function, and a stopping rule. The authors benchmarked 39 combinations of these components on 20 computational problems, including two finite-element structural models, with input dimensions from 2 to 100. The results show that no single combination is best for every problem, but using a surrogate with a sufficiently accurate reliability estimator is broadly beneficial. key_results: The benchmark tested 39 strategies on 20 problems, giving 11,700 repeated analyses; the comparison including two direct-simulation baselines comprised 12,300 analyses. Problems ranged from 2 to 100 input dimensions, with reference failure probabilities from about 3.14 × 10⁻² to 1.32 × 10⁻⁷. No strategy consistently led on every problem and metric, but polynomial-chaos Kriging, subset simulation, the deviation-number learning function, and either reliability-index bounds or the combined stopping rule were recommended overall. In an external black-box challenge covering 27 component- and system-reliability problems, the authors' selected approach was reported as the most accurate and efficient on 24 problems. The paper reports comparative rankings and error analyses, rather than one overall numerical accuracy or cost improvement applicable to all problems.

limitations_unstated: The benchmark mainly uses analytical test functions and includes only two finite-element structural examples, so its results may not transfer directly to diverse field structures or operational data. future_work_unstated: The methods could be tested against field measurements and independently implemented reliability solvers to assess transferability beyond the selected simulated problems. summary: Expensive simulator evaluations make it difficult to estimate rare failure probabilities, and a surrogate that misses parts of the failure boundary can produce a poor sampling distribution and unreliable estimates. The paper introduces the entropy-based contour locator (ECL), which chooses new inputs where a Gaussian process (GP) is uncertain about failure or non-failure, and extends the strategy to select batches of inputs. The authors combine these designs with multifidelity importance sampling (MFIS) to estimate failure probabilities. They evaluate the approach on simulated Branin-Hoo, Ishigami, and Hartmann-6 functions and on a simulated impact-damage model of a Z-2 spacesuit. ECL generally identifies failure regions and estimates their volumes more reliably than the tested alternatives, while requiring less computation for adaptive design.
key_results: Across 30 repetitions of each synthetic contour-finding test, ECL was among the best methods for sensitivity and failure-region volume error; on the six-dimensional Hartmann-6 test, its volume error was nearly an order of magnitude smaller than those of the other methods. For Hartmann-6, the average time to build the design was 4.40 minutes for ECL and 0.78 minutes for batch ECL, compared with 428.4 minutes for CLoVER. In the Ishigami and Hartmann-6 MFIS tests, ECL-based estimates were centered around the respective reported failure probabilities of about 1.9 × 10^-4 and 9.96 × 10^-6, whereas ordinary space-filling designs often produced zero estimates when failure classification used the GP mean. In the spacesuit example, the ECL-plus-MFIS estimate had the narrowest reported confidence interval among the three compared estimates, although the intervals overlapped.

future_work_unstated: Further evaluation could compare the estimates against physical impact tests and other field-relevant conditions for spacesuit materials. summary: High-dimensional structural reliability calculations can require many costly model evaluations, while conventional surrogate models can lose accuracy as input dimension grows. The paper proposes a method that uses a sparse polynomial chaos expansion to estimate the average gradient information and identify a lower-dimensional active subspace, then fits a hybrid polynomial correlated function expansion surrogate in that reduced space. The method is tested on simulated benchmark problems: a Sobol function with 10, 40, and 100 inputs, a 20-variable composite beam, and a 33-variable space truss. Its accuracy is compared with Monte Carlo estimates and established reliability methods. Across these examples, the proposed method gives close agreement with the Monte Carlo benchmarks while generally using fewer model evaluations than competing accurate approaches.
key_results: For the Sobol function with 10, 40, and 100 inputs, the proposed method's reported reliability-index errors relative to Monte Carlo were 0.82%, 0.3141%, and 1.011%, respectively; it identified a two-dimensional active subspace in each case. For the composite beam, the error was 0.8038% with 800 model evaluations, compared with 7.9520% for the first-order reliability method and 11.7580% for the sparse polynomial chaos expansion; the second-order reliability method did not converge after 10^4 evaluations. For the space truss, the proposed method had a 0.6751% error with 1,000 evaluations, compared with 3.8737% for polynomial chaos expansion, 27.1076% for the first-order reliability method, and 24.7368% for the second-order reliability method. future_work_stated: The authors propose combining the three stages into a simultaneous procedure, investigating nonlinear manifold-learning methods, and studying performance on dynamical systems.

summary: Disengagements during autonomous driving are used as a proxy for failures of the artificial intelligence system, with lower event rates taken to indicate greater reliability. The paper models these recurrent events with a nonhomogeneous Poisson process, adjusting the event intensity for each vehicle’s time-varying mileage. It compares established parametric models with a flexible monotone spline model, and uses likelihood estimation, bootstrap intervals, and a frailty model to assess uncertainty and differences among vehicles. The real data cover December 2017 through November 2019 for Waymo, Cruise, Pony AI, and Zoox; the paper also evaluates the methods using simulated data. The analysis finds decreasing event rates for three manufacturers, a roughly constant rate for Zoox, and little evidence of variation in event processes among vehicles within each manufacturer.
key_results: In the real-data analysis, the spline model had the lowest Akaike information criterion for Waymo, Cruise, and Pony AI: 2756.21, 2046.09, and 479.73, respectively; for Zoox its value was 688.78, slightly above the Musa-Okumoto model’s 687.69. The selected parametric models were Gompertz for Waymo and Cruise, Weibull for Pony AI, and Musa-Okumoto for Zoox. By the end of the study, the reported event rates were about 0.05 events per thousand miles for Waymo and Cruise and about 0.1 for Pony AI; Zoox had a roughly constant rate of about 0.6. Frailty-test p-values ranged from 0.8400 to 0.9972, indicating little evidence of population heterogeneity in these data. summary: This paper presents certifiable risk-based design optimization (CRiBDO) as an alternative to reliability-based design optimization (RBDO), which constrains the probability of failure (PoF). key_results: For the short-column example, the authors report that RBDO and bPoF-based optimization achieve nearly identical design frontiers when compared at similar estimated PoF or bPoF levels. For the short-column example, convexity gives the bPoF formulation a global-optimality guarantee for its sample-average optimization problem, whereas the RBDO solutions have no such guarantee in the paper.

limitations_stated: The authors state that estimating buffered probability of failure and superquantiles can be expensive. They also note that superquantile estimates can be less stable when rare, large tail outcomes have a strong influence, and that direct optimization can be nonsmooth.
limitations_unstated: The evaluation uses two simulated engineering examples and does not validate the proposed designs against field or operational data, so the results do not establish performance under real-world model error. summary: The paper studies how to compare the lifetimes of k-out-of-n systems, whose lifetimes are represented by order statistics of component lifetimes. limitations_unstated: The system comparisons assume independent, identically distributed component lifetimes from a common parent distribution in the one-sample setting; dependence between components and changing operating conditions are not addressed. summary: The paper proposes a Bayesian method for estimating recurrent failures in multiple repairable systems when different failure causes may be dependent. Each cause-specific failure stream is modelled with a power law process (PLP), and a shared frailty term represents system-to-system heterogeneity and induces dependence between causes. The frailty distribution is estimated flexibly using a Dirichlet process mixture (DPM), with a hybrid Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) and Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) procedure; closed-form posterior estimates are available for the PLP parameters. The method is evaluated using simulated failure histories and automobile warranty data with three failure causes. The analyses indicate accurate parameter estimates in the simulations and meaningful heterogeneity and dependence in the automobile data.
key_results: In simulations with 50,000 replications and 10, 50, or 100 systems, parameter-estimate biases were generally near zero, and mean squared errors (MSEs) decreased as the number of systems increased. For most PLP parameters, reported 95 percent interval coverage was around 0.94 to 0.95; coverage for frailty variance was lower in some small-sample settings, including 0.8395 when the variance was 0.5 and there were 10 systems. The warranty analysis used 439 automobiles, including 267 with no failures; the observed failure counts were 76, 87, and 111 for the three causes. Estimated shape parameters were 0.300, 0.409, and 0.698, all below 1, and the estimated frailty variance was 1.755 with a reported 95 percent interval of 1.050 to 2.777. The paper does not report a comparison against an alternative estimation method.
key_equations:
Cause-specific intensity with shared frailty: \[\lambda_q(t\mid Z_j)=Z_j\beta_q\alpha_q t^{\beta_q-1}T^{-\beta_q}\] The intensity lambda for cause q at time t in system j is multiplied by frailty Z_j; beta_q and alpha_q are the cause-specific shape and expected-count parameters, and T is the common observation endpoint.

Cumulative intensity at the observation endpoint: \[\Lambda_q(T\mid Z_j)=Z_j\alpha_q\] The cumulative intensity Lambda for cause q by endpoint T in system j equals frailty Z_j times the expected count alpha_q.

Closed-form posterior means for power law parameters: \[\hat{\alpha}_{q}^{Bayes}=\frac{n_q}{m},\qquad \hat{\beta}_{q}^{Bayes}=\frac{n_q+1-\zeta}{n_q}\hat{\beta}_q\] The posterior means of alpha and beta for cause q use n_q, the total count for that cause across m systems, the prior hyperparameter zeta, and beta_hat_q, the maximum-likelihood estimate of beta; the paper states that the estimators are unbiased when zeta equals 2.
limitations_stated: The authors assume identical systems, a common time-truncated observation period, minimal repair, and cause-specific failure processes that follow a power law process. They note that the power law intensity cannot represent non-monotonic failure behavior and propose extending the baseline intensity model and considering other repair types.
limitations_unstated: Dependence is represented through one shared multiplicative frailty per system, so other forms of cause-specific dependence may not be captured. The method is demonstrated on one automobile warranty dataset and the paper reports no external field validation or comparison of predictive performance against competing methods.
future_work_stated: The authors propose extending the approach to model the failure intensity nonparametrically, which could accommodate non-monotonic behavior. They also propose investigating perfect and imperfect repair settings.
future_work_unstated: Further work could include operating conditions and vehicle-level covariates, and assess whether distinct failure mechanisms need separate frailties. Evaluation on additional field datasets, along with out-of-sample prediction and maintenance-decision studies, would test the method's practical value.

summary: The paper studies online detection and classification of unusual logging activity in a computing center, rather than predicting equipment lifetime or physical failures. It models the severity of anomalous time windows with two evolving granular classifiers, which update their rules as log data arrive. The data are operational event-oriented logs from the StoRM back-end service at the Bologna computing center, converted into five activity measures and weak labels from a control chart. Each dataset contains 1,436 instances, and the analysis compares window lengths of 5, 15, 30, and 60 minutes. Accuracy generally improves with longer windows, and the evolving granular neural network achieves the strongest compact-model result at 96.17% accuracy with 60-minute windows.
key_results: For 60-minute windows, the evolving granular neural network reached 96.17% accuracy with a standard deviation of 0.78 percentage points, an average of 10.35 rules, and a processing time of 0.18 seconds; the fuzzy-set-based evolving model reached 85.64% accuracy with a standard deviation of 3.69 points, 12.63 rules, and 0.18 seconds. At 5 minutes, their reported accuracies were 85.00% and 67.27%, respectively. When the number of rules was not tightly constrained, the fuzzy-set-based model reached 96.1% accuracy with about 40 rules, while the neural network reached 96.2% with about 10 rules. limitations_stated: The authors characterize the automatically generated control-chart labels as weak and the classification problem as unbalanced. future_work_unstated: Evaluate the classifiers against independently verified incidents and maintenance records, including data from additional services and computing centers. Future studies could add log-message content and operating-context variables, test other failure mechanisms and system-level effects, and assess how classification outputs support maintenance decisions.

summary: Reliability-based design optimization can become computationally expensive when reliability constraints must be evaluated repeatedly during optimization. This paper proposes approximating the failure probability function (FPF) by estimating the density of design points associated with failure, using iterative partitions that focus additional sampling on low-density regions. Bayesian sequential partitioning estimates density within regions, and regression is used to smooth the result. The method is demonstrated with simulated data for a cantilever box beam, where failure occurs if its first natural frequency lies between 550 and 600 radians per second. The authors report that the resulting probability contours agree with direct simulation and that the method uses far fewer model evaluations in this example.
key_results: For the beam illustration, the authors report 36,000 model evaluations for the proposed method, compared with 5.68 × 10^7 for direct Monte Carlo simulation across the design grid. The probability contours from the proposed method were described as consistent with the direct Monte Carlo results, although no numerical error metric was reported. At allowable failure probabilities of 0.01, 10^-3, and 10^-4, the proposed method gave optimal mean width and height values of [30.0, 32.9], [30.0, 31.5], and [30.0, 30.4] millimeters, respectively; the corresponding direct simulation results were [30.0, 32.7], [30.0, 31.4], and [30.0, 30.4] millimeters.
key_equations: Failure probability from conditional failure-sample density: \[P_F(\boldsymbol{\varphi})=P(F\mid\boldsymbol{\varphi})=\frac{p(\boldsymbol{\varphi}\mid F)P(F)}{p(\boldsymbol{\varphi})}\] The failure probability at design phi equals the conditional failure probability and is the density of design samples given failure multiplied by the augmented-system failure probability and divided by the uniform design density.
limitations_stated: The authors state that selecting a regression function through model comparison is beyond the scope of the paper. They do not otherwise identify specific limitations.
limitations_unstated: The evaluation is a single simulated example with two design variables, and the paper reports no numerical error metric or validation against field or experimental data. It also gives no sampling convergence diagnostics for the modified Metropolis-Hastings procedure, so the impact of chain mixing and dependence on the density estimates is unclear.
future_work_stated: The authors propose conducting computer experiments for cases with more than two design variables.
future_work_unstated: Future studies could quantify approximation error and test the method against field or experimental measurements, including under operating conditions different from those used to build the surrogate. It would also be useful to study multiple failure mechanisms, dependent component failures, and how design decisions change when system-level reliability requirements are imposed.

glossary: REAK = Reliability analysis through Error rate-based Adaptive Kriging, the proposed method.|AK-MCS = Adaptive Kriging with Monte Carlo Simulation, a method used for comparison.|ISKRA = Improved Sequential Kriging Reliability Analysis, a method used for comparison.|ESR = Effective sampling regions, the portions of the input space prioritized by REAK.|MCS = Monte Carlo simulation.|epsilon = The relative error rate of the failure probability estimate; with a hat and max subscript, the estimated maximum error rate.|P_f = Probability of failure; a hat indicates the surrogate estimate.
summary: Estimating very small failure probabilities with costly engineering models can require many model evaluations. This paper proposes REAK, which uses a Kriging surrogate, prioritizes important parts of the input space, and estimates an upper bound on the failure-probability error to guide stopping. The method is evaluated using simulated model outputs for four reliability examples, including nonlinear systems with two, six, and nine random variables. Its estimated error bound is compared with observed error across repeated simulations and is generally conservative. The authors report fewer model evaluations than AK-MCS and ISKRA for most tested error targets, with the largest reported savings reaching 59 percent.
key_results: At a 5 percent target error rate, the paper reports that REAK reduced performance-function evaluations relative to AK-MCS and ISKRA by 52 percent and 50 percent for the four-boundary series example, 56 percent and 59 percent for the modified Rastrigin example, 51 percent and 50 percent for the nonlinear oscillator, and 33 percent and 21 percent for the cantilever tube. In 50 repeated simulations of the first example at that target, REAK averaged 58.36 evaluations, compared with 74.60 for ISKRA and 90.96 for AK-MCS. Across the examples, the estimated maximum error rate was generally larger than the observed error rate; reported probabilities that the bound covered the true error were near or above the nominal 95 percent in the cases discussed. For the cantilever example at a 1 percent target, however, REAK averaged 80.42 evaluations, more than ISKRA at 75.64.
key_equations:
Relative error rate: \[\epsilon=\left|\frac{\hat{P}_f}{P_f^{\mathrm{MCS}}}-1\right|\] Epsilon is the relative error rate, the hatted failure probability is the estimate from the surrogate, and the failure probability marked MCS is the estimate from crude Monte Carlo simulation on the same candidate samples.

Error-bound stopping rule: \[\hat{\epsilon}_{\max}\leq\epsilon_{\mathrm{target}}\] The hatted maximum epsilon is REAK's estimated upper bound on the error rate, and target epsilon is the user-prescribed error threshold that the bound must not exceed.
limitations_stated: The authors state that REAK is challenging to apply to very high-dimensional problems because Kriging requires repeated inversions of large covariance matrices. The method assumes that wrong-sign predictions at candidate points are independent; accounting for correlations may improve accuracy for higher error thresholds but would increase computational demands.
limitations_unstated: The evaluation uses simulated benchmark outputs rather than field or operational data, so the reported efficiency and error coverage are not demonstrated on real infrastructure models. The comparisons also rely on generated candidate samples and particular Kriging and sampling settings, leaving performance under different input distributions and modeling choices untested.
future_work_stated: The authors propose applying dimension-reduction techniques for high-dimensional problems and considering correlations among wrong-sign predictions. They also suggest combining REAK with importance sampling or subset simulation, and selecting multiple training points in parallel using unsupervised learning.
future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be validation using field-informed or experimentally measured structural data, including uncertainty in the model itself rather than only uncertainty in its inputs. Further work could also test how REAK behaves for time-dependent failure, competing failure mechanisms, and system-level reliability, then connect its error target to engineering decisions.

summary: The paper models a multi-component series system in which each component can be replaced individually after inspection, but failures between inspections may remain undetected and cause downtime. It represents gradual wear with gamma processes and adds shock damage to each component; in turn, accumulated degradation and previous shocks raise the shock arrival rate. The authors optimize each next inspection interval using the starting degradation of the components and a cost rate that includes inspection, replacement, and downtime costs. They illustrate the method with simulated results for a jet pipe servo-valve, using spool and sleeve components and 100,000 Monte Carlo replications. The mutually dependent model gives lower reliability and shorter optimal inspection intervals than the independent-shock comparison model.
key_results: The reliability curves show lower reliability for the mutually dependent model than for the model with independent Poisson shock arrivals; the paper reports this result qualitatively rather than as a single accuracy or error measure. With both components starting at zero degradation, the optimal interval is 1.432 times 10 to the minus 4 for the independent model and 0.741 times 10 to the minus 4 for the mutually dependent model. For the scenario with spool degradation 4.8 and sleeve degradation 5.5, the reported intervals are 0.023 times 10 to the minus 4 and 0.009 times 10 to the minus 4, respectively.
key_equations:
Shock arrival intensity: \[\lambda_m(t)=(1+\eta m)(\lambda_0+\gamma X_S(t))\] The shock intensity lambda_m(t) depends on time t, shock count m, facilitation factor eta, initial intensity lambda_0, dependence factor gamma, and total system degradation X_S(t).

Total system degradation: \[X_S(t)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(u_i+X_i(t)+\sum_{j=1}^{N(t)}Y_{ij}\right)\] Total degradation X_S(t) sums over n components indexed by i their starting degradation u_i, pure degradation X_i(t), and shock damages Y_ij for shocks j up to N(t) by time t.

Inspection cost rate: \[CR(\tau;u)=\frac{C_I+C_R(1-R(\tau;u))+C_\rho E[\rho]}{\tau}\] The cost rate CR uses inspection interval tau, component starting degradation vector u, inspection cost C_I, replacement cost C_R, reliability R, downtime cost rate C_rho, and expected downtime E[rho].
limitations_stated: The model assumes a series system, that every incoming shock damages the degradation of all components, and that replacement is the only maintenance action. limitations_unstated: The numerical illustration is not validated against field observations: several parameter values are assumed or taken from prior studies, and the paper reports no fitted parameters, confidence intervals, or uncertainty analysis. future_work_stated: The authors propose extending the dynamic inspection plan to system configurations other than series, distinguishing fatal from non-fatal shocks, considering imperfect or minimal repair, and allowing different shock patterns for components.
future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to estimate and validate the model using field degradation and failure records, including uncertainty in parameters and component starting condition. Further work could test changing operating environments and component covariates, and assess how inspection and replacement decisions change when system interactions or additional failure mechanisms are represented.

summary: The paper studies how to estimate software reliability growth when failures follow a power law process (PLP), a non-homogeneous Poisson process (NHPP) with a time-varying failure rate. It estimates the shape parameter using Bayesian analysis with the Higgins-Tsokos (H-T) loss function and examines several parametric and kernel-based prior distributions. The authors compare the Bayesian estimates with maximum likelihood estimates (MLEs) using simulated failure times and Crow’s 40 observed failure times from a developmental test. The comparisons use mean squared error (MSE) for the parameters and relative efficiency for intensity estimates. Across the tested simulations, the Bayesian approach generally has lower estimation error, but its results depend on the selected prior.
key_results: For the simulation with sample size 40 and scale parameter theta equal to 1.7441, the MSE for the Bayesian shape estimate with the Burr prior was 0.000516057, compared with 0.0110573 for the MLE. With true beta equal to 0.7054 and sample size 20, the reported average Bayesian estimate was 0.675263, compared with 0.784026 for the MLE; the true value was 0.7054. For the estimated intensity, the reported relative efficiency ratio for the Bayesian estimate versus the MLE was 0.0761919, with values below 1 favoring the Bayesian estimate under the paper’s criterion. For Crow’s failure data, the Bayesian estimates were beta equal to 0.501199 and theta equal to 2.07144; the paper reports a fitted intensity of 0.347933 times time to the power of negative 0.498801.
key_equations:
Power law process intensity: \[V(t;\beta,\theta)=\frac{\beta}{\theta}\left(\frac{t}{\theta}\right)^{\beta-1}\] V is the failure intensity, t is time, beta is the shape parameter, and theta is the scale parameter.

Bayesian estimate under the Higgins-Tsokos loss: \[\hat{\beta}_{B,HT}=\frac{1}{f_1+f_2}\ln\left(\frac{\int_0^\infty e^{f_1\beta}h(\beta\mid data)\,d\beta}{\int_0^\infty e^{-f_2\beta}h(\beta\mid data)\,d\beta}\right)\] The estimated beta is the Bayesian estimate, f_1 and f_2 are positive loss-function weights, beta is the shape parameter, and h is the posterior density of beta given the observed data.

Conditional reliability between successive failures: \[R_i=\exp\left(-\int_{t_{i-1}}^{t_i}V(x)\,dx\right)\] R_i is conditional reliability over the interval from preceding failure time t_{i-1} to current time t_i, V is the failure intensity, and x is the integration variable for time.
limitations_stated: The authors do not list study limitations explicitly. They do state that the Bayesian estimate is sensitive to prior selection and recommend Jeffreys or kernel priors when prior knowledge of the shape parameter is lacking.
limitations_unstated: The real-data demonstration uses one set of 40 failure times from a developmental test, so it does not establish performance across different software systems or field operating conditions. The simulations generate data under the assumed power law process and use a Burr distribution to generate the shape parameter, limiting how broadly the comparisons test model misspecification; the paper also does not report the computational cost of its numerical integration.
future_work_stated: The authors do not propose specific future research. Their stated practical recommendation is to use Jeffreys or kernel prior distributions when prior knowledge of the shape parameter is unavailable.
future_work_unstated: Further work could evaluate the method on independent field software failure records and test its robustness when the failure process departs from the power law assumption. It could also assess operating-condition covariates, compare prior choices using external validation, and connect reliability estimates to software release or maintenance decisions.

summary: Expensive evaluations of engineering performance functions make conventional reliability analysis costly, while first-order approximations can be inaccurate for nonlinear problems or multiple failure regions. The paper proposes Surrogates for Importance Sampling (S4IS), which adaptively selects evaluations of the original function in two stages: first to identify failure regions, then to focus on important regions and estimate failure probability more accurately. The method uses importance sampling (IS) and is designed to work with different surrogate types, although the examples use Gaussian processes (GPs). It is evaluated in five numerical examples using simulated inputs and computational model outputs, including system reliability, nonlinear limit states, rare failures, and problems with up to 50 random variables. Across these examples, S4IS generally achieves low estimation error with fewer evaluations than the adaptive Kriging-based importance-sampling method (AK-IS), and is more reliable than the first-order reliability method (FORM) in the challenging cases studied.
key_results: In the four-region series-system example, S4IS estimated failure probability with 0.5% relative error using 60.6 performance-function evaluations; the reported coefficient of variation (CoV) was 1.06%, compared with 73.6% relative error for AK-IS. For the nonlinear oscillator, S4IS had 0.9% relative error and CoV below 5.0% with 53.3 evaluations, about half the AK-IS evaluation count. In the example with 50 random variables, S4IS estimated failure probability with 1.0% relative error and CoV below 5.0% using 168.6 evaluations, compared with 1,845.2 evaluations for AK-IS. For the smallest failure probability reported, 9.485 × 10⁻⁷, S4IS achieved 4.7% relative error with 118.6 evaluations; the paper reports that FORM and AK-IS were inaccurate in that example.

summary: Traditional pavement condition inspections rely on visual surveys, which the paper identifies as a safety concern and a possible source of human error. The authors model the pavement condition index (PCI) from pavement deflection readings collected with a falling weight deflectometer (FWD), rather than estimating the score directly from a visual survey. The data are measurements from 236 flexible-pavement segments on the Tehran-Qom freeway in Iran, with PCI scores calculated for those segments. The combined model had the best overall error results among the models tested, supporting the potential use of deflection data to estimate PCI in this case study.
key_results: For the full dataset, the CMIS had an average percent relative error (APRE) of 2.3303%, an average absolute percent relative error (AAPRE) of 11.6768%, a root mean square error (RMSE) of 12.005653, and a standard error (SD) of 0.021081. The authors report that these overall results were better than those of the individual models; for example, the MLP optimized with Levenberg-Marquardt had an overall AAPRE of 14.4877% and RMSE of 14.499431. On the test data, the CMIS had an AAPRE of 11.9464% and RMSE of 11.807884. The authors also report that the largest relative error for the CMIS was below 33%.

summary: The paper develops optimal designs for accelerated degradation testing (ADT) when the goal is to estimate lifetime quantiles from degradation measurements rather than observed failure times. It models one response with a gamma degradation process and extends the method to two independent failure modes, using either two gamma processes or a gamma process together with a linear mixed-effects model (LMEM). The designs allocate test units across stress levels while keeping stress constant for each unit and using repeated measurements over time. The authors optimize the asymptotic variance of estimated failure-time quantiles using locally specified model parameters and a numerical multiplicative algorithm. Their numerical examples favor designs supported at the lowest and highest test stresses, and show high efficiency under many of the parameter misspecifications they examined.
key_results: In the single-response example, the optimal design assigns 0.79 of units to the lowest stress and 0.21 to the highest; at the stated normal-use condition, the uniform two-point and three-point designs have efficiencies of 75% and 55%, respectively, relative to the optimum. In the two-gamma-process example, the optimal allocation is 0.78 at the lowest stress and 0.22 at the highest. The same 0.78 and 0.22 allocation is obtained for the gamma-plus-LMEM example. For that latter example, the authors report efficiency of about 0.9936 at the largest considered gamma intercept value of 1.92; they also report that the univariate design is more sensitive to misspecification of the slope than of the intercept.
key_equations:
Stress-dependent gamma-process rate: \[\gamma(x)=\exp(\beta_0+\beta_1 x)\] The gamma-process rate at stress x is gamma of x, with intercept beta zero and stress slope beta one.

Quantile estimation variance criterion: \[\operatorname{avar}(\widehat{t}_\alpha)=c^{T}M(\xi)^{-1}c\] The asymptotic variance of the estimated alpha failure-time quantile is determined by its parameter-gradient vector c and the inverse information matrix M for design xi.
limitations_stated: The authors state that their models assume stress is constant within each test unit, the same measurement-time plan is used for all units, and the marginal response components are uncorrelated. They consider gamma processes and linear mixed-effects models as marginal degradation models, while noting that other model families could be considered.
limitations_unstated: The evaluation consists of numerical illustrations rather than validation with field or product-test data, so the performance of the designs under real degradation behavior is unknown. The independence assumptions and the use of nominal parameters for locally optimal designs may be consequential when failure modes interact or when the stress-acceleration relationship is misspecified; the paper does not quantify those effects beyond its sensitivity examples.
future_work_stated: The authors propose extending the methods to other marginal degradation models, including Wiener processes, inverse Gaussian processes, and nonlinear mixed-effects degradation models. They also propose optimality criteria for simultaneous estimation of multiple failure-time distribution characteristics.
future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to validate the proposed allocations using field or product-test data and to study correlated failure modes, additional operating-condition covariates, and changes in stress over time. Decision-focused extensions could optimize test cost or reliability decisions, while reporting computational effort and comparing the numerical solutions with alternative optimization methods.

summary: This paper presents an extension of Attribute Oriented Induction (AOI) for predictive maintenance of turbine engines. The method groups sensor readings into weighted clusters and turns those weights into a function intended to track machine wear. An Exponentially Weighted Moving Average (EWMA) chart detects changes, while a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) model forecasts the function and Western Electric Rules (WER) determine when an anomaly is reached and estimate Remaining Useful Life (RUL). The experiments use simulated turbine-engine data from a public NASA Ames dataset, with 100 training runs ending after failure and 100 test runs ending before failure. The authors report that changes were detected before failure in all cases, while RUL accuracy was weaker when change was detected very early.
key_results: The selected fourth Western Electric Rule had a mean absolute error of 6.26 cycles and a mean squared error of 72.74 when estimating failure timing; the corresponding errors for the first, second, and third rules were 56.0 and 8518.48, 33.25 and 4125.35, and 17.55 and 1084.13. The LSTM prediction of the quantification function had a reported root mean square error of 0.036021. For the overall system, the reported RUL mean absolute error was 39.02 cycles, improving to 13.30 when considering only runs whose change point occurred after the first 40 cycles. Change points were detected before failure in 100% of cases. The paper does not report a comparison against a separate prognostics method or a field-data evaluation.

limitations_stated: The experiments did not use domain experts, so the generalization hierarchies and attribute weights were not based on expert knowledge. The authors also note that the LSTM requires further tuning and that RUL error depends on its predictive accuracy.
limitations_unstated: The test runs end before failure, and the paper says their cycles to failure are not recorded; it does not clearly explain how independent ground-truth RUL values were obtained for the overall error evaluation. The results also come from simulated runs with one failure type, and no field-data validation or comparison with another prognostics method is reported.
future_work_stated: The authors propose adding root cause analysis to the methodology. They also suggest using domain-expert knowledge to set the hierarchies and weights and further tuning the LSTM model.
future_work_unstated: Evaluate the method on field sensor data with documented failure times and report performance separately on fully observed and right-censored runs. Further studies could test different failure mechanisms and operating conditions, and assess how the predictions support maintenance decisions at the system level.

summary: Multifidelity Efficient Global Reliability Analysis (mfEGRA) addresses the high computational cost of estimating failure probability when evaluations of the most accurate model are expensive. It builds a Gaussian process (GP) surrogate that combines high- and low-fidelity models, then adaptively chooses both where to sample and which model to evaluate. The method uses the expected feasibility function (EFF) to target the failure boundary and a cost-adjusted, weighted lookahead information gain to choose an information source. The authors test it on an analytic multimodal problem and on simulated acoustic-horn models, including a rarer failure case with manufacturing uncertainty. In these examples, mfEGRA reaches the reported accuracy with fewer equivalent high-fidelity evaluations than single-fidelity EGRA, with savings depending on model discrepancy and relative evaluation costs.
key_results: On the analytic problem, mfEGRA reached median relative failure-probability error below 10^-3 at a cost of 26 equivalent high-fidelity evaluations, compared with 48 for EGRA, a reported 46% reduction. For the three-dimensional acoustic horn, it required 19 evaluations versus 25 for EGRA to reach the same error threshold, a 24% reduction; restricting candidate locations to pre-drawn Monte Carlo samples increased the saving to 45%, with 12 versus 22 evaluations. For the rarer four-dimensional acoustic-horn case, the methods required 25 versus 48 evaluations, a reported 48% saving, to reach median relative error below 10^-3. The analytic results used 100 initial designs for comparison, and each acoustic-horn comparison used 10 initial designs.
key_equations:
Failure probability: \[p_F = \Pr(g(Z)>0)\] p sub F is the probability of failure, Pr denotes probability, g is the limit state function, and Z is the vector of random inputs.

Multifidelity model relationship: \[g_l(z)=g_0(z)+\delta_l(z)\] g sub l is the model at information source l, g sub zero is the high-fidelity model, z is an input location, and delta sub l is the discrepancy associated with source l.

Location selection: \[z^* = \arg\max_z \operatorname{EFF}(z)\] z star is the selected input location, arg max means the value that maximizes the criterion, and EFF is the expected feasibility function.

Information-source selection: \[l^* = \arg\max_l \frac{\operatorname{information\_gain}(l)}{\operatorname{cost}(l)}\] l star is the selected information source, l indexes the available sources, information gain is the weighted lookahead gain, and cost is the evaluation cost for that source.
limitations_stated: The authors note that GP training cost grows cubically with the number of samples and that their method does not address this scaling issue. They also identify high-dimensional space coverage as a challenge and state that parallel multifidelity adaptive sampling needs further exploration.
limitations_unstated: The evaluation is based on an analytic test and simulated acoustic-horn models; the paper does not validate the method against field or operational data. The surrogate formulation assumes independent GP discrepancy processes, and the reported demonstrations use fixed model costs and specific input distributions, so performance under dependent errors, changing costs, or substantial distribution shift remains untested.
future_work_stated: The authors suggest investigating GP sparsification to reduce surrogate-training cost and exploring parallel multifidelity adaptive sampling. They also identify Monte Carlo variance-reduction methods as a way to improve efficiency for still rarer failure probabilities and note that other stopping criteria could be explored.
future_work_unstated: Future studies could assess the method with measured engineering data and with lower-fidelity models whose errors or costs vary across operating conditions. They could also test additional failure mechanisms and system-level reliability problems, and connect the estimated failure probabilities to engineering decisions such as design acceptance or risk-based resource allocation.

summary: The paper presents a method for grouping subjects according to their underlying lifetime distributions, including settings where termination events are right-censored or cannot be observed. A neural network assigns subjects to clusters using their covariates and activity measurements from an initial period, while training aims to make the clusters’ empirical lifetime distributions as distinct as possible. The method estimates those distributions with a modified Kaplan–Meier estimator and uses a bounded Kuiper-test p-value as its clustering objective. The authors evaluate it on simulated data, Friendster activity records, and patient data from MIMIC III. They report that the proposed method generally produces more distinct and more predictive lifetime clusters than the comparison methods, while a different divergence baseline can produce empty or very small clusters.
key_results: On the synthetic three-cluster dataset, DeepCLife with the Kuiper bound achieved a C-index of 68.96% and an adjusted Rand index of 73.61%, compared with 63.77% and 47.67% for the strongest listed alternative on those measures. On Friendster with two clusters, it achieved a C-index of 75.58%, an integrated Brier score of 20.13%, and a logrank score of 47,837.25; the best comparison values were 67.49%, 22.04%, and 27,642.60, respectively. With four Friendster clusters, the corresponding results were 77.04%, 18.99%, and 59,236.36, compared with the strongest alternative values of 76.55%, 20.64%, and 40,703.01. On MIMIC III with two clusters, it achieved a C-index of 66.30% and a logrank score of 20,525.26, versus 64.93% and 17,193.38 for the strongest comparison; its Brier score was 15.50%, while another method scored 15.03%. summary: The paper proposes ASTPA, a method for estimating small failure probabilities in reliability problems. It guides sampling toward likely failure regions by combining the original parameter distribution with a likelihood based on the limit-state function, then adjusts the estimate using inverse importance sampling. The sampling uses HMCMC, including a Quasi-Newton preconditioned version intended to improve exploration in high-dimensional problems. The authors test the approach on four simulated structural reliability benchmarks, including static limit-state examples and dynamic oscillator models. They report that the Quasi-Newton version often estimates failure probabilities more accurately and with less variation than the comparison methods at similar numbers of model evaluations.
key_results: Results are based on 500 independent simulations per example. For the undamped oscillator with an exact failure probability of 1.55E-8, the Quasi-Newton method estimated 1.51E-8 with a coefficient of variation of 0.15; the standard Hamiltonian method estimated 1.52E-8 with 0.21, while the two Subset Simulation estimates were 1.67E-8 and 1.50E-8 with coefficients of variation of 0.77 and 0.70. For the 101-variable white-noise oscillator with an exact probability of 2.53E-6, the Quasi-Newton estimate was 2.55E-6 with a coefficient of variation of 0.24, compared with 2.57E-6 and 0.30 for standard Hamiltonian sampling and 2.58E-6 and 0.32 for uniform-proposal Subset Simulation. In the two-variable parabolic example, the Quasi-Newton estimate was 3.47E-5 with a coefficient of variation of 0.39, compared with 3.86E-5 and 0.35 for standard Hamiltonian sampling and coefficients of variation of 0.62 and 0.65 for the two Subset Simulation variants.
key_equations:
Approximate target density: \[q(\theta)\propto\pi_\theta(\theta)\exp\left[-\frac{g(\theta)^2}{2g_c^2\sigma^2}\right]\] The approximate target density q for parameter vector θ is proportional to the original joint density πθ, weighted by the limit-state function g, its scaling constant gc, and the likelihood dispersion factor σ.

Failure probability: \[P_F=\int I_F(\theta)\pi_\theta(\theta)\,d\theta\] The failure probability P_F is the integral over parameter vector θ of the failure indicator I_F multiplied by the joint density πθ.
limitations_stated: The authors state that the analyses rely on analytical gradients. They caution that when numerical gradient evaluations are needed, the Hamiltonian methods will not be competitive with Subset Simulation. They also note that the ASTPA parameters used in the examples were not optimized for each case.
limitations_unstated: The evaluation covers four simulated benchmark problems rather than field data, so performance on operational infrastructure models is not established. The post-processing density is fitted from the sampled points; if the sampler misses a relevant failure mode, that fit could also miss it and affect the probability estimate.
future_work_stated: The authors propose exploring additional ASTPA variants and estimating first-passage problems under a range of settings, including high-dimensional parameter spaces.
future_work_unstated: Further evaluation could test dependent and non-normal input variables, uncertain model parameters, and additional failure mechanisms on field or experimentally measured data. System-level applications could also assess how estimates inform reliability decisions when components share dependencies or multiple failure modes interact.

summary: This chapter reviews reliability methods for data that include covariates changing over time, alongside methods for planning accelerated tests. It covers failure-time prediction, degradation, and recurrent events, and explains how covariate histories can be incorporated into each type of model. The examples use field records from office machines and repairable industrial systems, outdoor coating measurements, and laboratory fatigue tests on glass fiber. It also describes Bayesian sequential test planning, which updates test conditions as results arrive. In the fatigue-test illustration, this planning approach produced a substantially lower average estimated variance than a local design based on a small amount of historical data.
key_results: In the office-machine data, 69 of 1,800 units failed during 70 weeks; predictions account for the 1,731 units still at risk. summary: The paper addresses the difficulty of choosing an order for reliability growth tasks when evaluating every possible sequence is too computationally expensive. It models uncertainty about whether identified system concerns are faults and whether planned tasks will detect them, then evaluates the expected utility of sequences using cost, time, and the chance of meeting a reliability target. The authors approximate these utilities with a surrogate based on the Benter model, fitted to a limited set of evaluated sequences. Their reliability example uses an elicited aerospace-style task and concern matrix, while the broader performance evaluation uses simulated scenarios rather than field data. The method often identifies high-utility task sequences with far fewer utility evaluations than exhaustive search, especially when paired with Pearson correlation fitting.
key_results: In the nine-task illustration, the regression-adjusted surrogate had a Pearson correlation of 0.993 with the training utilities, and correlation was 0.990 across all 362,880 sequences. With 60 training evaluations and 40 evaluations of top surrogate candidates, the method found the exact optimal sequence; its expected utility was 0.919, and the authors estimate about a 75% chance of finding the optimum in similar problems. In the simulation comparison for nine tasks, the Benter surrogate with Pearson correlation found the optimum in 0.95 of runs with 50 training sequences and 200 candidate evaluations, compared with 0.80 for reverse Plackett–Luce and 0.70 for Plackett–Luce. Evaluating all surrogate values for the illustration took about 17 seconds, compared with 102 seconds to evaluate all expected utilities.

Surrogate fitting criterion: \[\hat{\psi}=\arg\max_{\psi}\operatorname{Cor}(\eta,f_{\psi}),\qquad \eta_i=\log\left(\frac{u_i}{1-u_i}\right)\] Here psi is the surrogate parameter set, psi-hat is its fitted value, Cor is the chosen correlation, eta_i is the logit of expected utility u_i for observation i, and f_psi is the surrogate evaluated at that observation.

Reliability after planned tasks: \[R_{\mathrm{plan}}(t)=\prod_{i=1}^{I}\left[1-(1-R_i(t))\lambda_i\prod_{j=1}^{J}(1-p_{i,j})^{\kappa_j}\right]\] Here R_plan is planned-program reliability at time t, R_i is reliability for concern i, lambda_i is its prior fault probability, p_i,j is the detection probability for task j, kappa_j indicates whether task j is performed, and I and J count concerns and tasks.

Expected-utility sequence objective: \[x^*=\arg\max_x\mathbb{E}\left[q_1U(C(x,z))+q_2U(T(x,z))+q_3U(C(x,z))U(T(x,z))\right]\] Here x-star is the selected task sequence, x ranges over sequences, E is expectation over uncertainty z, U is utility, C and T are sequence cost and time, and q1, q2, and q3 weight cost, time, and their interaction.
limitations_stated: The authors state that the Benter-based surrogate is unimodal and will emulate around only one mode when the utility function is multimodal. limitations_unstated: The reliability calculations assume independent concern fault states and independent task outcomes, and assume that a detected fault is designed out with certainty; departures from these assumptions could change the preferred sequence. future_work_stated: The authors propose extending the method to allow tasks to be carried out in parallel and investigating mixtures of Benter models for multimodal utility functions. future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to validate the concern, detection, and reliability assumptions using field or development-program data, including checking how elicitation uncertainty affects task order.
